# GuitarHub: full text

> GuitarHub (https://guitarhub.org) is the Suede AI guitar lessons site: a step-by-step curriculum for beginners through advanced players, a four-stage practice method, free browser practice tools and a free Advanced Lab of scored drills.

This file carries the full text of GuitarHub's public pages, generated from the same page components the site renders. The shorter index is https://guitarhub.org/llms.txt. Cite the specific page URL given under each section.

Key facts: 135 guitar lessons in the curriculum; 23 free drills in the Advanced Lab; free tools in the browser with no account; lifetime lesson access is $79 USD, one time, in GuitarHub: Guitar Lessons for iPhone (https://apps.apple.com/us/app/guitarhub-guitar-lessons/id6806770875). Published by Suede AI (https://suedeai.ai), founded by Jason Colapietro.

## Practice guitar with a plan you can prove.

Source: https://guitarhub.org

GuitarHub · beginner to advanced

Pick one thing you can't play yet. Get a four-week plan, free tools to run it, and a recording on day 1 and day 30 that shows exactly what changed. Free in your browser, no account.

Brand new to guitar? Follow the 105-lesson path from stage 1, unlocked with $79 lifetime access in GuitarHub for iPhone.

How it works

### One goal, thirty days, two recordings.

#### Pick a goal

Name one thing you can't play yet: a chord change that stalls, a solo that falls apart at tempo, a song you can't finish. One goal, written down.

#### Record day 1

Play it once on your phone, mistakes included. That take is the baseline every later attempt is measured against.

#### Run the plan

Repair the piece that breaks, then put it back into the full song, the click or the backing track. The free tools time, pace and log each session.

#### Record day 30

Play the same take again and listen beside day 1. The difference is your proof, and it sets the next goal.

### Seven free tools to run it. No account.

Each one runs in your browser. Nothing is uploaded and nothing is emailed. What you type stays on the device you typed it on.

#### Guitar tuner and metronome

Check each open string with pitch feedback and reference tones, then practice with a steady four-beat click.

#### 30-day breakthrough planner

Choose one finish line and turn it into a four-week practice sequence you can run this month.

#### Practice plateau diagnostic

Answer a short set of questions and name the part of your practice that stopped producing change.

#### Practice session builder

Turn the minutes you actually have into timed blocks, weighted toward the one thing you are fixing.

#### Tempo ladder builder

Turn one difficult passage into a tempo ladder with a starting speed, a target, and steps between them.

#### Song readiness score

Check a song against the parts that break under pressure before you call it finished.

#### Practice evidence log

Log one line per session and read what actually moved, with no streak counter and no direction under three sessions.

### Free field guides for the music stand

Every practice guide as a free PDF, from the method to clean tone. Pick the problem you have this week and keep the guide on your phone or the music stand.

Guided lessons · $79 lifetime access

### Learning from scratch? Follow the lesson path.

105 guided lessons in seven stages take you from your first clean note to barre chords, the blues and your own solos, with 30 song companions along the way. Start the first module free in GuitarHub: Guitar Lessons for iPhone, then unlock every lesson with lifetime access: $79 one time.

- [Stages 1–2 New to guitar You have a guitar and maybe a chord or two. Hold, tune and pick cleanly, then your first two chords in time. Start at stage 1 →](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar#stage-1)
- [Stages 3–5 Know your open chords You change between open chords and can strum a song through. Scales, alternate picking, barre chords, twelve-bar blues and your first solos. Jump to stage 3 →](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar#stage-3)
- [Advanced Advanced player Barre chords, the pentatonic box and a few solos are already under your fingers. Scored drills for modes, arpeggios, legato, in-tune bends, funk sixteenths and triplet feels. Open the Advanced Lab →](https://guitarhub.org/advanced)

Not sure where you fit? [Take the five-question level check](https://guitarhub.org/start) · [Try the free A-to-D chord routine](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/routine)

Advanced Lab · free

### Already good? Get clean at tempo.

23 scored drills across the 8 skill areas a complete player needs. Practice mode waits for every note; Play mode scores the whole pass and tells you when to push the tempo.

- [Technique Legato, sweeps, string skipping and in-tune bends at tempo.](https://guitarhub.org/advanced#technique)
- [Theory Arpeggios, guide tones and modes you can hear and play, not just name.](https://guitarhub.org/advanced#theory)
- [Rhythm & timing Syncopated sixteenths, triplets and displaced phrases against a steady grid.](https://guitarhub.org/advanced#rhythm)
- [Ear training Hear a sound, then find it on the neck before you look.](https://guitarhub.org/advanced#ear)
- [Fretboard knowledge Every note, every octave, and movable shapes anywhere on the neck.](https://guitarhub.org/advanced#fretboard)
- [Improvisation Land on chord tones, enclose targets and add color notes on purpose.](https://guitarhub.org/advanced#improvisation)
- [Repertoire Original etudes that put the skills into complete pieces.](https://guitarhub.org/advanced#repertoire)
- [Tone Vibrato control and pick dynamics, the parts of tone your hands own.](https://guitarhub.org/advanced#tone)

The founding room

### Want a coach's ear on your playing?

We're forming a group of 8–12 players. Each week you bring one recording and get back one specific correction for your next session. Applying is free, and you'll see the schedule and price before you commit.

#### 8–12 players

Matched by goal and a schedule that works, so your playing gets heard.

#### Private by default

Corrections stay private. Progress proof is shared only when you choose.

#### One weekly studio

Bring one recording, leave with one correction for the next session.

#### No infinite feed

Every check-in exists to change your next attempt.

#### Apply to the founding room

Tell us where your playing is and name one change you can prove in 30 days. No payment is taken here.

## About GuitarHub.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/about

The guitar lessons site from Suede AI: meet the founder, explore the lessons and practice method, and learn how your practice data stays private.

Updated October 10, 2026

GuitarHub is where Suede AI teaches guitar. The [guitar path](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar) starts at the first foundations, how to hold the instrument, tune it, and get one clean note, and works up through chords, reading, rhythm and the whole neck. The guided lessons open with lifetime access, $79 one time in [GuitarHub: Guitar Lessons](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/guitarhub-guitar-lessons/id6806770875) for iPhone, and your place on the web is kept in this browser. The voice lessons moved to [Suede Sing](https://sing.suedeai.ai/learn/voice), where all of them are free. Pricing, access and data questions are answered in [the GuitarHub FAQ](https://guitarhub.org/faq).

Lessons on their own tell you what to do next. They do not tell you whether the last one worked, so the site pairs the curriculum with a practice method and a set of tools built to answer that question. Choose one change you can prove in thirty days. Record where you are before you start fixing it. Find the single thing that breaks the result and repair that one thing. Put the repair back under real pressure. Then record the same performance again, put the two takes side by side, and let them settle whether anything moved. The full argument, with the exit test for each stage, is on [the method page](https://guitarhub.org/method).

### Who built this

GuitarHub is made by [Suede AI](https://suedeai.ai), a studio founded by Jason Colapietro. Suede AI also builds [Strumly](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides), the AI guitar coach with its practice tools, its book and guides, and a music data API that AI agents pay for per call, and [Suede AI Social](https://social.suedeai.ai), where the guitar conversation happens. GuitarHub is the lessons site. It owns the curriculum, the practice method, and the job the other two leave open: deciding what to practice next, and proving it worked.

The position behind the site is his. A player with a shelf of finished courses and no finished songs has not failed at practice. They were handed material and no way to check their own work, which is a different problem with a different fix. The fix is unglamorous: fewer goals, a recording at each end of the month, and a straight comparison of the two.

The lesson paths and the practice tools serve different needs. A new player can follow the opening instruction and let the site keep the order. A returning player can skip the lessons and use the planner or the practice log alongside material they already follow.

### What GuitarHub is

**Guitar lessons, in order.** 105 guided lessons across seven stages, plus 30 popular-song practice companions. The opening lessons guide setup, tuning, and single-note practice; the wider curriculum covers chords, reading, rhythm and the whole neck, with a step for each and a place kept between visits. Listening demonstrations, self-reported practice, visual reading results, and microphone scores are labeled separately, so you always know which kind of check you are looking at.

**Voice lessons**, built the same way, from the room you sing in and a steady tone, through registers and the break, to agility and a sound of your own, live on [Suede Sing](https://sing.suedeai.ai/learn/voice), next to the rooms that measure them.

**A method.** One loop, run against one goal at a time, in four stages: baseline, isolate, reconnect, prove. The site presents it as four weeks, one stage per week, but the week is a default rather than a rule. Each stage has a test that tells you it is finished.

**The Advanced Lab**, 23 free scored drills for experienced players across technique, theory, rhythm, ear training, fretboard, improvisation, repertoire and tone. [Open the Advanced Lab](https://guitarhub.org/advanced).

**Seven free tools**, each running in your browser:

- [The guitar tuner and metronome](https://guitarhub.org/practice) checks each open string with pitch feedback and reference tones, then keeps a steady four-beat click at your tempo.
- [The 30-day breakthrough planner](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough) turns one finish line into a four-week sequence you can start today.
- [The practice plateau diagnostic](https://guitarhub.org/diagnose) ends by naming the part of your practice that stopped producing change, rather than by giving you a score.
- [The practice session builder](https://guitarhub.org/session) turns the minutes you have into timed blocks, weighted toward the one thing you are fixing.
- [The tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) turns one difficult passage into a starting speed, a target, and the steps between them.
- [The song readiness score](https://guitarhub.org/readiness) checks a song against the parts that break under pressure, before you decide it is finished.
- [The practice evidence log](https://guitarhub.org/log) takes one line per session and reports what moved, with no streak counter and no direction drawn through fewer than three sessions.

**Written guides**, covering the method itself, how to practice effectively, why progress plateaus once the beginner gains run out, what deliberate practice means at the instrument, how to run a 30-day challenge that ends in evidence, an intermediate weekly routine, how long to practice each day, a schedule that survives a real week, why speed has a ceiling, how to memorize a song, and how to work with a metronome. They are linked from the site footer.

**An application to a founding room**, described below.

### Make each practice count

Start with the opening module of a path and the free browser tools. Use the practice loop to choose one goal, capture a baseline on your phone, and bring a recording and a specific question to your next lesson. Apply for the founding room for a personal response about your playing goals.

### How this fits with Strumly and Suede AI Social

GuitarHub teaches and runs your practice. Strumly coaches. Suede AI Social carries the wider conversation. All three are Suede AI products.

In practice that means a lesson or a plan here decides what you work on this week, and GuitarHub's own tuner, metronome and Advanced Lab drills cover the daily work. Strumly adds the AI coach that listens to you play, along with chord references, scale maps and ear training. The [Strumly guides](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides) go deep on gear, tone, signal chain and the rights to your music. Strumly also sells its music data to AI agents one call at a time. That is Strumly's business, and it runs on the same chord, key and song knowledge the lessons here are built on.

The GuitarHub community meets on [Suede AI Social](https://social.suedeai.ai), where players post rigs and talk to each other.

### Apply for the founding room

Applications for the founding room are open and reviewed personally. Tell us what you want to improve and what your practice week looks like.

The intent is a small room, 8 to 12 players, assembled around one rule: a check-in has to change the next practice. Members would be matched by goal and by a schedule that works in a real week, corrections would stay private, and progress proof would be shared only when a player chooses to share it. The founding-room design puts focused practice and personal feedback at the center.

Applying sends four things: your name, your email address, a line about your playing experience, and one sentence naming the change you want to prove in thirty days. It arrives as an email at info@suedeai.ai and it is read personally. It takes no payment, asks for no card, and creates no commitment on either side. You will receive a personal response about your goal and the next step.

You see the schedule, review capacity, and price before you are asked to commit to anything. [The application form is on the home page.](https://guitarhub.org/#apply)

### What happens to what you type

The lessons and the tools keep their state in your own browser, in local storage. Close the tab and the work is still there next time; clear your browser data and it is gone. The planning tools send nothing to a server. If you sign in on the account page and explicitly turn on practice sync, new lesson-attempt results are saved to your account; earlier records stay on your device.

There is no analytics script and no third-party tracker on this site, which you can confirm from the page source. The tuner, lesson exercises and Advanced Lab drills listen through your microphone only after you start them and analyze the sound on your device; raw audio is never uploaded. When the method tells you to record a baseline, record it on your phone and keep it yourself.

The application form sends the four fields you fill in through Resend to info@suedeai.ai. The website host also processes ordinary connection information to deliver and protect the site. The [Privacy Policy](https://guitarhub.org/privacy) explains microphone use, local records, purchases, hosting, and messages in more detail.

### Corrections and contact

One address for everything, including press: [info@suedeai.ai](mailto:info@suedeai.ai).

Corrections to the lessons or the method go to the same address and get a personal reply. The method is an argument about how playing gets learned, and it is built to be tested against your own recordings: run it for a month and compare the two takes.

## Learn guitar in order, and practice it every day.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/learn

GuitarHub teaches guitar as a path: 105 guided lessons in seven stages, each one building on the last, with free tools for the days between lessons. Start with the curriculum if you are new, run the free routine on any day you pick up the guitar, and move to the Advanced Lab when the fundamentals are under your fingers. Not sure which fits? [Find your level in five questions](https://guitarhub.org/start).

Guitar curriculum · $79 lifetime access

### From your first clean note to songs you can play for anyone.

105 lessons in seven stages · 30 song companions · Lifetime access $79 one time

- Stage 1 Sound Check Guitar in tune, hands in place, one clean note you can repeat.
- Stage 2 Two Chords, First Study Learn A and D, count your changes, and play an original two-chord study.
- Stage 3 The Open Eight Eight open chords, a capo, and any three-chord song you like.
- Stage 4 The First Scale Single notes, alternate picking, and the shape every solo starts from.
- Stage 5 Barre Line The chord that stops most players, the blues form, and your first solo.
- Stage 6 Whole Neck Barre shapes everywhere, the major scale in five positions, eight bars of your own.
- Stage 7 Signature Style, tone, and three songs you can play for anyone.

Every stage pairs written instruction with practice you can check: chord diagrams, timed change counts, studies to play through and, where a lesson has one, a microphone exercise that listens to your attempt. The 30 song companions sit beside the stages with original studies for recognizable songs. Start the first module free in [GuitarHub: Guitar Lessons](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/guitarhub-guitar-lessons/id6806770875) for iPhone, then unlock every lesson with lifetime access for $79 one time.

### Free to use today

No account and no purchase: each of these runs in your browser and keeps its history on your device.

#### The A-to-D chord routine

Seven timed blocks, 21 minutes by default, for the first chord change most players learn: tune, check A and D string by string, practice the silent anchor move, count changes starting from each chord and finish on two-chord songs. Edit any block to fit the time you have; your history stays in this browser.

#### The Advanced Lab

23 scored drills across eight skill areas, from modes and arpeggios to bends, legato and rhythm feels. Practice mode waits for every note; Play mode scores the whole pass and tells you when to raise the tempo.

#### The 30-day plan

Name one thing you can't play yet and get four weeks of focused practice around it, with a recording on day 1 and day 30 so you can hear what changed.

Voice

### Singing lives on Suede Sing.

The voice path, from an easy breath to a steady tone, comfortable pitch matching and your first song, is on Suede Sing, where all seven stages are free. Two pages stay here for players who started voice on GuitarHub: your [saved voice takes](https://guitarhub.org/learn/voice/recordings), which this browser kept and never uploaded, and the lifetime [voice practice library](https://guitarhub.org/learn/voice/materials) of studies and readings.

### Learn it. Practice it. Try it through.

Written lessons give each session a focus. Where a microphone exercise is available, you can practice first and then play a measured attempt. For other lessons, you record your own assessment. A completed session records that you practiced, and a measured attempt shows what you can play. Web progress is saved in this browser. [How lifetime access works](https://guitarhub.org/faq#how-to-get-lifetime-access)

## Beginner guitar lessons, step by step.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar

Every guided lesson opens with lifetime access: $79 one time in GuitarHub: Guitar Lessons for iPhone, with the first module free in the app. Restore Purchases brings your access back on a new iPhone. Questions about pricing, access or your data are answered in [the GuitarHub FAQ](https://guitarhub.org/faq).

New to the vocabulary? [The glossary](https://guitarhub.org/glossary) defines every word this curriculum uses, in one sentence each.

7 stages, starting with first notes, open chords, strumming, and songs. Browse the curriculum, then continue into later stages as your playing develops.

Already know A and D? [Practice A-to-D chord changes with the free routine](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/routine), or [build a practice session around your available time](https://guitarhub.org/session).

Every lesson requires verified lifetime access. Browse the curriculum below. Progress saves in this browser.

## A-to-D chord practice routine.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/routine

A little practice, often

Practice changing between A and D guitar chords: check each chord, try light anchor movement, count changes, and play song sections. Seven blocks, 21 minutes. Adjust the time to fit today.

A free practice companion. Your history stays in this browser as guest history. Counts and reflections come from you and are saved separately from lesson checks and microphone results.

### Before the routine

Review the GuitarHub instruction first. Saved lesson evidence can satisfy preparation, or confirm that you already understand the exercise. These confirmations describe your preparation, not a skill test.

- **Tune and recheck all six strings** [GuitarHub curriculum preview (new tab)](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/g-l1-m1-02) I understand this exercise and am ready to practice it.
- **Form D and check each sounding string** [GuitarHub curriculum preview (new tab)](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/g-l2-m1-01) I understand this exercise and am ready to practice it.
- **Form A and check each sounding string** [GuitarHub curriculum preview (new tab)](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/g-l2-m1-01) I understand this exercise and am ready to practice it.
- **Move between D and A with a light anchor** [GuitarHub curriculum preview (new tab)](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/g-l2-m3-01) I understand this exercise and am ready to practice it.
- **Understand how to count alternating changes** [GuitarHub curriculum preview (new tab)](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/g-l2-m3-02) I understand this exercise and am ready to practice it.
- **Count four beats and attempt suitable A/D songs** [GuitarHub curriculum preview (new tab)](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/g-l2-m2-01) I understand this exercise and am ready to practice it.

### Today’s plan

Adjust any block in seconds while the timer is paused. A little practice each day helps the movements become familiar.

- 1 **Tune** Tune planned seconds sec
- 2 **D chord accuracy** D chord accuracy planned seconds sec
- 3 **A chord accuracy** A chord accuracy planned seconds sec
- 4 **Silent A/D anchor movement** Silent A/D anchor movement planned seconds sec
- 5 **Changes, starting on A** Changes, starting on A planned seconds sec
- 6 **Changes, starting on D** Changes, starting on D planned seconds sec
- 7 **Two-chord songs** Two-chord songs planned seconds sec

Complete preparation above to use the timer. The plan remains available to review.

### Your practice history

Saved in this browser as guest history. Routine history is not cloud-synced. Returning restores paused time; closed-tab or background time is never added. Counts and reflections are kept as separate attempts.

## Five questions. One place to start.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/start

Find your level

Answer for what your hands can do on an ordinary practice day. Your answers point to one starting point, stage 1 of the lesson path, stage 3, or the free Advanced Lab, and the first thing to work on when you get there. Nothing you choose here is saved or sent.

- 1. Can you play G, C, D and E minor with every string ringing clearly? Not yetMost of them, with a buzz or twoYes, without looking
- 2. Can you switch between two open chords and keep a steady strum going? Not yetWith a pause before each changeYes, at song tempo
- 3. Can you play an F barre chord with every note sounding? Not yetOn a good dayYes, and I move it up the neck
- 4. Can you improvise a phrase over a blues with the minor pentatonic? Not yetI know the box, but it sounds like a scaleYes, in more than one position
- 5. Can you play one complete song from start to finish without stopping? Not yetA simple strummed songYes, riffs or solo included

Answer all 5 questions for your starting point.

### Where each answer sends you

#### Stages 1–2

- **Stage 1 · Sound Check.** Guitar in tune, hands in place, one clean note you can repeat.
- **Stage 2 · Two Chords, First Study.** Learn A and D, count your changes, and play an original two-chord study.

#### Stages 3–5

- **Stage 3 · The Open Eight.** Eight open chords, a capo, and any three-chord song you like.
- **Stage 4 · The First Scale.** Single notes, alternate picking, and the shape every solo starts from.
- **Stage 5 · Barre Line.** The chord that stops most players, the blues form, and your first solo.

#### Advanced Lab · free

23 scored drills across eight skill areas: technique, theory, rhythm & timing, ear training, fretboard knowledge, improvisation, repertoire, tone. Each drill listens through your microphone, waits for every note in Practice mode and scores the whole pass in Play mode.

The guided lessons in every stage unlock with lifetime access, $79 one time in GuitarHub for iPhone, and the first module is free in the app. The Advanced Lab, the [A-to-D chord routine](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/routine) and the [practice tools](https://guitarhub.org/tools) are free.

### Getting an accurate answer

- Answer for a normal day, cold, without warming up on the thing you are being asked about. Your best take on a good night is not where your next lesson should start.
- Count “on a good day” as partly. A skill that works half the time still needs the lessons that make it automatic.
- Between two results, take the lower one. Starting low costs you a few quick sessions; starting high means practicing on top of a gap for weeks.
- Already know the one thing you want to fix? Skip placement and [build a 30-day plan around it](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough).

## Past the basics. Now make it clean at tempo.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/advanced

Advanced Lab · free

23 drills across the 8 skill areas a complete player needs. Practice mode waits for every note. Play mode scores the whole pass at tempo, and the coach tells you when to push faster.

The coach listens through your microphone, so a quiet room works best. Nothing is recorded or uploaded, and results stay in this browser.

### Technique

Legato, sweeps, string skipping and in-tune bends at tempo.

#### Three Notes a String, G Major

Pick once per string and hammer the next two, up four strings and back.

#### A Minor Sweep, Five Strings

One continuous pick stroke across five strings, each note separate and clean.

#### String Skipping in Octaves

Jump over a string on every move: root, octave, third, octave through C, Am, F and G.

#### Bends That Land in Tune

Play the target note fretted, then bend from a lower fret up to the exact same pitch, a whole step or a half step.

### Theory

Arpeggios, guide tones and modes you can hear and play, not just name.

#### ii–V–I Arpeggios in C

Spell Dm7, G7 and Cmaj7 note by note in one position.

#### Guide Tones Through a ii–V–I

Play only the third and seventh of each chord and hear the progression move by half steps.

#### One Root, Two Modes

Play A Aeolian, then A Dorian, and hear what one changed note does.

### Rhythm & timing

Syncopated sixteenths, triplets and displaced phrases against a steady grid.

#### Syncopated Sixteenths

Keep your hand moving in sixteenths and let only the written hits sound.

#### Three Over Two

Play quarter-note triplets, three even hits across every two beats.

#### Gear Shift: Triplets to Sixteenths

One bar of eighth-note triplets, one bar of sixteenths, back and forth.

#### Dotted-Eighth Displacement

Hits every three sixteenths, so the accent walks across the beat for three bars.

### Ear training

Hear a sound, then find it on the neck before you look.

#### Hear It, Find It: Intervals from A

Press Hear target, then find the note by ear before you look at the diagram.

#### An Eight-Note Phrase by Ear

An original E minor phrase, learned one note at a time from the reference tone.

### Fretboard knowledge

Every note, every octave, and movable shapes anywhere on the neck.

#### The Musical Alphabet on One String

Every natural note on string 6, up to the 12th fret and back down.

#### Your First Movable Shape

Find the root on string 6 or 5 for eight chords, the way you would place a power or barre chord.

#### Find Every C

The same note in seven places across three octaves.

### Improvisation

Land on chord tones, enclose targets and add color notes on purpose.

#### Land on the Chord Tone

Short blues phrases that resolve to the third of A7, D7 and E7.

#### Enclosures

Approach each target from the note above and a half step below, then land on it.

#### Add the Dorian Sixth

A minor pentatonic phrase with one added note, F sharp, that changes its color.

### Repertoire

Original etudes that put the skills into complete pieces.

#### Night Drive, an E Minor Etude

An original sixteen-note melody with long and short notes, played in time.

#### Alternating Bass Etude

Thumb on the bass, fingers on the melody, over C and G.

### Tone

Vibrato control and pick dynamics, the parts of tone your hands own.

#### Controlled Vibrato

Four long notes with vibrato that stays recognizably on pitch.

#### Dynamics Without Rushing

Alternate soft and loud bars while the timing stays exactly the same.

## The loop: baseline, isolate, reconnect, prove.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/method

One goal at a time, four stages, and an exit test for each one. This is the method the tools and guides on this site are built around.

Updated August 29, 2026

Field Guide No. 01

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

The GuitarHub method is a four-stage loop you run against one goal at a time: baseline, isolate, reconnect, prove. You record where you actually are. You cut the problem down to the smallest piece that still fails. You put that repaired piece back under the pressure of a full performance. Then you record the same thing again and compare the two takes. Each stage has an exit test, so you can tell when it is finished instead of guessing, and the last stage hands you the first stage of the next loop.

It is a loop rather than a curriculum. The useful information arrives late. You cannot know which transition is costing you the song until you have played the song badly onto a recording. Run the stages out of order and you get the most common failure in adult practice: four weeks of honest work on the part that was not the problem.

### Stage one: Baseline

Pick one finish line specific enough that a recording can settle it. Play the song from the count-in to the last chord without stopping is a finish line. Get better at rhythm is not. Then record one take: start to finish, no restarts, at a tempo you would actually attempt. Listen once, all the way through, and write down where it breaks.

- **Done badly: warming up first.** A baseline taken after twenty minutes on the hard part measures your best conditions, which you will not have in week four.
- **Done badly: stopping when it goes wrong.** The restart is the information. A take that survives to the end shows which failures cascade and which ones you play through.
- **Done badly: keeping the best of eight takes.** Best of eight is a ceiling. What the month has to move is the floor.

**The question this stage answers:** where does this fall apart, and when? Not how good you are, which is a rating you can argue with. A timestamp is not.

**Move on when** you can name the failure in one sentence containing a location. The chorus-to-bridge change drops a beat. If your sentence has no location in it, listen again. If you can hear that something is wrong but cannot place it, the [practice plateau diagnostic](https://guitarhub.org/diagnose) ends with a named blocker, which is the sentence this stage exists to produce.

### Stage two: Isolate

Shrink the failure until it stops failing, along two axes at once. Cut the length, down to the smallest unit that still contains the problem, which for a transition is often one beat either side of the join. Then set the tempo in two gears. First find the edge: the tempo where the failure shows up about half the time, which is where you can see exactly what goes wrong. Then build the fix one gear down, at the tempo where you play it correctly on purpose rather than correctly by luck, and every attempt is clean. Repeat it there until correct is boring, not until it is occasionally right. Occasionally right is what you already had.

- **Done badly: playing the whole song slowly.** That is the same problem at a lower speed, plus many repetitions of everything that was already fine.
- **Done badly: snapping the tempo back after one clean repetition.** One clean repetition is a coincidence until it repeats.
- **Done badly: editing the problem away.** Simplifying the voicing or switching to an easier fingering is a legitimate arrangement decision and a dishonest fix. Decide out loud which one you are making.

**The question this stage answers:** what is the smallest change that fixes this?

**Move on when** you can play the fragment correctly several times in a row, cold: first thing in a session, no run-up. Cold is the test. In performance the passage arrives unannounced, with your hands wherever the previous bar left them.

Write the tempo down, or the next session starts from a guess. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) turns one passage into a starting speed, a target, and the steps between. For a join between chords, Strumly's guide to [smoother chord transitions](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/smoother-chord-transitions) covers what to change while you are down there.

### Stage three: Reconnect

Put the repaired fragment back and add the pressure you removed, one layer at a time: the bars either side, then the full section, then the full piece, then a click, then a backing track, then one take with no restarts, then a camera.

This is the stage most players skip, and it is why a part works in practice and falls apart in the song. A fragment drilled in isolation comes with its own on-ramp: you know it is coming and your hand is already in position. In the piece it arrives with no warning, with your attention already moving to the next thing.

- **Done badly: adding every layer at once.** Straight from the isolated loop to a full take with a click and a camera. It falls apart, you decide the fix failed, and you go back to drilling the fragment, which was already fine.
- **Done badly: never leaving the loop.** The isolated fragment is now the part that feels good, so the week quietly becomes more of it.

**The question this stage answers:** does the fix survive contact with the music around it?

**Move on when** you can play the full section at a tempo where the whole thing survives and the repaired spot is no longer what breaks. It does not have to be the best part. It has to stop being the worst one.

Where those layers sit in a week is a scheduling problem too. Strumly's guide to [designing a practice routine](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine) covers building the week around them. For the session in front of you, the [practice session builder](https://guitarhub.org/session) turns the minutes you have and the failure you named into blocks that add up exactly, then points its largest block at the repair.

### Stage four: Prove

Record the same thing you recorded in week one, the same way: same start and end point, same one-take rule, same tempo range, same point in a session. Then listen to both, in order, once through.

The comparison only works if the conditions match. A cold single take in week one against take nine after a warm-up in week four proves only that take nine beats take one.

- **Done badly: deciding from memory.** Your memory of week one is generous. You have heard the improved version many more times since.
- **Done badly: recording and never listening back.** The file is not the evidence. The comparison is.
- **Done badly: letting the finish line drift.** A goal quietly rewritten mid-month to whatever now looks reachable will always be met.

**The question this stage answers:** what changed, and can I hear it?

**Move on when** you can state the change in a sentence a stranger could check by listening to both files. The bridge transition no longer drops a beat is a claim the recordings settle. It feels smoother is not. Then write down what is now the worst thing: that sentence is the finish line for the next loop.

The [song readiness score](https://guitarhub.org/readiness) pressure-tests whether the finished version survives outside the practice chair. The [practice evidence log](https://guitarhub.org/log) keeps the tempo or clean-pass result beside the session that produced it, and withholds a direction until the same focus has enough sessions to support one.

### Why the loop is closed

Each stage produces exactly what the next one consumes. That is what makes this a loop and not a list of good advice.

- **Baseline produces the target.** Without it, isolate is a guess, and the guess is reliably the part that is most enjoyable to play.
- **Isolate produces a fragment that works.** Without it, reconnect is playing the whole piece again and hoping.
- **Reconnect produces a version that holds up.** Without it, prove records a performance that collapses in the same place it always did.
- **Prove produces the next baseline.** The worst-thing sentence at the end of stage four is the finish line at the start of the next stage one.

The underlying principle is not original to GuitarHub. Practice works when it targets a specific weakness at the edge of what you can currently do, with feedback on whether the attempt worked. That is usually called deliberate practice. What the loop adds is a shape, so target a specific weakness becomes a step you can tell you have finished. There is more on [what that looks like at the instrument](https://guitarhub.org/deliberate-practice-guitar).

### What the method leaves out

Three familiar measurements are missing on purpose. Each measures something real. None measures whether you can play.

#### Lesson collecting

Saving a lesson is not acquiring a skill, and new material is the cheapest thing available to acquire. Material enters when the loop asks for it. Once the isolate stage has produced the question how do I get from this shape to that one without a gap, a lesson answers a question you already have. Browsing a library first answers questions you never asked, and the pile grows faster than you can play it down.

#### Watch time

Hours watched measures attendance at somebody else's playing. The unit of progress here is a recording of yours, and no counter here tracks how long you spent. Watching is an input, and inputs are not evidence.

#### Streaks

A streak measures showing up, which is real and weak. You can run a sixty-day streak playing only what you already play well, and that is the more comfortable option, so a streak biases each session toward whatever is easiest to finish. The loop counts weeks that ended with evidence instead. A week without a recording produced no evidence, which is a fact about the week and not a verdict on you.

### Common questions

#### How long is one loop?

Four weeks, one stage per week. That is the cadence the planner builds, and it is a default rather than a rule. The exit tests govern the handoff: a stage that meets its test on Tuesday hands off on Tuesday, and one that has not met its test has not finished.

#### What do I need in order to record myself?

A phone. A voice memo is enough to hear a dropped beat, a missed change, or a tempo that sags. GuitarHub does not upload, store, or listen to your recordings. The planner keeps only your goal and the actions you have checked, in your own browser.

#### Does this replace a teacher?

No. A good teacher can do the isolate stage for you in about a minute, which is most of what you are paying for. The loop is a structure for the other six days, and it makes lessons more useful. You arrive with a recording and a specific question.

#### What if week four shows no change?

Then you have learned something specific and cheap. Either the finish line was wrong for a month of work, or the isolate stage had no real target, or the fix was not reconnected under pressure. Each points at a different next month, and a clear negative result beats a feeling.

### Where to start

If you already know your finish line, build the four weeks. The [30-day breakthrough planner](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough) turns one goal into a week-by-week sequence and names the evidence each week has to produce. It needs no account.

If you do not know what to work on, start at the other end. The [practice plateau diagnostic](https://guitarhub.org/diagnose) ends with a named blocker, which is the input the baseline stage needs anyway.

## How to practice guitar effectively.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-effectively

The answer is not more hours. It is a smaller target, a slower tempo, and a way to tell whether the last thirty minutes changed anything.

Updated August 29, 2026

Field Guide No. 02

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

Practice guitar effectively by isolating the exact spot that fails, slowing it until you play it correctly every attempt, and repeating against a named target instead of a rep count. Keep one hard thing per session, put the repaired passage back in context, and write down where you stopped. Correction produces change. Time at the instrument does not.

This page is about the inside of one session: what to isolate, how slow to take it, and what order the parts go in. How long the session should run is answered on [how long to practice each day](https://guitarhub.org/how-long-to-practice-guitar-each-day), and where the sessions sit in a week on [the practice schedule](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-schedule).

### Practice the failure, not the song

Most of a practice hour goes to material that already works. You start at the top, play until something breaks, and start at the top again. Ten passes through a three-minute song give you ten attempts at the bar that fails and ten run-throughs of everything that never did.

The fix is unglamorous. Find the smallest unit that contains the problem and work on that alone. Usually it is two beats, one chord change, one string crossing, or a single reach your hand cannot make in the time available. If you cannot name the unit, you have not found it yet. The chorus is sloppy is a feeling, not a target. One size check: you should be able to play the isolated unit in a few seconds.

Locating it takes a deliberate pass. Play at a tempo where the section mostly holds and stop at the first thing that is not clean. Pushing through to the end is a stage habit, and it hides where the fault is. Mark the bar, then play only the two beats around it.

Some failures have a known repair. A chord change that arrives late usually breaks at one specific finger, not at the whole shape. Strumly's guide to [smoother chord transitions](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/smoother-chord-transitions) covers how to find which one.

### What slow enough actually means

Slow practice is advice everyone gives and almost nobody defines. Tempo has two jobs, so use two gears. The diagnostic gear is the edge: the tempo where the error shows up about half the time. A few attempts there show you exactly which move fails and how. The build gear is where the fix gets made: slow enough that you play the passage correctly on the first attempt, and on every attempt after it, with no mid-phrase recovery.

That last clause is the whole thing. If your hand arrives late and catches up, if a note buzzes and you re-press it, if you flinch and the beat stretches, the tempo is too fast regardless of how it sounded to you. A recovered mistake is still a mistake, and the recovery is part of what you teach your hands.

There is a second marker, more reliable than the first. At the correct tempo you can see the next move before you make it: your fingers are already traveling toward the next shape while the current one is still sounding. If the next chord is a surprise, slow down.

Expect this to feel absurdly slow, and expect to be bored. Boredom is roughly where the tempo starts being useful. The real mistake is drilling at the speed where it almost works. That tempo is for finding the error, not for fixing it: repeat there and you rehearse the error at high fidelity.

From there you climb. Raise the tempo in small increments, hold each step until you get two or three clean passes in a row, and drop back a step the moment a pass is not clean. Dropping back is not a punishment; it is the mechanism. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) turns one passage into that sequence so you are not choosing numbers mid-session.

### Repetition without a target does nothing

Playing something twenty times is not practice. It is twenty samples of your current ability, and it will average toward whatever you already do. A repetition changes something only when it is aimed at a specific correction.

So name the failure before you repeat it. Not it sounds bad. Which finger, which beat, which direction. A short list of what it usually turns out to be:

- **Timing.** The notes are right and land in the wrong place. Play against a click and find out whether you rush or drag; those need opposite fixes.
- **Fretting.** A note buzzes or dies. Find the finger and the reason: not enough pressure, the wrong part of the fingertip, or a finger lying flat across a string it should clear.
- **Picking.** The hand crosses strings late, or catches two when it wants one. Watch the picking hand for a few passes instead of the fretting hand. Most players never do.
- **The reach.** The shape is possible but your hand cannot get there in time. That is a preparation problem, and the fix belongs in the bar before the one that fails.
- **Attention.** You can play it while watching your hands and cannot when you are not. The passage is not learned yet, only supervised.

Once it has a name, the repetition gets a criterion. Instead of play it again, it becomes play it with the index finger landing steep enough to clear the next string. Now every pass has a verdict: it met the criterion or it did not, and three passes tell you something instead of nothing.

A criterion only works if something can tell you whether you met it, and your own ear mid-phrase is the least reliable judge you have available. That problem is large enough to have its own page: [deliberate practice on guitar](https://guitarhub.org/deliberate-practice-guitar) covers how to get an honest verdict on each attempt when there is no teacher in the room, which is the one part of this the structure below cannot supply.

### How to build the session

A session is not a to-do list of everything you want to be better at. It is one repair, protected from the rest of your playing. A structure that survives a real week:

- **Warm up on something that requires attention.** A few minutes on last session's passage at half its ladder tempo, or a slow chromatic run where you are actually watching your hand. A warm-up you can do while thinking about something else is not warming anything up.
- **Work one hard thing.** The isolated failure, at ladder tempo, with a named criterion. This is the part that changes your playing, so give it the middle of your attention span rather than the end. Twenty minutes is usually plenty; when the criterion stops improving, stop.
- **Put it back.** A bar that only works in isolation is not repaired. Play from four bars before the fix to four bars after, at a tempo where the fix survives. That is normally well below the top of your ladder.
- **Play something.** Finish with music rather than drilling. This is not a reward; it is the only part of the session that tests whether the work transfers to actual playing.

On a short day, do step two and step four and skip the rest. [An intermediate practice routine](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-routine-intermediate) scales this shape across a week, and Strumly's guide to [designing a practice routine](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine) is a reasonable week-level template to adapt.

### End the session so the next one starts well

The last five minutes decide the first ten of the next session, and most players spend them badly: push the tempo one more step, fail, push again, stop on the failure. Whatever you played last is what you rehearsed most recently, and it is what your hands offer up tomorrow.

So stop while it is working. When you get a clean pass at a new tempo step, take it and stop. Do not spend the win trying to prove it was not luck; you will find out tomorrow, which is the honest test anyway.

Then write two lines somewhere you will see them: the bar you were working on, the tempo you reached, and the specific thing that was still wrong. The next session starts by reading that instead of by wandering around the fretboard deciding what to do.

Record thirty seconds before you put the guitar down. Your phone is fine and nothing needs to be uploaded anywhere. The recording exists so next week you can hear what this week actually sounded like, which is reliably different from what you remember.

### How to tell the practice worked

How it felt is not evidence. Feeling is heavily influenced by how recently you played the passage, which is exactly the variable practice manipulates. Use markers you can check instead.

- **It survives cold.** Play it first, before any warm-up. A passage that only works after ten minutes of preparation is not learned yet.
- **It survives in context.** Play it inside the song, at the song's tempo, with whatever comes immediately before it. Isolation flatters everything.
- **It survives a surprise.** Something goes wrong (a buzz, a missed beat) and you keep going instead of stopping. Stopping means the passage is running on a memorized sequence rather than on control.
- **It survives a day.** Play it tomorrow without practicing it first. Same-day improvement is often short-term familiarity; what is left the next day is what you built.
- **The recording agrees.** Compare today's thirty seconds against the one you made at the start. It is the only marker that does not run through your own ears in real time.

Failing one of these hands you the next target, which is more useful than a vague sense of progress. The [song readiness score](https://guitarhub.org/readiness) runs a structured version of this check across a whole song.

### Common mistakes

- **Starting from the top every time.** The opening gets practiced far more than the part that needs it.
- **Counting reps instead of naming a target.** Twenty repetitions of an unspecified thing is twenty samples, not twenty corrections.
- **Adding new material before the old material holds.** New songs feel like progress and are the fastest way to accumulate half-finished pieces.
- **Warming up until the session is nearly over.** Twenty comfortable minutes followed by five on the hard thing is a session about avoidance.
- **Practicing with divided attention.** Playing with a screen running in front of you builds the ability to play with a screen running in front of you.

### Questions that come up

#### How long should a guitar practice session be?

Long enough to hold one repair, and no longer. Twenty to thirty focused minutes does more for a specific passage than an hour that starts from the top, because most of that hour lands on material that already works. If you have more time, run a second session later in the day rather than extending the first.

#### Is it better to practice every day or in longer sessions a few times a week?

More days is usually the better trade for anything technical. A passage is tested by whether it survives overnight, and practicing daily tests it daily. Longer sessions suit learning new material and playing, which is a different job from repairing.

#### Do I need a metronome for everything?

No. Use it when the problem is timing, when you are climbing a tempo ladder, and when you need an outside opinion on whether you rush. Turn it off when you are working on tone, on a reach, or on anything where subdividing in your head is part of what you are learning.

#### How do I know if I am practicing too slowly?

There is one real symptom. Below a certain tempo the passage becomes a different physical motion: you place fingers one at a time where you would normally move the whole shape at once. At that point you are rehearsing a motion you will never use. Speed up until the motion matches the passage, then stay there.

## Why guitar practice plateaus, and how to break one.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-plateau

You have played for years and the playing stopped changing. More hours will not fix that on their own. What the hours contain is the thing to change.

Updated August 29, 2026

Field Guide No. 03

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

Guitar practice plateaus when the difficulty of what you play stops rising while the hours keep going in. Adding time to a session that contains nothing difficult produces more of the same playing. Six causes are worth ruling out first: practicing what already sounds good, never playing at performance tempo, never hearing yourself from outside your own head, having no single target you could pass or fail, starting new material before the last piece is finished, and working around a technique problem instead of repairing it. Each one has a tell you can check in your own playing and a fix you can start this week.

This is the written account of the six causes, so you can read them and recognize your own. It does not rank them for you. The [practice plateau diagnostic](https://guitarhub.org/diagnose) asks nine questions about your last few sessions, scores five blockers against their own maximums, and returns the one your answers point at hardest, which is the part a page of prose cannot do. Read here to understand the causes. Go there to find out which one is yours.

### A plateau is a repetition problem, not a volume problem

The first stretch of playing improves on its own. Almost everything is new, so difficulty arrives without being scheduled: every chord shape, every strum pattern, every song is something you could not do last month. Then it stops arriving. You know enough shapes to get through most of what you attempt, and a session fills up with things you can already play at the speed you can already play them.

What improves is what is currently failing. Practice changes the playing at the edge where you can just barely hold it together, and nowhere else. A session with no failure in it maintains you at exactly the level you walked in with, which is why a plateau survives more practice. The hour was not wasted. It was spent on the part that was already finished.

Read the six statements below. Any that are true of your last three sessions are causes, not moods.

- You practiced things you can already play.
- You never reached the tempo the music is actually played at.
- You have not heard a recording of yourself in the last month.
- You cannot name one thing that would count as finished.
- You started something new before the last thing was done.
- You changed a fingering, a voicing, or an arrangement to avoid a movement you cannot make.

### The six causes, the tell, and the fix

#### You practice what already sounds good

Comfortable playing is the default, because it is the only part of practice that sounds like music. Nobody schedules it. It happens because starting from something familiar is easier than starting from something broken, and once the guitar is out and the sound is good, stopping to work on something that sounds bad takes a decision.

**The tell.** Your practice sounds good from the next room. If someone walking past would think you were playing rather than working, most of the hour was maintenance.

**The fix.** Put one thing in the session you cannot yet do: a passage that breaks down by the third bar, a change you miss more often than you land. Ten minutes of it, first, while your hands and your attention are fresh. Keep the comfortable playing. Move it to the end, where it belongs.

#### You never play at performance tempo

Slow practice is correct, and it is also where plateaus hide. A passage rehearsed only well under tempo never meets the problems that appear at full speed. The picking hand stiffens. The fretting hand starts arriving late. A shift that was comfortable becomes a jump. Those are not faster versions of the slow-tempo problems. They are different problems, and they exist only above a certain speed.

**The tell.** You know exactly how the passage feels at your practice tempo and have no idea how it feels at the real one, because you have not tried it there in weeks.

**The fix.** Play it at the target tempo once at the start of every session, badly if that is what happens. The failed attempt tells you which bar is the actual problem, and it is usually one bar rather than the whole passage. Then work in steps below it and return to the top before you stop. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) lays those steps out for a passage you choose.

#### You never hear yourself from outside

You cannot hear your own timing while you are producing it. Your ears are busy predicting what your hands are about to do, and the prediction smooths over the gaps. A recording removes the prediction.

The first one is unpleasant. It is also the most information you will get all week: a transition that rushes, a chord that never fully rings, a fill landing half a beat late, dynamics that sit flat from the first bar to the last. None of that is audible from behind the guitar.

**The tell.** You describe your sessions in feelings. Good days and bad days, rather than a specific thing that got better.

**The fix.** Record one take a week on your phone. One attempt, no edit, no second try. Listen once and write down the first thing that is wrong. That becomes the difficult ten minutes of the next session. The recording matters less than the comparison: a take from four weeks ago is the only honest evidence that anything changed.

#### You have no single target you could pass or fail

“Get better at soloing” cannot be finished, so it cannot be practiced. It has no end and no test, which makes every session equally defensible and none of them aimed. A target that works is one a stranger could score. “Play the intro at full tempo, twice through, no stops, no buzzes” is a target. “Improve my rhythm” is a subject heading.

That is the whole difference between [deliberate practice](https://guitarhub.org/deliberate-practice-guitar) and playing something again. The first has a standard it can fail.

**The tell.** Asked what you are working on, you name a subject rather than a passage. Scales. Timing. Theory. Speed.

**The fix.** Write one sentence containing a specific piece of music, a specific tempo, and a specific standard for clean, with a date on it four weeks out. One sentence, not five.

#### You start new material before the last piece is finished

Beginning is the enjoyable part. The first days on a new song produce visible progress every time you sit down, because everything in it is new. The end of a piece is the opposite: slow, unglamorous, four bars that still fall apart while the rest is fine. There is always another song more interesting than those four bars.

A shelf of nearly finished pieces feels like a repertoire and behaves like nothing. Under any pressure, a room, a camera, another player, the unfinished parts are precisely what breaks, because they were never taken past the point where they hold.

**The tell.** You can start twenty songs and play none of them all the way through at tempo.

**The fix.** Finish one. Pick the closest to done, decide in advance what finished means, and start nothing new until it holds. The [song readiness score](https://guitarhub.org/readiness) checks a song against the parts that break under pressure, which is usually not the part you have been practicing.

#### You worked around a technique problem instead of repairing it

Every guitarist carries some technique debt. The barre that never rings, so you play the three-string version. The pinky you stopped using early and never brought back. The alternate picking that turns into all downstrokes once the tempo rises. The shift you avoid by choosing another position. Each substitution was reasonable at the time, and each one let you keep playing.

The debt stays invisible while the workaround holds. It becomes visible when a piece requires the thing you routed around, and by then it is not one piece. It is a category of music you quietly stopped attempting.

**The tell.** There are songs you decided you do not like, and they happen to require the same movement.

**The fix.** Name the movement and practice it away from any song, a few minutes at the start of the session. The barre on its own. The pinky on its own. Isolated technique is dull, and it is the only way the debt gets paid. Chord changes respond particularly well to isolation, and the Strumly guide to [smoother chord transitions](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/smoother-chord-transitions) takes one change apart.

### Change one thing, not six

Six causes is a diagnosis, not a task list. Rebuilding an entire routine in a week fails the way a crash diet fails: none of it survives a bad Tuesday. Pick the cause whose tell was most obviously true, and change one thing about how the session runs.

- Record a baseline take before you change anything. One attempt, at the tempo you can currently manage.
- Choose the single cause whose tell you recognized fastest. The fast recognition is usually the honest one.
- Change one thing about the session, and write the change down so you cannot renegotiate it midweek.
- Run the changed session for a week without adjusting it again, and log one line per session in the free [practice evidence log](https://guitarhub.org/log), which shows whether the focus is moving once it has three sessions.
- Record the same take at the end of the week and listen to the two back to back.

If the two recordings sound the same, the change was the wrong one or it was too small. That is worth knowing, and it took a week to find out. If you need a shape for the rest of the week around that one change, the Strumly guide to [designing a practice routine](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine) covers the ordering.

### How you will know the plateau broke

Not by feeling better. Feeling is the least reliable instrument in the room, and it moves with sleep, mood, and how the guitar happens to be set up that day.

The plateau broke when something you could not play a month ago is something you can play now, at tempo, on demand, with a recording at each end to prove it. That is a small claim. It is also a real one, and it repeats: a month later, on the next thing you could not do.

If more than one of the six tells was true and you cannot decide where to start, the [practice plateau diagnostic](https://guitarhub.org/diagnose) asks a short set of questions and names the part of your practice that stopped producing change. It takes a couple of minutes, needs no account, and nothing leaves your browser.

## Deliberate practice, at the instrument.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/deliberate-practice-guitar

One target you cannot hit yet, a difficulty where you keep missing, and something outside your own ear judging each attempt. Here is how to run that without a teacher in the room.

Updated August 29, 2026

Field Guide No. 04

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

Deliberate practice on guitar means working on one thing you cannot yet play, at a difficulty where you keep failing, with something outside your own ear judging each attempt. Playing is what you do with material you already own. Deliberate practice is what you do with material you do not. Both belong in a week at the instrument, but only one of them is built to move what is currently out of reach.

This page is about the part of practice you cannot supply by deciding to: an honest verdict on each attempt when nobody else is listening. The target, the tempo and the order of the session are a separate problem, and [how to practice guitar effectively](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-effectively) is the page that solves it. Read that one for the shape of the hour. Read this one for how to tell whether the hour worked.

### Playing and practicing feel similar and are not

Sit down with a guitar and the default is playing. Your hands reach for the riff you always open with and the two songs you can get through without thinking. Nothing is wrong with that. It is most of why you own the instrument.

Deliberate practice starts somewhere else. You name a failure, and you name it narrowly. Not “get better at barre chords.” The B-flat in the second verse buzzes on the third string every time you arrive from an open G. The second sentence is a target. The first is a mood.

Three questions separate them, and you can answer all three about the hour you just finished:

- What was failing when you sat down, and is it still failing now?
- How many times did you stop mid-phrase because something was wrong?
- Could you have played most of that hour while thinking about something else?

If nothing was failing, if you never stopped, and if your attention was free the whole time, you played. That is a legitimate way to spend an hour. It is just not the hour that moves the thing you are stuck on.

### Feedback is the mechanism, not an extra

Repetition on its own does not sort good attempts from bad ones. It installs whatever you actually did, at whatever accuracy you actually did it. If your timing drifted late on every pass through a phrase and nothing told you, you rehearsed the drift. This is how practice can feel diligent and change nothing.

A teacher is, mechanically, a feedback machine: a second set of ears that is not busy playing. You do not have one in the room, so you build that function out of parts you already have.

#### Record the attempt, then listen to it cold

Your ear while playing is occupied. It is running the next chord change, watching your fretting hand, and quietly forgiving you. Your ear on playback has none of those jobs and is much harder to fool.

Record one take on your phone. Then listen for one thing only: was the timing steady, or was the chord clean, or was the bend in tune. One question per listen. The errors you hear on playback were mostly inaudible to you thirty seconds earlier, and that gap is the entire reason to record.

#### Let the metronome judge instead of accompany

Most players treat a click as a pacer to follow. Use it as a judge instead. Play the passage and pay attention to where you and the click separate, because that tells you which beat is actually causing the problem. Rushing into a hard bar and dragging out of it is a different diagnosis than being late the whole way through.

A click on every beat hides small drift, since you get corrected four times a bar before the error can accumulate. Move the click to beats two and four, or to beat one only, and the drift becomes obvious. If you cannot hear yourself against it, the click is too quiet or the tempo is too fast.

#### Use a tool that reports something you cannot hear

Software that listens while you play can flag notes and timing you would argue with on your own. It does not know what you are trying to sound like, so it is not a replacement for your judgment. It is useful for the narrow question of whether what you played matches what you intended. [Strumly's guide to practicing with an AI coach](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/practicing-guitar-with-an-ai-coach) is a longer read on where that fits into a session.

### Work at the edge of what you can do

The edge is the level where you fail some of the time, about half the time. Not most of the time, and not never. It is the diagnostic gear: the place you find out what fails. The fix itself gets built one gear down, at the tempo where every attempt is clean.

Far below the edge, on material you already own, you are playing. The attempts come out clean because they were always going to come out clean, and nothing about your playing had to change to produce them.

Above the edge you are generating noise. When every attempt collapses, you cannot tell which one was closer, so there is nothing to correct toward. Practice above the edge feels like hard work and returns almost no information.

The edge has a specific discomfort to it: you can nearly do the thing. You get it, lose it, and get it again. That instability is the point. It means the thing is still being built rather than already built or not yet started.

Finding it is mechanical, and the arithmetic of climbing back up from it belongs to the session rather than to this page: the tempo work is laid out in [how to practice guitar effectively](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-effectively). What matters here is that the edge is a place you have to locate by ear before any of it starts, because a tempo you chose for being comfortable is not a tempo that tells you anything.

The edge also moves. A tempo that was hard last week becomes a warm-up, which means practicing at last week's edge is playing. Re-find it every few sessions instead of assuming it stayed put.

### It is meant to be short, and it is meant to be uncomfortable

Attention is the constraint here, not time. Deliberate practice asks you to hold a target in mind, notice a specific error, and change something on the next attempt. That kind of attention runs out well before your hands do.

When it runs out, the session does not visibly fall apart. It degrades quietly. You keep repeating the passage, you stop catching the errors, and you start banking attempts at an accuracy you would not have accepted twenty minutes earlier. Stopping is the right move and also the hard one, because the guitar is still in your hands and the room is still quiet.

The discomfort is not a virtue and it is not the goal. It is a location signal. A practice block that is entirely comfortable has drifted below the edge, which means you are playing. A block that is grim start to finish is above it.

### Twenty deliberate minutes against two unfocused hours

The difference is not willpower or talent. It is how many attempts got judged.

Two unfocused hours can contain hundreds of repetitions. Most of them are of material you already play, at a tempo you already own, and none of them were checked against anything. The four bars that are actually broken get a handful of passes on the way by, usually inside the whole song, usually at full speed, usually with the same error each time.

Twenty deliberate minutes might contain thirty attempts. Each one is aimed at a single target, at a tempo where the outcome is in doubt, and each one is followed by a decision about what to change.

Here is what those twenty minutes can look like:

- Two minutes: play the passage once at full speed and record it. That take is your before.
- Three minutes: listen back and name one error. Not three. One.
- Ten minutes: find the tempo where that error shows up about half the time and watch what fails. Then drop to the tempo where the fix comes out clean every time, changing one thing per attempt. A fingering, an anchor finger, where the shift starts, where you breathe. Climb back toward the edge as it holds.
- Three minutes: return to full speed and record the same passage again.
- Two minutes: write down what changed and what you will start with tomorrow.

The two hours are not wasted. They are how songs get into your hands and how playing stays worth doing. But if a month of them has produced no change in the thing you cannot play, the missing ingredient is the twenty minutes rather than more hours. That is the usual shape of a [practice plateau](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-plateau).

### What deliberate practice does not mean

- **Not more hours.** It describes what a block of practice contains, not how long you sit with the guitar.
- **Not drills instead of songs.** A song is fine material. The deliberate part is what you do with the four bars of it that keep collapsing.
- **Not a daily obligation.** A short focused block a few times a week is deliberate practice. A daily streak of unfocused repetition is not.
- **Not gear or software dependent.** It needs a target, a tempo you can move, and a way to hear yourself back. A phone covers the third one.
- **Not the whole session.** Fifteen focused minutes followed by an hour of playing is a good session. Ninety minutes of half-attention is one long warm-up.

### Where to point it

The method is useless without a target, and picking one is the part most players skip. If you are not sure where to aim, the [practice plateau diagnostic](https://guitarhub.org/diagnose) asks the questions that usually surface it. If you already know the target and want the structure that goes around the deliberate block, [how to practice guitar effectively](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-effectively) covers the rest of the session, and [Strumly's guide to designing a practice routine](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine) covers the weekly shape around that.

### Common questions

#### Is deliberate practice just practicing slowly?

No. Slowing down is one way to reach the edge, and often the right one, but a slow repetition with no target and no feedback is still just a repetition. What matters is whether each attempt is aimed at something specific and checked afterward, not the number on the metronome.

#### How long should a deliberate practice block be?

Short enough that your attention holds for the whole of it. Twenty minutes on one target is a reasonable place to start, less on a tired day. When you stop hearing your own mistakes, the block is finished, whatever the clock says.

#### Can you practice deliberately without a teacher?

Yes, but you have to replace what a teacher supplies: a target chosen for you, an honest read on each attempt, and a decision about what to change next. The target and the decision you can supply yourself. The honest read is the part to hand off, to a recording, to a metronome, or to software that listens while you play.

#### Does this mean playing for fun is a waste of practice time?

No. Playing is the reason for the practice, and it is how songs settle into your hands. The two just do different jobs, so a week containing only one of them gets only one of the two results.

## The 30-day guitar challenge that actually works.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/30-day-guitar-challenge

Streak challenges measure attendance. This one measures playing: one finish line, a day 1 baseline, four weeks that each do a different job, and two recordings you compare at the end.

Updated August 29, 2026

Field Guide No. 05

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

A 30-day guitar challenge works when it ends with two recordings you can play back to back: one from day 1, one from day 30, of the same thing, under the same conditions. Everything else is scaffolding. Choose one finish line narrow enough that someone could listen for a minute and say whether you hit it. Record it before you practice. Spend the four weeks on the four stages of the GuitarHub method: baseline what breaks, isolate and repair that one thing, reconnect it under pressure, and prove it with the final take. The daily streak is not the measure. The pair of recordings is.

This is the written guide: how to choose a finish line narrow enough to prove, and how to judge the day 30 recording. It does not build the four weeks for you, because the sequencing is arithmetic and the judgment is not. The [30-day breakthrough planner](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough) does the arithmetic, sized to the days and minutes you actually have. Read this page to decide what you are proving, then hand the month to the planner.

### Why most 30-day challenges fail

The common format asks you to play every day for 30 days. It is easy to explain, easy to start, and it measures the wrong thing. Attendance and change are not the same, and a challenge scored on attendance cannot tell them apart. Four failure modes account for most of it.

- **The streak becomes the scoreboard.** A checked box records that you picked up the guitar, not what you did with it. Thirty checked boxes can describe 30 sessions of playing the parts you already play well.
- **The goal is too broad to judge.** Get better at rhythm has no finish line. On day 30 you will argue with yourself about whether it happened, and there is no evidence in the argument.
- **There is no baseline.** Without a day 1 recording, the comparison at the end runs against your memory of how you sounded, and memory bends toward whatever you already believe.
- **One missed day ends the run.** All-or-nothing framing turns a single skipped evening into a reason to abandon the remaining three weeks.

### Choose a finish line narrow enough to prove

A finish line is one sentence describing a performance you can either deliver or not. The test is whether a person who knows nothing about your practice could listen to a recording and answer yes or no without a follow-up question. If the answer needs context from you, the finish line is still a wish.

- Get faster becomes play the main riff cleanly at 120 BPM, up from the 88 BPM I can hold today.
- Get better at rhythm becomes play two minutes of this groove against a click without losing the pulse.
- Learn the fretboard becomes find and play the same phrase in three neck positions without hunting for the notes.
- Finish a song becomes record this song from count-in to final chord in one take, no restarts.

Two sizing rules. The finish line has to be something you cannot do today, or there is nothing to prove. It also has to be close enough that four focused weeks could plausibly reach it, which usually means taking a piece of a large goal rather than the goal. Play the solo is often a month of work. Play the whole song at tempo is often not.

The [30-day breakthrough planner](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough) holds you to one finish line and turns it into a week-by-week sequence with the evidence each week has to produce. It runs in your browser and needs no account.

### Record the baseline before you practice

Day 1 is a recording day. Play the thing once, all the way through, before you have warmed up on it and before you have started fixing anything. One take. Keep the mistakes.

A phone on a table is enough. The recording does not have to sound good, but it does have to be repeatable, so write the conditions beside it: tempo, where you started, whether a click was running, what room you were in. You repeat those conditions on day 30, because a comparison between two different setups proves nothing.
