While it is fresh, write one line naming the exact bar, transition, or beat where the performance first came apart. That line is your week 1 diagnosis, and most of the month depends on it being specific. The chorus is messy is not specific. The change out of the fourth bar of the chorus arrives half a beat late is.

### The four-week arc

Each week does a different job. Running the same practice for four weeks is how a challenge turns into 30 repetitions of the same plateau.

#### Week 1 · Baseline: find where it breaks

Find the single place the performance breaks, not the list of everything imperfect. Play the whole thing a few times and watch for the failure that repeats. If two candidates keep competing, take the earlier one. An error near the start compounds into everything after it.

#### Week 2 · Isolate: repair one thing

Take the broken piece out of its context and work it alone, in two gears. First find the edge, the tempo where the error shows up about half the time, and watch exactly what fails. Then drop to the tempo where every attempt is clean, slow enough that playing it correctly is boring, and build the fix there before stepping the speed up. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) turns one passage into a starting speed, a target, and the steps between them. Put the piece back into the song at the end of each session so you are repairing the join and not just the fragment. If the break is a chord change, the Strumly guide to [smoother chord transitions](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/smoother-chord-transitions) covers the mechanics.

#### Week 3 · Reconnect: add real pressure

A repaired passage played alone at a comfortable tempo is not yet a repaired performance. Put it back under the conditions that will exist on day 30: full length, real tempo, a click or a backing track, and a cold start with no warm-up run first. Work that holds in isolation often falls apart here, and finding that out in week 3 leaves time to respond.

#### Week 4 · Prove: perform and compare

Stop making changes. Rehearse the version you have, record the final take under the day 1 conditions, and put the two recordings side by side. Week 4 is not for one last improvement. It is for making the result repeatable.

### What to record, and when

- **Day 1.** The baseline take, before practicing, plus the written conditions and the first breakdown point.
- **End of week 2.** The repaired piece on its own, at the fastest tempo where it stays clean. That number is the one you are trying to move.
- **End of week 3.** A full run under pressure. Expect it to be worse than the isolated take from week 2. The size of that gap is your week 4 workload.
- **Day 30.** The final take, under the day 1 conditions, recorded whether or not it goes well.

Between those points, one line per session is enough: what you worked on, at what tempo, and what changed. The log exists so that on day 30 you can tell whether a result came from the work or from a good night. How you structure the session itself is a separate problem, and the Strumly guide to [designing a practice routine](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine) covers it.

### Missing a day is not failure

A missed day costs one session. Quitting on day 12 costs the other 18. Streak framing makes those feel like the same size of mistake, which is the most expensive thing about it.

So drop the streak. The month is scored on whether the day 30 recording differs from the day 1 recording in the way you predicted. Four missed days with the other 26 spent on the actual blocker beats 30 days of running the whole song from the top.

What genuinely breaks a 30-day run is changing the finish line partway through. Week 2 is uncomfortable by design, because week 2 is where you work slowly and alone on the one thing you are worst at. Switching goals at that point feels like progress and resets the month to zero. If the finish line was chosen badly, write that down, finish the 30 days anyway, and choose better next time.

### Judging day 30 honestly

Play the day 1 recording first, then the final take, once each. Then answer three questions.

- Is the thing you named on day 1 still the first thing that breaks? If it is, the month did not reach the target, whatever else improved along the way.
- Can the difference be heard without knowing where to listen? Play both takes for someone who has not been told what changed. If they cannot hear it, the change may still be real, but it is small.
- Can you repeat the final take right now? A performance you produced once out of nine attempts is a good sign, not a finished skill.

If the finish line was a song, the [song readiness score](https://guitarhub.org/readiness) checks it against the parts that tend to break under pressure, which is a useful second opinion before you call the month done.

### If it did not work

Missing the finish line is a result, not a wasted month. The log usually tells you which of a small number of things happened.

- **The finish line was too broad.** Effort spread across a goal containing several independent problems. Cut it to the smallest piece still worth playing and run that.
- **You practiced the whole thing instead of the broken part.** Common, comfortable, and easy to spot in the log: sessions that describe playing through rather than working on. Week 2 is the week that got skipped.
- **You never found the real blocker.** What you repaired was not what was breaking the performance. The [practice plateau diagnostic](https://guitarhub.org/diagnose) is built for this case, and walks you to the part of your practice that stopped producing change.
- **It is working, slower than 30 days.** Tempo up, error count down, target not yet reached. Keep the same finish line and run a second month rather than starting over on something new.

### Common questions

#### Does missing a day mean starting the challenge over?

No. Missing a day costs one session. The challenge is judged on whether the day 30 recording differs from the day 1 recording, not on how many days in a row you practiced.

#### How long should each practice session be?

Long enough to do the repair work rather than only warm up and play through. The GuitarHub planner accepts sessions of 15 to 60 minutes, three to six days a week, and builds the same four-week sequence at any of those settings.

#### Can I work on more than one finish line in the same 30 days?

Pick one. Two finish lines split the month into two fortnights, and a fortnight is rarely enough to get through diagnosis and repair on either. Write the second one down and run it next month.

#### What if I cannot record myself properly?

A phone voice memo is enough. The recording is a measurement, not a release. What matters is that the day 1 and day 30 takes exist, were played under the same conditions, and can be listened to back to back.

The [30-day breakthrough planner](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough) takes a finish line, the days you have, and your session length, and lays out the four weeks with the evidence each one has to produce. Record day 1 before you build the plan. The baseline is the part people skip, and it is the part the whole month gets measured against.

## An intermediate guitar practice routine that changes every week.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-routine-intermediate

Five blocks with different jobs, in a 25-minute and a 50-minute version. The structure stays fixed. The material inside it moves as the evidence moves.

Updated August 29, 2026

Field Guide No. 06

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

An intermediate practice routine works when the session is split into five blocks with different jobs: a warm-up with a stated intent, one repair target, tempo work on that target, repertoire played under pressure, and a cold-start test. A 50-minute session runs 5 / 15 / 10 / 15 / 5 minutes. A 25-minute session runs 3 / 10 / 8 / 4, with the tempo ladder folded into the repair block. Keep the five blocks fixed and change the material inside them as the evidence changes. A routine that is identical in week four to week one has stopped producing change, because the fault it was built to fix is either fixed by now or was never the real one.

This page is about what a session contains once you are past the beginner stage, in five blocks with separate jobs. [The practice schedule](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-schedule) decides which days these sessions land on and which one you defend when the week goes wrong, and this page decides what happens inside one of them. In your first three months, the [beginner guitar practice routine](https://guitarhub.org/beginner-guitar-practice-routine) lays out the 90-day plan, and the [A-to-D chord practice routine](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/routine) times each session for you.

### Why the intermediate stall is a structure problem

You can almost play a hundred things and fully play none. That is rarely a talent ceiling and it is usually not a discipline problem either. It is what happens when every session is built from the same material: the songs you can already mostly play, at the speed you can already mostly play them, stopping and restarting whenever a bar goes wrong.

That session feels like work and produces very little, because nothing in it is aimed at a specific fault and nothing in it measures whether the fault moved. The five blocks below exist to give each part of the hour one job and one output. If the sessions have stopped producing any change at all, read [why guitar practice plateaus](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-plateau) first, because a plateau needs a diagnosis before it needs a routine.

### The five blocks, and what each one is for

Run them in this order. Each block hands its output to the next, and the last block generates the input for tomorrow.

#### 1. Warm-up with intent, 5 minutes

This block gets your hands and ears working and commits you to the one thing the session will fix.

Use material that matches the motion your repair target needs. If the target is a barre change, warm up moving between barre shapes slowly and cleanly. If it is string crossing at speed, cross strings at a tempo where nothing misfires. A warm-up made of unrelated scale patterns is just the first five minutes of playing.

End the block by naming the target out loud or writing it down. If you cannot finish the sentence “today I am fixing ___”, you do not have a session yet. You have practice time.

#### 2. The one repair target, 15 minutes

This block makes one specific thing measurably better. It is the only block that is allowed to feel bad.

Take the smallest unit that actually breaks. Usually that is two bars, one chord change, one position shift, or one string crossing. Not a section, and never a whole song. Work it well under performance speed with your phone recording the entire block, so you are judging the take instead of the memory of the take.

The test is countable: five correct repetitions in a row, counted, not “it is mostly there now”. If you cannot get five, the unit is too big or the tempo is too high. Halve the unit before you lower the tempo again.

Choose the target from your own evidence, not from a video you saw: the place the pressure block collapsed last session, or the break point the cold-start test exposed. The [practice plateau diagnostic](https://guitarhub.org/diagnose) is a faster route to it when the recording is ambiguous. For chord changes specifically, Strumly's guide to [smoother chord transitions](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/smoother-chord-transitions) breaks the motion into the parts worth isolating.

#### 3. Tempo work, 10 minutes

This block finds the speed at which the repaired unit falls apart, which is the real edge of the skill.

Build a ladder: a starting tempo where the unit is genuinely clean, the tempo the music actually runs at, and steps between them. Climb one step at a time. When the fault reappears, drop two steps, play it clean three times, and climb again. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) lays out the steps if you would rather not do the arithmetic mid-session.

Two rules keep this block honest. The top of the ladder is the song's tempo, not a personal record, because playing faster than the music requires is a separate skill and it is not the one that finishes your song. And clean at a slow tempo counts for nothing if you never climb. The point is to move the break point, not to enjoy the bottom rung.

#### 4. Repertoire under pressure, 15 minutes

This block proves the repair survives contact with the actual song.

Pressure is anything that removes your ability to stop and restart. A click. A backing track. One take with no restarts. Standing up. Recording. Another person in the room. Pick one constraint and keep it for the whole week so the sessions stay comparable.

The failure this block catches is specific: the passage is clean in isolation and still collapses inside the song, because the bar before it and the bar after it were never part of the repair. Play into the passage and out of it, not just through it.

#### 5. The cold-start test, 5 minutes

This block measures what survives with no runway.

Play one piece you claim to know, once, cold, with no practice run and no restart. Everyone plays better on the third attempt. The first attempt is what you would have on a stage, at a jam, or when someone hands you a guitar.

Keep a rotating list of four to six cold-start pieces and note two things after each: whether you finished, and where it broke. That break point becomes a candidate target for the next session, which is how the routine feeds itself. The [song readiness score](https://guitarhub.org/readiness) checks the same piece against the parts that usually fail under pressure.

This is the cheapest block and the only one that measures anything. When the session gets cut short, cut something else.

### The two session lengths, side by side

The 50-minute session:

- **5 minutes.** Warm-up with intent.
- **15 minutes.** The one repair target.
- **10 minutes.** Tempo work on that unit.
- **15 minutes.** Repertoire under pressure.
- **5 minutes.** The cold-start test.

The 25-minute session:

- **3 minutes.** Warm-up with intent.
- **10 minutes.** The repair target, with the tempo ladder run inside it.
- **8 minutes.** Repertoire under pressure.
- **4 minutes.** The cold-start test.

Notice what did not happen: the short session is not the long session halved. Tempo work merges into repair because both are working the same unit, and that merge absorbs most of the cut: together the two blocks go from 25 minutes to 10. The pressure block gives up 7 minutes, roughly half its length, because it is the block that tolerates being short. The warm-up gives up 2. The cold-start test gives up one minute, because removing it saves almost nothing and costs you the only measurement in the session.

### How to swap material in without rebuilding the routine

Only the inputs change. The blocks do not.

- **Warm-up.** The motion your repair target needs, at a tempo where it is clean.
- **Repair.** The smallest failing unit from last session's pressure block or cold start.
- **Tempo.** That repaired unit, plus the tempo the song actually runs at.
- **Pressure.** The song the unit belongs to, played under the one constraint you kept all week.
- **Cold start.** The next piece on your rotating list.

The repair input is the one that matters. It should come out of your own last session, not out of a feed. If you cannot say where this week's target came from, you picked it because it looked interesting, and the routine has quietly turned back into lesson collecting. Strumly's guide to [designing a practice routine](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine) covers the same problem from the routine-design side.

Retire a cold-start piece once it survives three cold starts in a row and put a harder one in its place. A list you always finish has stopped telling you anything.

### What should change week to week

The blocks hold their shape across a month. The emphasis inside them moves.

- **Week 1.** Record a baseline before deciding anything. The repair target is whatever that recording exposes, not what you assumed on the way to the guitar.
- **Week 2.** Same target, bigger unit. Two bars become the phrase; the phrase becomes the section it sits in.
- **Week 3.** The target moves to the seams, meaning the bar before and the bar after. Pressure gets the longest block this week.
- **Week 4.** No new repair. The session is pressure and cold start only. Record the final take beside the baseline and name the change the two recordings actually support.

Change one variable at a time. If you swap the target, the tempo ceiling, and the song in the same week, the routine can no longer tell you which change did anything.

Three signals say a target has finished its work: the error rate stops dropping across two consecutive sessions, the unit stays clean at the song's tempo for three sessions running, or the cold-start test starts breaking somewhere else. Any one of them means pick a new target. Two of them mean you should have picked one already.

### The ten-minute day

Do not run all five blocks at two minutes each. A two-minute repair block is not practice, it is a checklist you ticked. What follows is which of these five blocks survives a short day, not a general ten minute session: that one is on [how long to practice each day](https://guitarhub.org/how-long-to-practice-guitar-each-day).

A ten-minute day is a repair day:

- **2 minutes.** Warm up on the exact motion the target needs.
- **6 minutes.** The repair unit, recorded, and nothing else.
- **2 minutes.** One cold start, one piece, no second attempt.

The tempo ladder and the pressure block are gone for the day, and that is correct. Both need enough repetitions to mean something, and neither survives being handed ninety seconds.

Mark the session short in whatever you use to log it. A week with three ten-minute days and two full sessions is a fine week, but if the log does not say so, you will read the flat cold-start results as a plateau instead of as a short week.

### Questions about this routine

#### How long should an intermediate guitar practice session be?

Long enough to hold a real repair block. Fifty minutes fits all five blocks comfortably. Twenty-five works if you run the tempo ladder inside the repair block and take the time out of the pressure block rather than out of the cold-start test.

#### Should scales be part of an intermediate practice routine?

Only inside a block that needs them. A scale is warm-up material when it matches the motion your repair target requires, and it is repair material when the failing unit is a position shift or a string crossing inside that scale. A scale run attached to no target belongs outside the session.

#### What should I do if I cannot identify a repair target?

Record one cold take of a song you claim to know, listen to it once, and write down the first place it broke. That is the target. If nothing broke, the piece is too easy to diagnose anything and you need a harder one on the list.

#### How often should the routine itself change?

The five blocks stay. The material inside them changes when the evidence says so: when the error rate stops dropping across two consecutive sessions, when the unit has been clean at the song's tempo for three sessions, or when the cold-start test starts breaking somewhere new.

## How long should you practice guitar each day?

Source: https://guitarhub.org/how-long-to-practice-guitar-each-day

Duration is the wrong variable. Here is the right one, how to tell when a session has stopped working, and what to do with 10, 25 or 60 minutes.

Updated August 29, 2026

Field Guide No. 07

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

There is no correct number of minutes. Duration is the wrong variable; attention is the right one. A focused twenty minutes changes your playing more than an unfocused two hours, because practice only moves what you are paying attention to. Practice as long as you can stay specific about what you are fixing, then stop.

If you want a number to start from, take twenty to forty minutes on most days over ninety minutes twice a week. Not because short sessions are special. Because a repair has to survive a night's sleep before you know it held, and the only way to run that test often is to practice often.

This page is about one session: how long it stays useful, and what belongs in ten, twenty-five or sixty minutes. It is the page that sizes a session and fills it. How those sessions are arranged across a week, which one you defend and what you cut when the week goes wrong, is [the practice schedule](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-schedule)'s question rather than this one.

### The limit is concentration, not fingers

Ask a player why they stopped and the answer is usually physical: tired hand, sore fingertips. Sore fingertips are real in the first few weeks and stop being the limit after that. What runs out first, for nearly everyone past that stage, is the ability to hold one specific target in mind and evaluate each attempt against it.

That evaluation is the expensive part of a session and the part that does the work. A repetition you did not evaluate still taught you something, just not the thing you chose. An hour of unevaluated repetition teaches you whatever your hands happened to do.

So the useful question is not how many minutes you can sit with the instrument. It is how many minutes you can stay specific. The third finger lands late on the C, listen for it, fix it is practice. Run the song again is a fine way to spend an evening and a poor way to fix a bar.

### How to tell a session has stopped producing change

Sessions rarely end. They decay, and the decay is hard to notice from inside because it feels exactly like continuing. Any one of these tells can be a bad minute; two at once means the useful part of the session is behind you.

- **You cannot say what you are fixing.** Answer out loud. If it takes more than a second, or comes out as the name of a song rather than a location inside it, you are no longer aiming at anything.
- **Repetitions stop getting a verdict.** Early on you know instantly whether a pass was clean. Later the pass ends and you have no opinion. That is the evaluation shutting down, and it shuts down well before the hands do.
- **A mistake you had fixed comes back.** Not a new one — the old one, returning. You have dropped below the attention the fix requires, and every repetition from here argues with it.
- **You drift toward what already works.** The bar you came to repair gets shorter run-ups and the intro gets longer ones. Nobody decides to do this.
- **You raise the tempo out of boredom.** The honest reason to move up a rung is that the current one is clean and cold. Being tired of it is a different reason wearing the same clothes.
- **You start negotiating.** One more good one and I will stop, said twice, is a coin flip you keep re-flipping.

When two of those show up, stop. Stopping is the last measurement you take: a session that ends while you can still tell a clean pass from a dirty one ends with a result, and one that runs past that point ends with a fog.

### Why long sessions can move you backwards

A practice session does not record your intentions. It records what your hands actually did, and it weights the late repetitions as heavily as the early ones. In the last stretch of a long session, what your hands do is the sloppy version. You are not failing to make progress there; you are making progress on the wrong take. That is why a two-hour night can leave a passage worse than it was at the forty-minute mark.

There is a second cost, harder to see. A long session produces a strong memory of effort, and that memory buys patience with an approach that is not working. Three weeks of twenty-five-minute sessions are easy to abandon when the recording says they did nothing. Three weeks of two-hour nights are not.

The check takes ninety seconds and is worth running on any session past about forty minutes. Before you pack up, play the thing you were repairing once, cold. If it is worse than it was mid-session, the last stretch cost you something, and tomorrow should be shorter.

### Three session shapes

Time is the one budget you know in advance, so it is the sensible thing to plan against. All three shapes assume you already know your repair target. If you do not, the [GuitarHub method](https://guitarhub.org/method) covers how the target gets chosen and how you know when it is finished.

Ten, twenty-five and sixty are the common sizes, not the only ones. For a number that is none of those, the [practice session builder](https://guitarhub.org/session) splits whatever minutes you have into blocks that total exactly that length, weighted toward the one thing you named as broken. On a short evening it drops the blocks whose share came out too small to be worth starting, rather than shrinking all of them into setup time, and it tells you which ones went and why.

#### Ten minutes: one repair, recorded

Do not run a miniature version of your full routine. Five blocks at two minutes each is a checklist you ticked.

- **2 minutes.** The exact motion the target needs. Not general warm-up — that motion.
- **6 minutes.** The repair unit alone, at a tempo where you are correct on purpose rather than correct by luck.
- **2 minutes.** One cold pass of the passage in context, recorded, no second attempt.

The recording is what makes ten minutes count. Without it a short day leaves no trace, and a week of short days reads back as a plateau rather than a short week.

#### Twenty-five minutes: repair, then pressure

- **3 minutes.** The motion.
- **12 minutes.** The repair unit, tempo work folded into it. One target, not three. If you are climbing speeds, the [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) decides which rung this session owns, so you are not deciding it while tired.
- **7 minutes.** The repaired part back inside the music, at a tempo where the whole passage survives rather than the fragment.
- **3 minutes.** One cold pass, recorded.

Twenty-five is the shape most weekday sessions should take: long enough to repair something and test the repair in one sitting, short enough that your evaluation still works at the test.

#### Sixty minutes: two sessions, not one

An hour is not a longer version of twenty-five minutes. Treat it as two sessions with a real break between them: put the guitar down, leave the room, five to ten minutes.

- **First half.** Repair, exactly as above, on one target.
- **The break.** Load-bearing, not optional. Without it the second half is the decayed tail of the first.
- **Second half.** A different job: repertoire, the whole piece, new material, or a second target that uses a different skill.

Changing jobs is the point of the break: the first target has had all the attention it can use today, and another twenty minutes on it is repetition without evaluation. If both halves have to be repair, make the second structurally different — a timing problem after a fretting-hand problem.

### When a long session is the right call

None of this makes long sessions bad. It makes them bad at one job. Repair — slow, evaluated, one passage at a time — degrades with duration. Plenty of guitar work does not.

- **Playing.** Ninety minutes of songs you already know is not practice and does not need to be. It is why most people picked up the instrument.
- **Learning new material.** Reading through a piece, working out an arrangement, finding fingerings. Exploratory work tolerates length far better than repair.
- **Stamina.** If the goal involves a forty-minute set, at some point you have to play for forty minutes without stopping.
- **Playing with other people.** A rehearsal runs as long as it runs, and what it builds — listening, holding your part, recovering mid-song — is not available alone in a room.

The mistake is counting those hours as practice and then wondering why the stuck bar is still stuck. Keep them in a separate column: a week with four hours of playing and eighty minutes of repair is a good week, and the eighty minutes is what moves the bar.

### Days with almost no time

Some days you have four minutes between two obligations. Four minutes beats zero, but only if all four go to one thing.

- **3 minutes.** The single hardest join in what you are working on, slowly, correctly. Nothing else gets touched.
- **1 minute.** One cold pass of it, no retries, so the day produces a verdict instead of a feeling.

Skip the warm-up, skip repertoire, skip the ladder: each needs more repetitions than four minutes contains.

On a day with genuinely no minutes, the useful move is not a guilty two minutes with the guitar on your lap. It is thirty seconds with a note: write tomorrow's target in a sentence containing a location. Choosing the target is the one part of practice that is easier away from the instrument.

### Making the number stick

Two counts matter more than session length: how many days a week you pick up the instrument, and how many end with a recorded verdict. Session length is what you adjust to protect those two. A forty-minute session that costs you the next two days was not really forty minutes.

For the weekly structure this sits inside — which blocks get cut first when the clock shrinks — see the [intermediate practice routine](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-routine-intermediate). For what to do inside the repair block once you are in it, [how to practice guitar effectively](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-effectively) is the companion piece to this one.

Strumly's guide to [designing a practice routine](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine) takes the same problem from the scheduling side, and it has a companion piece on [practicing guitar with an AI coach](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/practicing-guitar-with-an-ai-coach).

### Common questions

#### Is 30 minutes a day enough to get good at guitar?

Thirty attentive minutes a day is enough to keep moving, and for most players it is more than they currently get. It does not set the ceiling; the goal does that. Thirty minutes aimed at one passage will fix that passage, and the same thirty spread across five ambitions will fix none of them.

#### Should I practice every day, or take rest days?

Most days is the better default. Past the first few weeks, the limit on a session is attention rather than tissue recovery, so a day off is a scheduling decision. In the first weeks, fingertips are still toughening: keep sessions short, spread them across the day, and stop when a fingertip is sore. Pain at any stage is a reason to stop: hand, wrist or forearm pain gets looked at, not practiced through.

#### Does two hours a day improve you twice as fast as one?

No, because the attentive part of two hours is not twice the attentive part of one. Past the point where you can tell a clean repetition from a dirty one, the extra time rehearses the mistake instead of removing it. If you have two hours, split them and give the halves different jobs.

#### How long until I hear progress?

That depends on the goal, and no honest answer arrives in weeks. What you can do is make the answer checkable: record one passage today, work on it for four weeks, record it the same way again, and listen to both. That comparison settles it where a general number cannot.

## A guitar practice schedule that survives a real week.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-schedule

Built around a weekly minute total instead of a daily streak, with one session you defend, a cut order you decide in advance, and a ten-minute version that still does a job.

Updated August 29, 2026

Field Guide No. 08

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

A guitar practice schedule survives a real week when it is built around a weekly minute total instead of a daily streak. Pick a number of minutes you would hit in a bad week rather than a good one. Protect one anchor session at a fixed day and time and defend it the way you would defend a dentist appointment. Let every other session float. Decide in advance what gets cut when the week goes wrong, so that decision is not made at ten at night by whichever part of practice feels worst. Keep a ten-minute version that does one job properly. Then judge the week on whether the minutes landed on the thing you are trying to change — missed days included, because they happen in every real week and are not failure.

The schedule that collapses on Wednesday usually collapsed on paper, before the week started. It was designed for the week you meant to have.

This page is about the week: the minutes it holds, the one session you defend, and the order you cut things in. What goes inside a session is a different question with two different answers depending on where you are: [how long to practice each day](https://guitarhub.org/how-long-to-practice-guitar-each-day) sizes a single session and says what belongs in ten, twenty-five or sixty minutes, and [the intermediate practice routine](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-routine-intermediate) gives the five blocks a session holds once the beginner gains have run out. This page is the container for both.

### Why rigid daily schedules break

Thirty minutes every day at the same time describes what a settled practice looks like from the outside, which makes it a poor instruction for building one. Three things go wrong.

**It cannot represent a partial day.** A schedule that only knows practiced and did not practice turns a fifteen-minute Tuesday into a miss, and being marked a failure for showing up is a reliable way to stop showing up.

**Every session is the same size.** So the work that needs a long block — recording a full take, deciding what actually breaks, resetting a tempo ladder — never gets scheduled on purpose. It lands on whichever evening feels roomy, which is to say rarely.

**It fails all at once.** Miss two days and the plan is no longer the plan you agreed to, and there is no defined way back into it. Most people do not resume a broken schedule. They wait for Monday, then for the first of the month.

### Design the week around a total, not a streak

Replace thirty minutes a day with a weekly figure: a hundred and fifty minutes this week. The unit of the plan becomes the week, and the day becomes a place to put minutes. A skipped Tuesday is no longer a hole; it is minutes still on the table, and minutes can move. A streak cannot move — it can only break.

Pick the number from evidence, not intention. Count what you actually did over the last three weeks, including the fifteen-minute evenings, and make the worst of the three your budget. A budget you clear is a schedule you keep. A budget set from your best week is the streak problem with extra arithmetic.

Then make the sessions unequal on purpose. A hundred and fifty minutes might be one forty-five, two twenty-fives, and the rest in tens. Expensive work goes in the long session; cheap, repeatable work goes in the short ones.

One rule keeps this from becoming an accounting exercise: minutes count only when they went to the thing you are trying to change. Twenty minutes playing what you already play well is a good evening, and it is not a deposit. Strumly's guide to [designing a practice routine](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine) covers what belongs inside the blocks once the week has a shape.

### Protect one anchor session

An anchor is one session a week with a fixed day, a fixed time, and a job that justifies its length. Everything else floats around it. One anchor, not three: a second is not twice the protection, it is a session you feel guilty about.

#### Choosing the slot

- **Fewest dependencies wins.** A slot that needs nobody else's cooperation survives more weeks than a better one that needs three people to hold their plans.
- **Earlier than feels necessary.** Sunday morning survives. Thursday at nine at night competes with a whole week of accumulated tiredness.
- **Not against something you would rather do.** A slot that makes you win an argument with yourself every week will eventually lose one.

#### What goes in it

The work that cannot be done in fragments. One full take of the piece, recorded and listened back. Naming the single repair target for the week. Setting or resetting a [tempo ladder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) for the passage that is failing. Anything that needs a run-up, or that produces a decision the short sessions spend the week executing.

The rule that makes it an anchor: if exactly one session happens this week, it is this one. Which means when Wednesday comes under threat, you do not move the anchor to cover it. You let Wednesday go.

### Decide the cut order before you need it

At ten at night on a bad Wednesday you will cut whatever is least pleasant, and that is almost always the repair work — the one part that changes your playing. So the order gets decided in daylight, once.

- **New material goes first.** Starting a new song is the most expensive item in the week and the least urgent. It is also the hardest to give up, because opening something new feels like progress.
- **Then the long warm-up.** Keep two minutes of it. A warm-up is a ramp onto the work; a twelve-minute one has quietly become the session.
- **Then full run-throughs.** A run-through is measurement, and measurement is expensive in minutes. One a week is enough to see whether the repair is holding.
- **Then volume on the repair target**, but never the target itself. Six attentive repetitions beat twenty distracted ones, and six fit inside a short session.

Two things never get cut: the anchor session, and the recording that makes the month comparable at the end.

Writing the order down means a bad week produces a smaller version of the same plan instead of a different plan. That is the whole trick. Plans rarely die of one bad week. They die of being improvised four weeks in a row.

### Where a ten-minute day sits in the week

A ten-minute session is not a compressed full session, and the scheduling question about it is narrower than what to put in it. It is whether the ten minutes count. They do, on one condition: that the minutes came out of the week total rather than out of nowhere, so a run of short days shows up as a light week instead of as a plateau.

So log it as ten, not as a session. Four ten-minute days and one anchor is a real ninety-minute week and should be read as one. The same week recorded as five sessions reads like a productive one that somehow produced nothing, and the next decision you make from it will be the wrong one.

What those ten minutes should actually contain is the other page's question, and [how long to practice each day](https://guitarhub.org/how-long-to-practice-guitar-each-day) answers it in a shape you can run. For sizes in between, the odd thirty-five a real week hands you, the [practice session builder](https://guitarhub.org/session) takes the minutes you have and the one thing you are fixing and returns blocks that add up to exactly that number, dropping the ones whose share came out too small to be worth starting rather than shrinking all of them.

### Missed days are part of the plan

You will miss days. Work, illness, family, travel, and plain flatness. A schedule that treats those as anomalies will be wrong most weeks, and a plan that is wrong most weeks stops being consulted.

Take the same week under both designs: you practice on four days out of seven and the minutes add up to what you intended. Under a daily schedule that is three failures. Under a weekly total it is a completed week. Same playing, two verdicts, and only one is still in use next Monday.

A streak also gets more expensive the longer it runs, so a single break starts to feel like an ending rather than a Tuesday. A weekly total has nothing to break; its worst outcome is a week under budget, which is a number and not a verdict on you. The only miss that costs you the month is the one you convert into a decision to stop.

### Restarting after a week you missed

Do not start the plan over. It is the most expensive response to a cheap event, and it resets the thing that took real work to build: knowing exactly what is broken and how slowly you have to play it. Assume the week cost you some tempo and none of the diagnosis.

- **Keep the goal.** A missed week is the worst moment to choose a new finish line. The new one looks exciting and the old one now smells of failure, which is a feeling about last week rather than a fact about the goal.
- **Re-take the last thing you were working on, cold.** Write down the tempo. It will be lower than where you left off. That is information about where to start, not a judgment.
- **Drop the ladder a few steps, not to the bottom.** Climb from the tempo you just measured, not the one you remember.
- **Repeat the last week you completed**, not the week the calendar says you are on. A repeated week costs seven days. A restart costs the month.
- **Do not double next week to catch up.** A double week is a heavy week, a heavy week fails on Wednesday, and that manufactures the second missed week.

It is also why a month of practice is counted in weeks of the plan rather than consecutive calendar days. The [30-day guitar challenge](https://guitarhub.org/30-day-guitar-challenge) is judged on two recordings of the same thing under the same conditions. A missed week moves the second date; it does not void the first recording.

### What this looks like on paper

One week at a hundred and fifty minutes, for a player working on a single failing passage.

- **Sunday, 45 minutes — the anchor.** Full take, recorded and listened back. Name this week's repair target. Set the tempo ladder for it.
- **Tuesday, 25 minutes.** Repair target, climbing the ladder. No run-through.
- **Thursday, 25 minutes.** Repair target, then reconnect it to the section around it.
- **Two floating tens.** One repair each, on whichever two days actually exist.
- **One open 35.** Repertoire, new material, or a session that got missed. Deliberately the largest block after the anchor and the first on the cut list, so a bad week has somewhere to take its losses.

The bad-week version is the anchor cut to thirty minutes, two tens, and nothing else: fifty minutes, still pointed at the same passage, still ending with a tempo written down. The same plan at a smaller size, which is the property that matters.

### The schedule is only a container

A week with good structure and nothing worth putting in it is still wasted. The schedule decides when you practice and how the week absorbs damage. What goes inside comes from a diagnosis: one finish line, one thing that breaks, one repair target at a time.

The [30-day breakthrough planner](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough) turns one goal into four weeks and names the evidence each week has to produce — the material this schedule carries. It needs no account. If the harder question is what to work on rather than when, Strumly's guide to [practicing guitar with an AI coach](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/practicing-guitar-with-an-ai-coach) covers turning a vague sense that something is off into a specific answer.

Build the week from the worst version of itself. A schedule that only works on a good week has not been tested against the only kind of week you reliably get.

## Why you cannot play it fast yet.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/why-cant-i-play-guitar-fast

A speed ceiling is a diagnosis, not a verdict. Five causes, the tell that reveals each one in your own playing, and the fix that moves it.

Updated August 29, 2026

Field Guide No. 09

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

You cannot play it fast yet because the motion you are repeating is not the motion the tempo needs. A speed ceiling is almost never a talent limit or a rep-count problem. It is one of five things: practicing at a tempo where the motion has already broken down, tension in the fretting or picking hand, the two hands landing at different moments, speeding up a passage that is not yet accurate, and never spending time in the narrow band just below the ceiling. Each has a tell you can check today and a different fix. More of the same practice will not move any of them.

### A ceiling is a fact about the motion

Fast playing is mostly the same motion made smaller, timed more exactly, and produced with less effort. What changes most between 90 and 160 BPM is the tolerance. A finger that travels an inch has time for that at 90 and does not at 160, so a motion that fit before stops fitting and the passage breaks in the same place every time. Some motions do not scale at all: above a certain speed the hand may need a different motion, such as a picking stroke that moves from the wrist or forearm instead of the fingers, and slowing the old one down will not reveal the new one. A ceiling belongs to a motion, not to a player: you might run sixteenths at 130 in one riff and stall at 95 in another.

### Why “just play it slow” is incomplete

Slow practice helps only if the slow motion is the same motion, and often it is not. At a comfortable tempo you have time to lift fingers high, press harder than the note needs, re-aim the pick, and gather yourself before the hard bar. None of that fits at speed, and repetition builds whatever you repeat: slow practice full of large motions builds a motion with a low ceiling, and builds it well.

Two questions make slow practice honest.

- **Is this a smaller version of the fast motion, or a different one?** Fingers stay near the strings, the pick keeps its angle and its short distance, and nothing pauses before the difficult bar. If any of that is untrue, you are rehearsing something that cannot scale.
- **Does the shape survive one step up?** Add a small increase and watch the same list. If the fingers start flying or the wrist locks, the tempo you own is lower than the number you use.

The click is what makes any of this measurable: [practicing guitar with a metronome](https://guitarhub.org/practicing-guitar-with-a-metronome) covers using one honestly, and [how to practice guitar effectively](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-effectively) covers the rest of the session.

### The five causes, the tell, and the fix

#### 1. You practice at a tempo where the motion is already wrong

**The tell.** You can name the tempo where it gets messy, and most of your repetitions happen within a few clicks of it, because that is where the passage feels like work.

**The fix.** Find the tempo you own, as a measurement rather than an opinion: three passes in a row, cold, at the start of a session, no missed notes, no rushing, no mid-phrase recovery. A pass you saved is not a clean pass. Whatever survives is the bottom of your ladder, normally well below the number you called your tempo.

#### 2. You are holding tension you cannot feel

Speed is the rate at which a motion can reverse. A finger pressing harder than the note needs has to stop pressing before it can leave; a locked hand has to be overcome before the pick can change direction. Tension caps how fast a motion turns around, and it accumulates.

**The tells.**

- The forearm burns or the hand cramps within half a minute.
- The pick rotates in your fingers, or you regrip between phrases.
- Passes get worse across a set instead of better. Technique does not degrade over five repetitions; tension does.
- The note after the difficult bit lands late even though the difficult bit worked.

**The fix.** Find your pressure floor: fret a note, release until it buzzes, add back the least pressure that clears it, and play there. Drop the volume too, since loud playing recruits tension in both hands. Scan where you have attention to spare: jaw, shoulder, fretting thumb, pick grip, breath. And end a repetition when the tension arrives rather than pushing to the end of the bar. Pushing through is a repetition of playing tense.

#### 3. Your hands are not landing together

Each hand can be individually competent and jointly wrong. At a low tempo the window for arriving together is wide enough that nobody notices the gap; as the tempo climbs the window narrows and the gap does not. The sound is not wrong notes but a smear: the tail of the previous note under the new attack, or a muted click where the pick beat the finger.

**The tells.**

- Slowly, every note is right. Fast, it is sloppy, and you cannot name which note is wrong.
- It is acceptable clean and unusable with gain. Distortion amplifies what happens between notes, which is where a sync problem lives.
- Picked passages break down while legato ones survive, or the reverse. The failure is in the join.

**The fix** is to take the hands apart at the tempo you want, then rejoin them below it. Mute the strings and play the picking pattern alone at the target tempo: if it is uneven there, the problem is the pattern, not the sync. Then play the passage with no pick, hammering every note: if it is uneven here, the fretting hand is out of time. Put them together slowly enough to hear each attack separately. The tempo where you can hear the seam is where you can close it.

To check the fretting hand on its own with a scorer listening, run the free [three-notes-per-string legato drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/three-note-legato-g-major): one pick per string, two hammer-ons, every note checked for pitch in order, and a coach that tells you when to push the tempo.

One more test: start the passage on an upstroke. If it works one way and collapses the other, the pick direction was never decided. Where the join is between chord shapes, Strumly's guide to [smoother chord transitions](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/smoother-chord-transitions) covers what the hands have to agree on.

#### 4. The passage is not accurate yet

Speed does not produce accuracy. It removes the time you were quietly using to correct.

**The tell, and the most useful one here:** watch where the errors land across four or five passes. A failure in the same place every time is a mechanical problem at that spot, and one of the three causes above will name it. A failure that moves means the passage is not learned yet. The two feel identical from inside the room and need different weeks.

A second tell: you cannot say out loud which finger plays each note, where the shift happens, and which way each pick stroke goes. A passage that was never decided cannot be made automatic, because you play a slightly different one every time.

**The fix.** Decide it — position, fingering, shift points, pick direction — and leave it alone for the week. Then take one pass at the comfortable tempo, no run-up. If you miss, the passage is still under construction, and that is this week's work.

#### 5. You never spend time just under the ceiling

Two habits produce this and they look like opposites: living at the ceiling and nowhere else, so every repetition is a repetition of the passage failing, or living well below it and trying the song tempo once at the end of a session to see whether it has arrived.

Both leave the same range empty, and that range does the work: from a few rungs under your best clean tempo up to it. Fast enough that the motion has to become efficient, slow enough that it stays correct.

**The tell.** Your metronome has two numbers in it, the safe one and the song's one, and nothing between them has had a session of its own.

**The fix.** Put most of a session's tempo work inside that band, and move its top one rung at a time. Which is what a ladder is, and the [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) lays one out from your clean tempo to your target.

### The climb: capped steps, holds, and back-offs

A tempo ladder is the ordered set of tempos between the speed you own and the speed you want, one session per rung. The parts that are not a straight line are what make it hold.

- **The first rung is a measurement, not practice.** You are finding the fastest tempo you can play the passage three times cleanly in a row, cold. Start above it and every later rung is a guess.
- **Steps are capped, not averaged.** No rung asks for more than about a tenth of the tempo you are leaving, and never more than 10 BPM, because hands feel proportion rather than arithmetic.
- **Some rungs repeat the previous tempo.** Reaching a tempo once and owning it are different skills, and the second comes only from repetitions at a speed you reached.
- **One ladder per passage, not per song.** Three spots holding a song back is three ladders.

#### What a back-off rep is for

At least one session goes down on purpose. A back-off drops below the top tempo you reached and climbs back through the rungs you passed, inside one sitting. Three things happen there that a straight climb cannot produce.

- **It finds the rung you skipped.** A ladder climbed once leaves rungs you reached and never owned. Walking back up exposes the one that fails, and that tempo is what the next session works on.
- **It turns a ceiling into a floor.** A number you hit once, on a good day, after warming up, is a ceiling. A number you can arrive at from below, cold, is a floor, and the floor is what shows up when someone is listening.
- **It removes the incentive to protect the number.** Once the top tempo is something you re-earn, there is nothing to defend, and the quiet edits stop: the simplified voicing, the dropped note, the generous definition of clean.

The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) writes that sequence out: enter the tempo you already play cleanly and the tempo you want, choose how many sessions to spend, and it returns the rungs in order with a pass condition on each. Where those sessions sit in a week is a separate question, and Strumly's guide to [designing a practice routine](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine) covers it.

### Two checks before you commit a month

Count the recording against a metronome instead of trusting the number in your head; chasing a tempo the record never played is an avoidable way to fail. And check that you are playing the same part, because fast playing on records is often the easy version: an open string where you are shifting, hammer-ons where you are picking every note.

### What to do this week

- Pick one passage, not a song: the bar or two that breaks, plus a beat either side. Measure its baseline cold, first thing in a session, and write the number down.
- Run the tells. Do the errors sit in one place or move? Is the fifth pass worse than the first? Does the picking pattern hold on muted strings?
- Build the ladder from that baseline to a target you can reach this month, not automatically the tempo on the record.
- At the end, record one pass at the top tempo against a recording made today. That comparison is the evidence.

If nothing in your playing has moved for months, rather than this one passage, start with [why guitar practice plateaus](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-plateau). If you are not sure which it is, the [practice plateau diagnostic](https://guitarhub.org/diagnose) ends with a named blocker.

## How to memorize a song on guitar.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/how-to-memorize-songs-on-guitar

Close the page sooner than feels comfortable, learn the map before the notes, and drill the seams between sections rather than the sections themselves.

Updated August 29, 2026

Field Guide No. 10

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

Memorize a song on guitar by learning its form before its notes, working in named chunks of four to eight bars, drilling the joins between those chunks as items in their own right, and testing recall cold the next day with the tab out of sight. Reading the tab again is the one thing that feels like memorizing and is not: while the page is open it does the remembering for you. Memory is built at the moment you do not know what comes next and have to produce it anyway, and every glance at the page skips that moment.

### Why reading the tab on repeat does not stick

Playing from tab and playing from memory are different skills. With the page open you are converting symbols into motions in real time. Take it away and you have to produce the next bar with no prompt. The two feel similar while you do them, which is why a player can run a song many times off the page and still be lost the first time it is closed.

Recognition is cheap, and it feels exactly like knowing. Retrieval is the expensive version, and the only way to train it is to attempt it and be wrong sometimes. The pause where you cannot find the next chord is the repetition that counts.

So remove the cue earlier than is comfortable. Put the tablet face down or the sheet on the floor, because anything inside your eye-line gets used without a decision. Then withdraw the support in steps:

- Full tab or notation, where you start.
- Chord and section names only, on one line of paper.
- Section names only, in order, nothing about the notes.
- Nothing on the stand at all.

Playing along with the recording is the same crutch in audio form: it tells you what is coming and holds the tempo. Learn the song silent, then put the record on to find out whether you were right.

### Finger memory and knowing the form are two different things

When a song falls apart from memory it is usually the map that went rather than the notes, and the two fail in different ways.

#### Finger memory

Finger memory is a chain of motions, each one cued by the movement before it: fast, automatic, and needing no attention. It is brittle in one way. Break the chain and there is no obvious way back in, which is why one wrong chord can take the next thirty seconds of a part you have played hundreds of times.

#### The form

The form is the map you can say out loud away from the instrument: which sections exist, in what order, how many times each repeats, and how it ends. It is slower than finger memory, and it is what lets you re-enter after a break. Someone who knows the form can be lost for two bars and still arrive at the top of the chorus on time.

Write it on one line, with bar counts:

Intro 4 | Verse 16 | Chorus 8 | Verse 16 | Chorus 8 | Solo 16 | Chorus 8 | Chorus 8 | Outro 4

The repeat counts are worth being pedantic about. The thing that ends a song you would say you know is rarely a wrong note. It is one chorus too many, or leaving the second verse eight bars early because it felt like the first. Next to each change, note the cue that announces it: a drum fill, a word in the lyric, a chord that appears nowhere else. Where you hesitate saying the line out loud is where you will hesitate playing it.

The [song readiness score](https://guitarhub.org/readiness) keeps this as a check of its own, separate from anything about your hands. Reading the form and knowing it feel identical while the page is open.

### Chunk by section, not by however far you got

A chunk is a complete musical unit with a beginning and an end, usually four to eight bars. Not five minutes of work, and not the stretch you reached before you got bored. Give each chunk a name you would use out loud, and use the same names every session.

- **Two or three chunks per session, at most.** A chunk is done for the day once you can play it twice, cold, with nothing on the stand. More repetitions that afternoon measure how long you can hold something in the front of your mind.
- **Stop starting at the top.** Bar one every time gives the intro a repetition on every pass and the last section almost none. The intro of a half-learned song is always its strongest part, which tells you about the rehearsal order, not the song.
- **Learn it backwards.** Take the final chunk first, then add the one before it and play to the end. Every pass finishes on familiar ground, and endings stop being the part you have played twice.
- **Separate technical trouble from memory trouble.** A section that fails because it is hard is not a memory job. Take it out and repair it, which is what the [four-stage loop](https://guitarhub.org/method) is for, then bring it back.

### The joins are the song

The experience that sends people back to the tab: every section is fine on its own, and the song still stops. A section drilled in isolation comes with its own run-up. You knew it was coming, your hand was in position, the tempo was set. In the song it arrives cold, out of whatever the previous bar left behind.

So list the joins and practice those instead. Six sections gives five joins, plus one more for every repeat, and a chorus into a second chorus is its own item because the exit is different. That list is where the song breaks.

- **Shrink the join to two bars.** The last bar of one section and the first bar of the next. Loop it until the change is boring rather than occasionally correct.
- **Then widen to four.** Two bars either side, so approach and landing are both in the loop.
- **Chain forward one link at a time.** First into second, second into third, then first into second into third.
- **Give each join a cue.** The join is where you consult the map, so it needs something to consult: a lyric, a fill, a bass note, a hand shape.

If a join fails for physical reasons rather than memory ones, the fix is speed rather than repetition. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) turns one change into a starting speed, a target and the steps between, and Strumly covers what to change with your hands in its guide to [smoother chord transitions](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/smoother-chord-transitions).

### The cold-start test

A cold start is the first thing you do with the guitar that day: no warm-up, no run-up, no page, no backing track. Pick it up, name a section, and play from there. One attempt, because the second is a different and much easier test.

Run it the next day rather than the same session. Inside a session you are partly holding the song in the front of your mind, and that version evaporates overnight. It is also the honest question, because the moments when somebody asks you to play do not come with a warm-up.

The test gets harder in a fixed order:

- Start at the top, cold, and get to the end without stopping.
- Start from a middle section you choose, cold, with no run-up.
- Have somebody else name the section, so you cannot pick a favorite.

Score it pass or fail and write down where it came apart. Being able to start only from bar one is a diagnosis rather than a general weakness: the song is one long chain instead of a set of parts you know. The [readiness checklist](https://guitarhub.org/readiness) scores cold starts alongside nine other checks and hands back the single heaviest one you have not passed.

### Recover mid-song instead of restarting

Stopping at a mistake is a rehearsed skill like any other. If every repetition ends where the error is, the error is the ending you have practiced most. That is how a player arrives at playing for somebody with the first eight bars solid, the last eight barely known, and a reflex to stop the moment a chord goes wrong.

Recovery is not playing without mistakes. It is keeping time while your hands are wrong and re-entering at the next landmark. Two rules, both decided before the take.

- **Protect the beat, not the notes.** Strumming muted strings in time for two bars is a recovery. A silence while you find the shape is a breakdown, and more audible than the chord that caused it.
- **Aim at the next landmark.** The downbeat of the next bar if you can reach it, the top of the next section if you cannot. Going back to repair the note you dropped costs the four bars after it as well.

Practice it directly, because it will not turn up on its own: play the song through and fumble one chord on purpose while the strumming hand keeps moving. It feels ridiculous, which is the point. You are training the response, not the mistake.

### How to keep a song once you have it

Songs decay in a predictable order. The riff comes back quickly and the form goes first: section order, repeat counts, ending. A song learned in spring and untouched since midsummer is usually not lost. Its map has gone while the motions stayed.

Maintenance is therefore a cold take rather than a rehearsal. One pass, nothing on the stand, no restarts, early in the session, and then you stop whether or not it was any good. Running it again turns maintenance back into practice.

- **Keep a written list** of every song you would claim to know. Your memory of what you can play is as unreliable as your memory of the songs.
- **Rotate by neglect.** Two or three a session, chosen because you have not touched them in longest, not because they are the ones you enjoy.
- **Refresh the map, not the notes.** Every few weeks, say the form out loud away from the guitar. A minute per song, and it catches the thing that actually goes.
- **Repair the chunk, not the song.** When a maintenance take fails, fix the chunk or the join that broke. Relearning the whole thing is the expensive way to fix eight bars.

Where this sits in a week is a scheduling question. The [intermediate practice routine](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-routine-intermediate) gives repertoire under pressure and the cold-start test blocks of their own, and Strumly's guide to [designing a practice routine](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine) covers building the week around them.

### What to do this week

- Write the form of one song on a single line, with bar counts and the cue for each change. Say it out loud with the guitar down.
- List the joins, and loop the two worst as two-bar fragments.
- Tomorrow, pick the guitar up first thing and start from a middle section, cold, with nothing on the stand. Write down what happened.
- Play one take with a deliberate fumble in it, keeping the beat straight through the mistake.

None of that makes the song feel finished faster. It makes the point at which you can say you know it something you can check: page closed, on a day you did not warm up.

## How to actually practice with a metronome.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/practicing-guitar-with-a-metronome

Playing along with a click measures how well you follow a sound. Testing against it measures your time. This is how to run the second one.

Updated August 29, 2026

Field Guide No. 11

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

A metronome is a measuring instrument, not an accompanist. Playing along with it mostly tests how well you follow a sound, which is a different skill from keeping time. The version that changes your playing is the opposite: you keep the time, and the click checks it. Make the click sparse enough that the timekeeping is genuinely yours, put the passage against it, and listen to the gap between your note and the click. Where that gap opens is the fault. A metronome does not make you steady. It makes unsteadiness audible.

### What a click actually reveals

A metronome does one thing: it produces an event at a fixed interval. It has no opinion about your playing and no way to correct you. All of the information sits in the distance between the click and your note, and that distance carries three readings.

- **Direction.** Are you consistently in front of the click, or consistently behind it? The two have different causes and different fixes, and guessing wrong costs you the week.
- **Location.** Which beat, which bar, which side of a chord change. A timing problem that is really one transition is a small job. A timing problem everywhere is a different job.
- **Shape.** Does the gap grow steadily from the top, or open in one spot and close again? Steady growth is a tempo you cannot hold. A spike is a passage you cannot play yet.

A click on every beat gives you almost none of this. It re-anchors you four times a bar, so you never drift far enough for the drift to be visible. That is why quarter notes under a strummed song feel reassuring and teach so little: they confirm you can stay within a beat of a reference, which you already could.

### Subdivision is the part you are missing

Time is not the beats but the space between them, and that space is where almost everything you play lives. With the click on the beat, the beat is the only place you have a reference. Offbeats, sixteenths, the back half of a strum pattern, the moment you release a chord: all unsupervised.

So supervise it yourself. Count the subdivision out loud while you play, in whatever unit the passage moves in. Out loud matters, because counting in your head quietly stops when a bar gets hard, and the bar that stops you counting is the bar you were looking for.

Match the click to the passage, not to the smallest note in it. A click on every sixteenth under a sixteenth-note figure removes the thing you are building, which is your own even division of the beat. Click the eighths and let your hands own the sixteenths.

### Move the click to expose your real time-keeping

#### Beats two and four

Halve the metronome tempo and hear each click as the backbeat. For a piece at 120, set the metronome to 60 and count four beats with the clicks landing on two and four. Beats one and three are yours to place now. Getting in takes a few attempts, because starting against a click that is not beat one is genuinely harder, and drift shows up within a bar or two rather than never: a rushed beat one has nothing propping it up.

#### Beat one only

Quarter the tempo. At 120 that is a click at 30, one per bar in common time, near the bottom of the range on many metronomes. You are keeping three beats out of four, so one rushed bar puts your downbeat audibly in front of the click instead of merely feeling wrong. This is where most players find their time is fine in the easy bars and moves everywhere else.

#### Bars with no click at all

Sparser than one click per bar needs a metronome that can mute bars, a gap or silence setting if yours has one. Two bars of click, two bars of nothing, repeating. Play through the silence and find out whether you land back on the click or in front of it. For two bars there is no reference at all, and the verdict arrives at once.

#### The click on the offbeat

The hardest placement, and it tests what the others cannot: whether your subdivision is even. Keep the metronome at the quarter-note tempo, count one and two and over it, then flip the count so the clicks land on the ands rather than the numbers. It will invert on you the first several times, snapping back until the click sounds like a downbeat again. That inversion is the test: if your eighths are uneven, the flip has nothing steady to sit on.

### What playing ahead and dragging feel like

#### Playing ahead

The click seems to arrive a moment after you rather than with you, as though the metronome had slowed down. The passage feels urgent and the sensation is one of leaning. Rushing shows up in the easy bars, in the bar after a difficult one, and anywhere the music gets louder. Relief speeds people up as reliably as nerves do.

#### Dragging

The click seems to pull away, and playing feels like chasing something. Dragging sits in the physically expensive bar: the stretch, the barre, the position shift, the first chord after a change your fretting hand has not finished making. It also appears wherever you are still deciding what comes next, because deciding takes time the bar does not have.

#### The combination that costs you

The common pattern is both at once. Rush into the hard bar, drag through it, come out in front again. Across a take the errors cancel, so the average looks fine while the take sounds wrong. Nobody hears an average. They hear the two places where the pulse moved.

One cheap test for direction, once the click is sparse: turn it down until it is only just audible. Land exactly on it and your attack swallows the click, so it seems to vanish. Land off it and you hear two separate events, and their order tells you which way you went.

### Tempo is a measurement, not a target

A number on a metronome means nothing by itself. What makes it a measurement is the condition attached, so write that down beside it. Bars nine to twelve, 84 BPM, three passes in a row, cold, no missed notes and no stopping. That is a reading. Just 84 is a memory, and memory rounds in your favor.

Cold is the load-bearing word: first thing in the session, no run-up, no eight attempts. Best of eight is a ceiling, and a ceiling is not what shows up when you play for someone. What you can repeat cold is a floor, and the floor is the only number worth building on.

A number with no condition drifts upward on its own. The tempo you hit once on the twentieth try is your tempo by Thursday, and every session after it is built on a coincidence.

With a real floor and a target, the distance between them is a plan rather than a wish. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) turns those two numbers into an ordered set of sessions: every increase capped, some sessions repeating a tempo instead of adding to it, and at least one that drops below the top speed and climbs back. Reaching a tempo once and owning it are different events.

When the target refuses to arrive however patiently you climb, the ceiling is usually not made of tempo. [What actually limits speed](https://guitarhub.org/why-cant-i-play-guitar-fast) is worth reading before you turn the number up again.

### Four drills, each with a pass condition

Each takes a few minutes and returns a yes or a no. A drill with no pass condition is time near a metronome.

- **The cold three.** First thing in the session, no warm-up: three consecutive clean passes at one tempo. Pass: three in a row, not three out of five. Every other number depends on this one.
- **The silent bar.** Two bars of click, two bars muted, repeating. Pass: four cycles where the click returns exactly where you expected it.
- **The one-question listen.** Record thirty seconds against a sparse click, then listen back for one thing: ahead or behind, and where. Pass: you can name a bar.
- **The handover.** Play the passage with the click, then immediately without it, then a third time with it back on. Pass: the click comes back roughly where your playing left it. A large jump means the click was carrying you.

Run them on GuitarHub's free [tuner and metronome](https://guitarhub.org/practice), which keeps a steady four-beat click at any tempo you set. When you want a verdict on every attack, four free Advanced Lab drills time each hit against the grid through your microphone: [syncopated sixteenths](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/funk-sixteenths), [quarter-note triplets](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/quarter-note-triplets), [the shift from triplets to sixteenths](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/triplet-sixteenth-shift), and [dotted-eighth displacement](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/dotted-eighth-displacement).

### When not to use a metronome

A click answers one narrow question. Pointed at a different one it teaches something you then have to undo.

- **When the problem is not timing.** Tone, vibrato, whether a bend arrives in tune, the balance inside a voicing. A click holds no information about any of them and pulls your attention off what you sat down to fix.
- **When the motion does not exist yet.** A click is a deadline. Give one to a hand that has not made the movement and you get a tense approximation you then have to practice your way out of. Build the motion slowly and freely. Add the clock once it repeats.
- **When the music is not in strict time.** A rubato intro, a free ending, a passage meant to breathe. Practicing those to a click removes the thing they are.
- **When you are playing with a recording or with people.** The recording is the reference, and so is the drummer. A click running against a human is an argument you cannot win.
- **When you can no longer play the piece without one.** That is a dependency, and the handover drill is how you catch it. The cure is not more click. It is the sparse settings above, in order.
- **When you are playing for the pleasure of it.** Not every session is practice, and a measuring instrument is poor company.

### Where the click sits in a week

A metronome is one tool inside a session, not the session. It belongs to the moments when you are testing something specific and want an outside opinion, which is a narrow slice of the week. [The GuitarHub method](https://guitarhub.org/method) puts that slice in order: measure where you are, shrink the problem, put it back under pressure, then record and compare. A click earns its place in the first and third.

Practice moves when an attempt has a specific target and honest feedback attached, which is what a sparse click supplies. There is more on [what that looks like at the instrument](https://guitarhub.org/deliberate-practice-guitar), and on [how to spend a practice hour](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-effectively). Strumly's guide to [designing a practice routine](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine) covers the scheduling side.

One last thing a click cannot do. It tells you that you are late, not why, and the why is almost always somewhere else: a chord shape your hand reaches for a beat too late, a pick stroke starting on the wrong side of the string, a breath you stopped taking four bars ago. Naming that cause is a separate job. Strumly's guide to [practicing with an AI coach](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/practicing-guitar-with-an-ai-coach) covers what that kind of feedback is good for and where it stops.

## A beginner guitar practice routine for the first 90 days.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/beginner-guitar-practice-routine

Twenty minutes a day, three 30-day phases, and a recording on days 1, 30, 60 and 90 that shows you exactly what changed.

Updated October 10, 2026

A beginner guitar practice routine for the first 90 days is 15 to 25 minutes a day, five or six days a week, built from the same five blocks every time: tune, check one chord string by string, time one chord change, strum against a click, and finish by playing something musical. What changes across the 90 days is the material inside the blocks. Days 1 to 30 cover tuning and your first two chords. Days 31 to 60 add the rest of the open chords and a strumming hand that never stops. Days 61 to 90 end with one complete song. Record yourself on day 1 and again on days 30, 60 and 90, and the recordings tell you what worked.

This page is the plan for your first 90 days: what goes in a 20-minute session and how the material changes every 30 days. The lessons themselves live in the [GuitarHub guitar curriculum](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar), which this plan follows stage by stage, and the [A-to-D chord practice routine](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/routine) runs the timer for the daily blocks while you are on your first two chords. Once open chords and a steady strum hold up, the [intermediate guitar practice routine](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-routine-intermediate) takes over with five blocks built around one repair target.

### Why twenty minutes a day beats two hours on Saturday

Two things decide the dose for a beginner, and neither is willpower. The first is your fingertips. Steel strings press thin skin into the fret wire, and the skin toughens through repeated, moderate contact. Short daily sessions build calluses.
