A long weekend session builds blisters, and then a week off while they heal.

The second is sleep. In a 2002 study published in Neuron, Matthew Walker and colleagues trained people on a finger-tapping sequence and found they were faster after a night of sleep, with no additional practice. A chord change is a finger sequence too. Every day you practice gives you another night of that consolidation, which is why six short sessions move a beginner further than one long one with the same total minutes.

So the routine is built for a real weekday: twenty minutes that fit before work or after dinner, and a ten-minute version for the days that collapse.

### The daily twenty minutes

The five blocks stay the same for all 90 days. Only the chords and songs inside them change.

- **Tune (2 minutes).** Use the [guitar tuner](https://guitarhub.org/practice) and check all six strings, low to high: E, A, D, G, B, E. Recheck after every adjustment, because tightening one string pulls the neck and nudges the others.
- **One chord, string by string (3 minutes).** Form the chord, strum it once, then pick each string that belongs in it, one at a time. Any string that buzzes or dies gets fixed before you move on: a fingertip more upright, closer to the fret, or pressing a little firmer.
- **One change against the clock (5 minutes).** Pick one pair of chords and count how many clean changes you make in sixty seconds, strumming once on each arrival. Do two or three rounds and write down the best count. The [chord change guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-change-chords-faster) covers the finger moves that raise that number.
- **Strum against a click (7 minutes).** Set the [metronome](https://guitarhub.org/practice) between 60 and 80 BPM and play the current chords in time, starting with one downstroke per beat. The click decides whether the change arrived on time. Your ear in the moment is too generous.
- **Play something (3 minutes).** A study, a riff, or a song section, played start to finish without stopping. Then write one line: the chord pair, today's one-minute count, and the tempo. The [practice evidence log](https://guitarhub.org/log) keeps that line where you can read the trend.

On a short day, run blocks 1, 3 and 5. When you have more or less than twenty minutes, the [practice session builder](https://guitarhub.org/session) resizes the blocks to the time you actually have.

### Days 1 to 30: tune, hold, and two chords

The first month matches Stage 1 and Stage 2 of the curriculum: Sound Check, then Two Chords, First Study. The goal is small and specific. By day 30 you tune the guitar on your own, play D and A with every string ringing, and hold sixteen bars of steady downstrokes at 80 BPM.

- **Week 1.** How to hold the guitar and the pick, the six open strings by name, tuning, and reading tab and chord boxes. Record your day 1 take: the six open strings, picked one at a time, and whatever chord you can already make. It will sound rough. That is the point of keeping it.
- **Week 2.** The D chord and the A chord, each checked string by string. D sounds from string 4 down to string 1. A sounds from string 5 down to string 1.
- **Weeks 3 and 4.** The D-to-A change with one finger kept in place, one-minute changes every day, and four downstrokes per bar against the click. Finish the month with a two-chord study or song played start to finish.

The [A-to-D chord practice routine](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/routine) is built for exactly this stretch: seven timed blocks, from tuning to two-chord songs, with durations you can edit and your history kept in the browser.

### Days 31 to 60: the open eight and a hand that never stops

Month two matches Stage 3, The Open Eight. You add A minor, E minor and D minor, then the stretch chords E, C and G. With A and D that makes eight open chords, and with a capo they cover songs in many more keys.

The strumming hand changes job at the same time. Instead of one downstroke per beat, it moves down and up in a steady pendulum, down on every beat and up on every “and,” whether or not it touches the strings. That constant motion is what keeps time when a pattern skips a stroke. The [strumming guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-strumming) takes it from straight eighths to the patterns most songs use.

- **Weeks 5 and 6.** Am, Em and Dm, then C to Am and Am to Em as your one-minute pairs. C to Am keeps two fingers exactly where they are, so it climbs quickly.
- **Weeks 7 and 8.** E, C and G. G to C is the hardest change in this set, because no finger stays on the same string and fret, so give it its own one-minute rounds every day.
- **Day 30 and day 60 check.** Record the same passage you will record at the end of the month, at the same tempo, from the same spot. Listen to both takes back to back before you decide how the month went.

### Days 61 to 90: one finished song

The last month turns parts into a piece. Choose one song that uses three or four of your open chords and a strum you can already hold. The finish line is one take from the count-in to the last chord with no stops, recorded on day 90.

- Play the whole song once, slowly, and mark the change that breaks first. That is your target for the week.
- Put that one change on a tempo ladder. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) gives you a starting speed, a target, and the steps between them.
- Reconnect it: play two bars before the change and two bars after, then the whole section, then the whole song.
- Check the song with the [song readiness score](https://guitarhub.org/readiness) before you record the day 90 take, so you know which part is most likely to break.

If the song is solid before day 90, spend five minutes a day on the first scale shape. Stage 4 of the curriculum, The First Scale, picks up there with single notes and alternate picking.

### Run it as a loop: baseline, isolate, reconnect, prove

The 90 days use the same four-stage loop as every other plan on this site. The day 1 recording is your **baseline**. The daily one-minute changes and string checks **isolate** the single change or chord that fails. Playing the change back inside a study or song is where you **reconnect** it. The day 30, 60 and 90 recordings **prove** what moved. The [GuitarHub method](https://guitarhub.org/method) explains each stage and the exit test that tells you it is finished, and the [phone recording guide](https://guitarhub.org/record-guitar-practice-on-phone) covers how to make the four takes comparable.

### Common mistakes in the first 90 days

- **Learning a new chord every day.** A chord is learned when you can change into it in time, not when you can make the shape once. Two chords you can change between beat ten chords you can only hold.
- **Skipping the tuner.** Practicing on an out-of-tune guitar teaches your ear the wrong sound. Two minutes, every session.
- **Practicing through sharp pain.** Tender fingertips are normal in the first weeks. Sharp pain, numbness, or pain in the wrist are stop signals. The [finger pain guide](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-finger-pain) covers the difference and the guitar setup changes that help.
- **Stopping at every mistake.** In block 5, keep going through the error. Restarting trains restarting.
- **Judging progress by feel.** How a session felt depends on how tired you were. The recordings and the one-minute counts are the evidence.

For a second view of the beginner path, Strumly's [beginner guitar learning path](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/beginner-guitar-learning-path) lays out the same early skills in order. When you are ready to set one finish line for a month, the [30-day breakthrough planner](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough) turns it into four weeks of focused practice.

### Questions that come up

#### How long should a beginner practice guitar each day?

Fifteen to twenty-five minutes, five or six days a week. In the first month your fingertips set the limit more than your attention does, and two short sessions in one day beat one long one. Daily contact matters more than session length, because each night of sleep consolidates what the session started.

#### How long until I can play a whole song?

On this plan the first complete song is the target for days 61 to 90, after the eight open chords and steady strumming are in place. A two-chord song with A and D comes earlier, in the first month, and it counts: playing a short piece start to finish without stopping is the skill every later song uses.

#### Should a beginner learn chords or scales first?

Chords first. Open chords and a steady strum let you play real songs within weeks, and songs are what keep a beginner practicing. Single notes and the first scale arrive in the fourth stage of the GuitarHub curriculum, once changes and strumming hold up on their own.

#### What should I do on a day with only ten minutes?

Tune, run one set of one-minute changes on the chord pair you are working on, and play one song or study through once. That keeps the daily contact that builds calluses and consolidates the change, and it takes ten minutes.

## How to change chords faster.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/how-to-change-chords-faster

Fast changes come from moving less, not from moving harder. Keep what can stay, slide what can slide, move the rest as one shape, and leave early.

Updated October 10, 2026

To change chords faster on guitar, move fewer fingers a shorter distance. Keep any finger that sits on the same string and fret in both chords pressed down (an anchor finger). Slide any finger that stays on the same string but moves fret (a guide finger). Move the remaining fingers together as one shape instead of placing them one at a time, and start the move a beat early, while the old chord is still sounding. Measure it with one-minute changes: count how many clean changes you make in sixty seconds, every day, for each chord pair.

The fingerings below use string numbers: string 6 is the thickest, low E, and string 1 is the thinnest, high E. A chord written as x32010 lists the frets from string 6 to string 1, with x for a string you do not play and 0 for an open string.

### Why your changes are slow

A slow change is rarely a slow hand. It is usually one of four habits, and you can see all of them in a phone video of your fretting hand.

- **Fingers lift too far.** Every centimeter a finger travels away from the strings is a centimeter it has to travel back.
- **Fingers land one at a time.** First finger, check, second finger, check. Three separate placements take three times as long as one.
- **Fingers that could stay, leave.** Lifting a finger that belongs in both chords throws away the one landmark you had.
- **The move starts late.** If you only think about the next chord on the beat it is due, you are already behind.

### Anchor fingers: what stays down

An anchor finger sits on the same string and fret in both chords. It never lifts. It keeps your hand located on the neck and leaves fewer fingers to move. Look for anchors first, every time you learn a new pair.

- **C (x32010) and A minor (x02210).** In both shapes the index finger is on string 2 at fret 1 and the middle finger is on string 4 at fret 2. Only the ring finger moves, from string 5 at fret 3 to string 3 at fret 2.
- **D (xx0232) and A (x02220).** Play A with the middle finger on string 4, the index on string 3, and the ring on string 2, all at fret 2. The index is now on string 3 at fret 2 in both chords, so it stays down while the other two fingers trade places. This is the fingering the GuitarHub curriculum teaches for the first change.
- **G (320033) and D (xx0232).** In this version of G the ring finger plays string 2 at fret 3 and the pinky plays string 1 at fret 3. D also has the ring finger on string 2 at fret 3, so it becomes the anchor and the rest of the hand pivots around it.
- **E minor (022000) and G (320003).** Finger E minor with the index on string 5 and the middle finger on string 4. G puts the index on string 5 at fret 2 as well, so it stays while the middle finger moves to string 6 at fret 3 and the ring finger lands on string 1.

Notice that two of those depend on choosing a fingering. When a chord has more than one standard fingering, choose the one that shares a finger with the chords around it in the song.

### Guide fingers: slide, do not lift

A guide finger stays on the same string but moves to a different fret. Instead of lifting it, ease the pressure and slide it along the string, keeping light contact. The string acts as a rail, so the finger arrives in the right place without you looking for it.

The key of A shows it best. Using the A fingering above, the index finger is on string 3 at fret 2 for D, stays there for A, and slides back to fret 1 for E (022100). Across A, D and E, the one, four and five chords in the key of A, the index finger never leaves string 3.

### Shape moves: travel as one unit

When no finger can stay, the fingers that move should move together, already arranged in the next shape. Two pairs show how much of a change this removes.

- **A minor (x02210) to E (022100).** The fingers make the same shape in both chords, one string apart. A minor sits on strings 4, 3 and 2. E is the identical shape on strings 5, 4 and 3. Keep the shape locked and move the whole hand one string toward the ceiling.
- **G (320003) to C (x32010).** Play G with the ring finger on string 6, the middle on string 5, and the pinky on string 1. For C, the ring and middle fingers step across one string together, to string 5 at fret 3 and string 4 at fret 2, and the index lands on string 2 at fret 1. Two fingers moving as a pair is one move, not two.

A useful drill for any pair is the shape drop. Form the destination chord, lift every finger a few millimeters while keeping the shape, hold it in the air for a beat, and drop all the fingers at once. Then strum and check that every string rings. Ten clean drops trains the hand to arrive as a unit.

### Look ahead and leave early

The fretting hand should start moving before the new chord is due. On a four-beat bar, think the name of the next chord on beat 3, and start the move on the last “and” of the bar. Your strumming hand keeps going through the gap. If the last upstroke of the bar catches a few open strings while the fingers travel, that is normal and, at tempo, it sounds like part of the strum.

Your eyes lead too. Once a pair feels familiar, look at where the next chord's anchor or lowest finger lands, a beat before you need it, instead of watching the chord you are holding.

### One-minute changes: the number that tells you

The measurement for all of this is one-minute changes. It is in Stage 2 of the [GuitarHub guitar curriculum](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar), and it works for any pair of chords.

- Choose one pair of chords, for example D and A.
- Form the first chord. That position is zero.
- Start a sixty-second timer. Change to the second chord and strum once: that is one. Change back and strum: two. Keep alternating.
- Count only changes where the chord was fully formed when you strummed. Do not stop to fix a bad one. Just keep going.
- Write down the count with the date. Do two or three rounds per pair and keep the best.

Run it every day for the pairs in the song you are learning. The number moves day by day in a way that your sense of the change does not, and the [practice evidence log](https://guitarhub.org/log) shows the trend once you have three sessions in it. For D and A, the [A-to-D chord practice routine](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar/routine) times both directions for you, starting on A and starting on D.

### Put the change in time

A one-minute count measures speed. A song needs the change on the beat. Once a pair is climbing, move it to the [metronome](https://guitarhub.org/practice):

- At 60 BPM, strum each chord four times (one bar) and change. Four clean bars in a row moves you to the next step.
- Change every two beats.
- Change every beat. This is the hardest step and the one that makes the bar-length change easy at song tempo.
- Raise the tempo in small steps and repeat. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) sets the starting speed, the target, and the steps between.

When the change holds against the click, play it inside the song again: two bars before it, two bars after it, then the full section. The isolated drill only counts once it survives that.

### A ten-minute chord change session

- **1 minute:** check both chords string by string. Fix any string that buzzes.
- **2 minutes:** silent shape drops into each chord, anchors and guides held.
- **3 minutes:** one-minute changes, three rounds, best count written down.
- **3 minutes:** the change against the click, four beats, then two.
- **1 minute:** play the change inside the song or study it came from.

Strumly's guide to [smoother chord transitions](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/smoother-chord-transitions) goes further into finding which single finger is arriving late. When the change you need is into a barre chord, the [barre chord guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-play-barre-chords) covers the F chord and the moves in and out of it, and the [strumming guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-strumming) keeps the other hand steady while the changes speed up.

### Questions that come up

#### Is it OK to let the open strings ring while I change chords?

Yes. On the last eighth note before a new chord, many players lift the old shape and strum whatever is open while the fingers travel. At song tempo it reads as part of the strum. What does not work is stopping the strumming hand to wait for the fretting hand, because that breaks the time.

#### Should I look at my fretting hand during a change?

While you learn the shape, yes. Once the one-minute count for a pair is climbing, start looking at the next chord's position a beat early, then practice a round with your eyes up. A change you can only make while watching is not finished yet.

#### Which chord change should a beginner practice first?

D to A. The index finger can stay on string 3 at fret 2 for both shapes, so only two fingers move. It is the first change in the GuitarHub curriculum. After it, C to Am is a quick pair to add, because two fingers stay exactly where they are.

#### How many one-minute changes is good?

Work it out from the song. At 100 BPM in 4/4 there are 25 bars a minute, so a song that changes chord once per bar needs 25 changes a minute, and one that changes every two beats needs 50. Aim above the song's number, so the change has time to spare.

## Sore fingertips, hand pain, and when to stop.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/guitar-finger-pain

Tender fingertips in the first weeks are part of learning guitar. Pain anywhere else is information. Here is how to tell them apart and what to change.

Updated October 10, 2026

Sore fingertips are normal when you start guitar or come back after a break. Steel strings press the skin of your fingertip pads into the fret wire, and the skin responds by toughening into calluses over the first weeks of regular playing. Keep sessions short and frequent, press only as hard as the note needs, and have the guitar set up so the strings sit low. Sharp pain, numbness, tingling, or pain in your wrist, thumb, forearm or elbow is a different thing. Stop playing and, if it does not settle with rest, see a doctor or a hand therapist.

### The safety rule, first

Tenderness on the pads of the fretting fingertips is expected. These are stop signals:

- Sharp, stabbing or burning pain anywhere in the hand or arm.
- Numbness, tingling, or pins and needles in the fingers or thumb.
- Aching in the wrist, thumb base, forearm, elbow or shoulder that is still there the next day.
- Swelling, or a joint that looks or feels different.
- A finger that catches, clicks or locks as it bends.
- Weaker grip, or fingers that stop doing what you tell them.
- A blister or cracked fingertip that turns red, hot, swollen or weeps.

If any of these appear, stop playing for the day. If they persist after rest, or come back each time you play, book an appointment with your doctor, a sports medicine clinic, or a hand therapist (an occupational or physical therapist who specializes in hands). Some clinics specialize in performing arts medicine and treat musicians every day. Do not use painkillers to keep playing through pain. Pain is the signal that tells you what to change.

### Why fingertips hurt at the start

To sound a note, you press a string until it touches the fret. The string is a thin steel wire under tension, and all that force lands on a small patch of skin. The skin on an untrained fingertip is not built for it, so it gets tender, and if you overdo it, it blisters.

With repeated, moderate pressure, the outer layer of skin thickens into calluses. Calluses spread the load and make pressing painless. The key word is moderate. Too little playing and the skin never adapts. Too much at once and you get a blister, which forces days off and sends you back toward the start.

### The callus timeline

For most players who practice a little every day, the first week is the most tender, the sharp soreness fades over the following few weeks, and the calluses keep developing for months. Calluses soften when you stop playing, which is why a two-week break feels like a partial restart and why returning players feel it too.

The fastest route through this stage is frequency, not volume:

- **Play 10 to 15 minutes, two or three times a day** in the first weeks, instead of one long session. The [practice session builder](https://guitarhub.org/session) turns a short window into timed blocks so a ten-minute session still covers the important work.
- **Stop at the first sign of heat or stinging** in a fingertip. That is the point just before a blister.
- **Leave blisters alone.** Do not pop them and do not play on them. Let them heal fully before you play on that finger again.
- **Do not peel or bite calluses.** If a callus develops a rough edge that snags strings, smooth it gently with a fine nail file.
- **Keep fretting-hand nails short**, so you can press with the fingertip pad instead of the soft part further back.
- **Play before a long shower or dishes, not straight after.** Skin softened by hot water wears faster under the strings.

### Press less: the minimum-pressure test

Most beginners press several times harder than a note needs, and the extra force goes straight into the fingertip, the thumb and the wrist. Find the real number with this test:

- Fret a single note, for example string 3 at fret 2, and pick it repeatedly in a slow, steady rhythm.
- Gradually ease off the pressure until the note starts to buzz or choke.
- Add back just enough pressure for a clear note. That is all the note needs.
- Repeat on each finger, then on a whole chord.

Two placement details reduce the pressure further. Put the fingertip just behind the fret wire, not in the middle of the space between frets: the closer you are to the fret, the less force a clean note takes. And press with the tip of the finger, keeping the finger arched instead of letting it collapse flat.

Watch the thumb. A thumb clamped hard against the back of the neck is a common source of aching at the base of the thumb and in the web of the hand. The thumb is a counterweight, not a vise. On an electric guitar with a strap, or when seated with the guitar resting against your body, you can let the weight of your arm draw the fingers into the strings, which takes most of the load off the thumb.

### Fix the guitar, not just the hand

A guitar with high strings makes every note harder to press, and plenty of entry-level guitars leave the factory that way. A setup by a guitar technician adjusts the neck, the string height at the bridge, and the nut, and is one of the best-value changes a beginner can make.

- **High action.** If there is a visible gap between the strings and the frets up the neck, the action is likely high. A tech measures and lowers it.
- **High nut slots.** If chords near the headstock are much harder than the same shapes higher up, try a capo at fret 1. If the first-position chords suddenly feel easy, the nut slots are a likely cause, and a tech can lower them.
- **String gauge.** Lighter strings need less force. On an acoustic, a set labeled extra light or custom light is gentler than the common light gauge. Ask the tech to adjust the setup for the new strings.
- **Old strings.** Corroded strings feel rough and wear fingertips faster. Fresh strings feel smoother.
- **Nylon strings.** A classical guitar with nylon strings is much softer on the fingertips, and is a good choice for a player whose fingertips are the main obstacle.

### Warm up the whole hand

A short warm-up spreads the load before you ask the hand for barre chords or long stretches. Three to five minutes is enough:

- Open and close both hands slowly ten times, then let the arms hang and shake out loosely.
- Play a slow chromatic pattern on one string, frets 1, 2, 3 and 4 with fingers 1, 2, 3 and 4, at 60 BPM on the [metronome](https://guitarhub.org/practice), using the lightest pressure that gives a clean note.
- Strum a few easy open chords before any barre chord or stretch.

Posture matters as much as the warm-up. Keep the fretting wrist as close to neutral as the chord allows rather than sharply bent, keep the shoulders down, and take a short break every 20 to 30 minutes in longer sessions. When seated, a footstool or a strap set so the guitar sits at the same height as when you stand keeps the neck where your hand can reach it without the wrist folding.

### Barre chords are the next sore spot

The first barre chords bring a new kind of soreness: the side of the index finger and the base of the thumb. The fix is leverage rather than grip strength, and the [barre chord guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-play-barre-chords) covers it step by step. Aching that spreads into the wrist or forearm during barre practice is one of the stop signals above, not a sign to push harder.

### Coming back with a smaller dose

When you return after a blister, a sore week, or years away, start lower than feels necessary: two short sessions a day, easy chords, and the minimum-pressure test at the start of each one. The [guide to coming back to guitar](https://guitarhub.org/coming-back-to-guitar) lays out the first 30 days, and the [beginner practice routine](https://guitarhub.org/beginner-guitar-practice-routine) uses the same short daily blocks for the first 90.

### Questions that come up

#### Should I keep playing with sore fingertips?

Tender fingertips in your first weeks are expected, and short sessions through mild tenderness are how calluses form. Stop for the day when a fingertip feels hot, stinging or raw, or when a blister starts. Never play through a blister. Pain anywhere other than the fingertip pads is a different matter: stop and read the warning signs on this page.

#### How long until my fingers stop hurting?

For most players who practice briefly and often, the sharp soreness eases within the first few weeks, and calluses keep thickening for months after that. Long gaps reset part of the progress, because calluses soften when you stop playing. Daily short sessions get you through this stage fastest.

#### Do nylon strings hurt less than steel strings?

Yes. Nylon strings on a classical guitar sit at lower tension and are softer under the fingertip, so most beginners find them gentler. Lighter-gauge steel strings and a professional setup also reduce the pressure each note needs.

#### Is it normal for my wrist or thumb to hurt after playing?

No. Fingertip tenderness is normal; aching in the wrist, thumb, forearm or elbow is a warning sign that something in your posture, grip or guitar setup is overloading the hand. Rest it, check your thumb pressure and wrist angle, and if the pain is still there after a day or two of rest, see a doctor or a hand therapist.

## Record your practice on a phone, and hear what changed.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/record-guitar-practice-on-phone

The phone in your pocket is the most useful practice tool you own. Set it up once, record the same way every time, and every take becomes evidence.

Updated October 10, 2026

To record your guitar practice on a phone, put the phone about an arm's length in front of the guitar, pointed at the spot where the neck joins the body, with the end that holds its microphone toward the guitar. Set the level by playing your loudest part first and moving the phone back if it distorts. Then keep everything the same for every take: the spot, the distance, the room, the passage and the tempo. Record a full take on day 1 and the same take on day 30, listen to them back to back, and score both against the same five things: time, clean notes, changes, dynamics, and stops.

This page is about recording as practice evidence: takes you compare to measure progress. For how a recording space shapes your guitar sound, see [how to hear the room in a guitar recording](https://guitarhub.org/resources/recording-guitar-room-sound).

### Why a recording beats your memory

While you play, your attention is on the next chord, not on the last one, and you hear the guitar from behind it, through your own body. A recording puts you in the audience. The rushed change, the buzzing string and the gap before the chorus are obvious on playback and nearly invisible in the moment.

A recording also fixes the comparison problem. Memory of how you sounded a month ago drifts toward how you sound now, so progress disappears. Two takes recorded the same way do not drift. That is why the [GuitarHub method](https://guitarhub.org/method) starts and ends on a recording: the **baseline** stage is a take that shows where the playing breaks, and the **prove** stage is the same take a month later. The isolate and reconnect stages in between are the work the two takes measure.

### Set up once, then never change it

A comparison only works when the only thing that changed is your playing. Decide the setup once and write it down.

- **Acoustic guitar.** Phone about 60 to 90 centimeters (two to three feet) in front of the guitar, at the height of the neck joint, angled toward where the neck meets the body. Pointing straight into the sound hole gives a boomy, bass-heavy take.
- **Electric guitar through an amp.** Phone about 30 to 60 centimeters (one to two feet) in front of the speaker, at a volume you would practice at anyway. A loud amp right next to the phone distorts the microphone.
- **Video.** Landscape, on a stand or propped on a shelf, far enough back that both hands and the whole neck are in frame. You will learn as much from watching the hands as from listening.
- **Mark the spot.** A strip of tape on the floor or the shelf for the phone, and the same chair in the same place. Same room, and the same guitar if you have more than one.
- **Silence the phone.** Turn on Do Not Disturb or airplane mode before you record, so a notification does not land in the middle of your best take.

### Get the level right

Most phone recording apps adjust the input level automatically and offer few manual controls, so distance is your level control. Before the first take:

- Record ten seconds of the loudest thing you will play, usually a hard strum.
- Play it back. If it crackles or sounds squashed, move the phone back and try again. If you can barely hear quiet notes, move it closer.
- If the app shows a waveform, the loudest strums should come close to the edges without flattening against them.
- In the app's settings, choose the highest quality or lossless option if there is one, and switch off any noise-reduction or enhancement feature. Those features are built for speech and can smear note attacks and room sound.

Once the distance is right, it stays. Changing it between takes changes the sound more than a month of practice changes your playing.

### What to record

The comparison take is one passage, start to finish, at a tempo you would actually attempt, with no restarts. A restart is information: leave it on the recording. Before you play, say the date, the passage and the tempo out loud, for example “Day 1, verse and chorus, 72 BPM.” Then play a count-in on the [metronome](https://guitarhub.org/practice) and go.

Choose a passage you will still be working on in a month, ideally the part of a song you want to finish. If you are not sure which part, the [song readiness score](https://guitarhub.org/readiness) points at the sections most likely to break.

Between monthly takes, record one short take at the end of most sessions: thirty seconds of whatever you worked on. These catch problems while they are still small, and they show you whether the session's fix survived the end of the session.

### The day 1 versus day 30 comparison

- **Record day 30 exactly like day 1.** Same spot, same distance, same passage, same tempo, same count-in. Record it before you warm up on the passage, so it shows what you can do cold.
- **Listen to day 1 once, all the way through.** Write down the timestamp of every stop, stumble and buzz.
- **Listen to day 30 once, the same way.** Same notes, same timestamps.
- **Play the hardest bar from each take back to back.** This is where the change is easiest to hear.
- **Score both takes on the five checks below**, then write one sentence naming what improved and one naming what still breaks. The second sentence is next month's target.

The [practice evidence log](https://guitarhub.org/log) is a good place for those two sentences and the tempo. If you are running a month toward one finish line, the [30-day guitar challenge guide](https://guitarhub.org/30-day-guitar-challenge) covers how to judge the day 30 take, and the [30-day breakthrough planner](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough) sets the four weeks in between.

### What to listen for: five checks

- **Time.** Does the beat stay steady, especially at chord changes and the start of new sections? Rushing into a hard part and slowing down inside it are the classic timing faults. A quiet click on the recording makes both easy to hear.
- **Clean notes.** Count the buzzes, dead strings and notes that ring when they should be muted.
- **Changes.** Listen to the gap before each new chord. A clean change sounds continuous. A late one leaves a hole or a stretched beat.
- **Dynamics.** Does the chorus get louder than the verse, or does everything sit at one volume? Playing with dynamics on purpose is part of sounding like music.
- **Stops and recoveries.** Count the stops. Then listen to how you recover from a mistake: a recovery that keeps the beat is a skill, and it improves with practice like any other.

With video, add a sixth check: the hands. Look for fingers lifting far off the strings, a thumb pressing hard behind the neck, shoulders rising, and the moment your eyes drop to the fretboard. Those usually sit right before the problem you heard.

### File it so you can find it

Name each take with the date, the piece, the tempo and the day number, for example 2026-10-10 verse-chorus 72bpm day01, and keep them in one album or folder. The recordings stay on your phone. Nothing needs to be uploaded or shared for any of this to work, so you can be as rough as you need to be on day 1.

### Questions that come up

#### Should I record audio or video?

Video, when you can. Landscape video with both hands in frame gives you the audio and shows why a note failed: a finger lifting too early, a thumb clamping, a wrist folding. Audio alone is enough for checking time and clean notes, and it is quicker to listen to.

#### Do I need an external microphone?

No. For practice evidence, the phone's built-in microphone is enough, as long as the placement and level stay the same from take to take. An external microphone improves the sound, and you can add one later without changing anything else in this routine.

#### How often should I record my practice?

One short take at the end of most sessions, and one full baseline-style take every 30 days. The short takes catch problems while they are small. The monthly takes, recorded the same way each time, are the ones you compare.

#### Should the metronome be audible on the recording?

For timing checks, yes, quietly. A click you can hear on playback lets you hear exactly where you rush or drag. For the monthly comparison, record a count-in and then play without the click, so you can hear whether your own time holds.

## Learn the notes on the fretboard, then connect them with CAGED.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/learn-guitar-fretboard-notes

Two facts, two strings, four octave shapes and five chord shapes. That is the whole map, learned a few minutes a day.

Updated October 10, 2026

To learn the notes on the guitar fretboard, start with the musical alphabet and its two half steps, then learn the natural notes on string 6 and string 5 until you can name any of them instantly. Use octave shapes to carry those names to the other four strings, and drill one note in every position until the neck reads as a set of repeating patterns. Finally, connect the positions with the CAGED system: the five open chord shapes C, A, G, E and D, which link up the neck in that order. Five minutes a day, testing yourself without a diagram, does more than an hour of staring at a chart.

### The two facts the whole neck runs on

Music uses seven letter names: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, then back to A. Between most neighboring letters there is a whole step, which on guitar is two frets. There are exactly two exceptions: B to C and E to F are half steps, one fret apart. There is no sharp between them.

The second fact: twelve frets make an octave. The note at fret 12 has the same name as the open string, an octave higher, and the pattern from fret 12 to fret 24 repeats the pattern from the open string to fret 12. Learn frets 0 to 12 and you know the whole neck.

Everything in between follows from those two facts. The fret above any natural note is its sharp, and the fret below is its flat, so the note at fret 6 on string 6 is called both A sharp and B flat.

### Step 1: string 6 and string 5

Start with the two lowest strings, because every movable chord and scale shape is placed from a root on one of them. The natural notes are:

- **String 6 (low E):** E at the open string, F at fret 1, G at 3, A at 5, B at 7, C at 8, D at 10, and E again at 12.
- **String 5 (A):** A open, B at 2, C at 3, D at 5, E at 7, F at 8, G at 10, and A again at 12.

Use the fret markers as landmarks. Most guitars have dots at frets 3, 5, 7, 9 and 12. On string 6 that gives you G, A, B, C sharp and E, and on string 5, C, D, E, F sharp and A. Anchor the naturals to those dots and the gaps fill in.

The [musical alphabet on one string drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/musical-alphabet-low-e) walks string 6 from the open string to fret 12 and back, and listens to each note through your microphone. Then the [first movable shape drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/movable-shape-roots) calls out chord names and has you find each root on string 6 or 5, the way you place a power chord or barre chord.

### Step 2: octave shapes carry the names everywhere

You do not memorize strings 4 to 1 note by note. You reach them from strings 6 and 5 with octave shapes, which are fixed distances that always land on the same note name.

- **From string 6:** skip one string to string 4 and go up two frets. G at string 6, fret 3 is also G at string 4, fret 5.
- **From string 5:** skip one string to string 3 and go up two frets. C at string 5, fret 3 is also C at string 3, fret 5.
- **From string 4:** skip one string to string 2 and go up three frets. E at string 4, fret 2 is also E at string 2, fret 5. The extra fret comes from the B string, which is tuned a major third above the G string while every other neighboring pair is a fourth apart.
- **From string 3:** skip one string to string 1 and go up three frets, for the same reason. A at string 3, fret 2 is also A at string 1, fret 5.
- **Strings 6 and 1:** both are E strings, two octaves apart, so every fret has the same note name on both.

With those five rules, knowing strings 6 and 5 means you can find any note on any string in one move.

### Step 3: one note, everywhere

Now turn the map around. Instead of naming the note under your finger, pick a note and find every place it lives between the open strings and fret 12. C, for example, sits at string 5 fret 3, string 3 fret 5, string 2 fret 1, string 6 fret 8, string 4 fret 10, and string 1 fret 8, among others.

The [Find Every C drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/every-c) runs exactly this, across three octaves, and checks the pitch and octave of each note you play. Once C is automatic, do the same with one new note each day. A good order is the cycle of fourths, C, F, B flat, E flat, A flat, D flat, G flat, B, E, A, D, G, because it walks through every note and matches how many chord progressions move.

Test yourself rather than reviewing. In a 2006 study, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that students who practiced recalling a passage remembered more of it a week later than students who spent the same time rereading it. On the fretboard, that means naming notes from memory and checking afterward, not reading them off a chart.

### Step 4: CAGED connects the shapes

The CAGED system takes the five open chord shapes, C, A, G, E and D, and treats each one as a movable shape. Your index finger, or a barre, takes over the job of the nut, and the shape can then be played anywhere on the neck. The five shapes fit together up the neck in the order of the name, C, A, G, E, D, and then the cycle repeats an octave higher.

Here is C major played five ways, moving up the neck:

- **C shape, open position:** x32010. Root on string 5, fret 3.
- **A shape, barre at fret 3:** x35553. Root on string 5, fret 3.
- **G shape, around frets 5 to 8:** 875558. Roots on string 6 fret 8, string 3 fret 5 and string 1 fret 8.
- **E shape, barre at fret 8:** 8 10 10 9 8 8. Root on string 6, fret 8.
- **D shape, around frets 10 to 13:** xx 10 12 13 12. Root on string 4, fret 10.

After the D shape, the C shape returns at fret 12, an octave above where you started. Every major chord works the same way. For G, the cycle starts on a different letter but keeps the order: the open G shape, the E shape barred at fret 3, the D shape at fret 5, the C shape around frets 7 to 10, and the A shape barred at fret 10.

The full G and C shapes are awkward to fret as complete chords higher up the neck, and players often use partial versions of them. Their real value is as a map: each shape tells you where the roots, thirds and fifths of the chord sit in that region of the neck, and each one sits inside a position of the major scale. That is what connects chords, arpeggios and scales into one picture.

The E and A shapes are the two barre chords most players learn first, and the [barre chord guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-play-barre-chords) covers them in detail. Stage 6 of the [GuitarHub guitar curriculum](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar), Whole Neck, teaches both barre shapes in every position along with the major scale in five positions.

### A ten-minute daily fretboard session

- **2 minutes:** name the natural notes on string 6, then string 5, up and back, out loud, without looking at a chart.
- **3 minutes:** today's note, everywhere from the open strings to fret 12, using the octave shapes to jump between strings.
- **3 minutes:** one major chord through all five CAGED shapes, saying the shape name as you play it.
- **2 minutes:** random calls. Pick a string and a note name at random and find it. Use a [metronome](https://guitarhub.org/practice) at 40 BPM and aim to land each note on the next click.

The click turns recall into a timed test, and timed recall is what you need in a song, where the next chord does not wait for you to count up from the nut.

With the notes and shapes in place, the [scale practice guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-scales) turns positions into music, and the [improvisation guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-improvisation) uses the same roots and chord tones to make up phrases over chords.

### Questions that come up

#### How long does it take to learn the notes on the fretboard?

Strings 6 and 5 come first and come fastest, because every movable chord and scale shape is placed from a root on one of them. Give them a few minutes every day for two weeks before adding octave shapes. The full neck builds over the following weeks as you use the octave shapes and one-note-everywhere drill daily.

#### Do I need to learn sharps and flats too?

Learn the natural notes first. Every sharp or flat is one fret away from a natural: the fret above a note is its sharp, and the fret below is its flat. Once the naturals are instant, the sharps and flats come for free.

#### Is the CAGED system necessary?

It is a widely taught map for connecting chord shapes, arpeggios and scale positions across the whole neck. You can learn the notes without it, and CAGED is far more useful once you know the notes, because it tells you where each shape's roots are.

#### Should I learn the notes or the scales first?

Start with the notes on strings 6 and 5, then learn scales. A scale shape is much easier to move to a new key when you can put its root on the right fret immediately.

## How to practice strumming so the groove holds.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-strumming

Rhythm guitar is a hand that never stops and a choice about which strokes touch the strings. Practice those two things and every pattern gets easier.

Updated October 10, 2026

To practice strumming, keep your strumming hand moving down and up in a constant, even motion locked to the beat: down on every beat and up on every “and” between them. A strumming pattern is just a choice about which of those strokes hit the strings and which pass just above them. Count out loud, start at 60 to 70 BPM on a metronome, learn five patterns in order from straight quarter notes to syncopation, and record yourself to check that the beat holds through the chord changes.

### The pendulum rule

Picture the strumming hand as a pendulum. In a song counted in eighth notes, it moves down on each number (1, 2, 3, 4) and up on each “and” between them, at an even speed, for the whole song. It never stops and never changes direction early.

When a pattern leaves out a stroke, the hand still makes the motion, it just passes above the strings. These are ghost strums, and they are the central idea in rhythm guitar. They keep your place in the bar for you. A hand that stops between strokes has to restart from rest and guess when to come back in, which is a common source of rushing and dragging.

Stage 3 of the [GuitarHub guitar curriculum](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar) teaches this as its own module, Up and Down, with lessons on the hand that never stops and on ghost strums.

### Count out loud

Say the count while you play: “1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and.” It feels clumsy for a few days and then becomes the fastest way to learn any pattern, because you can say where each stroke goes before your hand knows it. If you lose the count, you have found the spot to slow down.

### Five patterns, in order

Learn these one at a time, each on a single chord first, then on a two-chord change. D is a downstroke, U is an upstroke, and a dash is a ghost strum where the hand moves but misses the strings.

- **Quarter notes: D - D - D - D -.** One downstroke on each beat, with the up motion silent. This is the first strum in the curriculum, and Stage 2 checks it at sixteen bars at 80 BPM.
- **Straight eighths: D U D U D U D U.** Every stroke hits. Keep the downs and ups the same volume, then try accenting the downs.
- **Down, down-up: D - D U D - D U.** Counted 1, 2-and, 3, 4-and. The first pattern with a ghost strum in it.
- **The syncopated pattern: D - D U - U D U.** Counted 1, 2-and, and-4-and. Beat 3 is a ghost strum, so the upstroke on the “and” of 2 rings across it. This pattern fits a wide range of songs in 4/4.
- **Sixteenths: 1 e and a.** The hand moves twice as fast, down on 1 and “and”, up on “e” and “a”. Start with all sixteen strokes muted, then let only some of them sound. This is the engine of funk rhythm guitar.

Songs in 3/4 and 6/8 use the same pendulum with a different count: “1 and 2 and 3 and” for 3/4, and “1 2 3 4 5 6” with a stress on 1 and 4 for 6/8. Stage 3 of the curriculum covers both meters.

### The metronome: slow first, then move the click to 2 and 4

Set the [metronome](https://guitarhub.org/practice) between 60 and 70 BPM and play each pattern until you can do four bars in a row with every stroke on time and the count still in your mouth. Then raise the tempo in steps of 5 BPM. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) lays out the steps for a specific passage.

Once a pattern holds at 80 to 90 BPM, try this. Set the metronome to half your tempo and hear each click as beat 2 and beat 4 of the bar. At a song tempo of 100 BPM, set the click to 50. Now the click is the backbeat, the snare drum's job in most pop and rock, and you supply beats 1 and 3 yourself. It is harder, and it is much closer to playing with a drummer. The [metronome guide](https://guitarhub.org/practicing-guitar-with-a-metronome) covers more ways to use the click as a test instead of a crutch.

### Accents make it groove

A pattern played at one even volume sounds mechanical. Once the strokes are in place, add accents: dig in slightly on beats 2 and 4 for a rock or pop backbeat feel, or on the first stroke of each bar for a folk feel. Change only how deep the pick goes into the strings, not the size or speed of the motion, or the timing will move with the volume.

The [Dynamics Without Rushing drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/pick-dynamics) trains exactly this: alternating soft and loud bars while the microphone checks that the timing stays put.

### Mechanics that keep the motion easy

- **Move from the wrist and forearm together**, with a loose rotation like shaking water off your hand, not a stiff arm swing from the shoulder.
- **Hold the pick loosely**, just firmly enough that it does not fly out of your hand. A loose grip lets the pick give a little as it crosses the strings, which smooths the sound.
- **Aim the strokes.** Downstrokes usually favor the bass strings and upstrokes catch the top three or four. You rarely need all six strings on an upstroke.
- **Strum over the sound hole or the neck pickup area.** Strumming near the bridge sounds thinner and is harder to control.

### Changing chords without breaking the strum

The strumming hand is the timekeeper, so it never waits for the fretting hand. If the new chord is not ready, the strum still happens on time. To give the fretting hand room, lift the old chord on the last upstroke of the bar and let that stroke catch the open strings. At tempo it sounds like part of the pattern.

If the change is the reason the strum breaks down, isolate the change itself. The [chord change guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-change-chords-faster) covers anchor fingers, one-minute changes and how to put the change on the beat.

### Record it and check the time

Your sense of time in the moment is generous. Record thirty seconds of each pattern with the click audible and listen back. Listen for the strum drifting ahead of the click on upstrokes, for a stretched beat at each chord change, and for downs that are much louder than ups. The [phone recording guide](https://guitarhub.org/record-guitar-practice-on-phone) covers placement and what to listen for.

### A fifteen-minute rhythm session

- **3 minutes:** ghost-strum warm-up. The pendulum on muted strings at 60 BPM, counting out loud.
- **5 minutes:** today's pattern on one chord, then on a two-chord change, four bars clean before you raise the tempo.
- **4 minutes:** the same pattern with the click on 2 and 4, or with accents if that is still too hard.
- **3 minutes:** a song section with the pattern, recorded.

### Beyond the basics: the rhythm drills

When the five patterns are solid, the Advanced Lab has four rhythm drills that listen to the timing of each attack through your microphone:

- [Syncopated Sixteenths](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/funk-sixteenths): constant sixteenth-note motion with only the written hits sounding.
- [Gear Shift: Triplets to Sixteenths](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/triplet-sixteenth-shift): switching subdivisions while the beat stays still.
- [Three Over Two](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/quarter-note-triplets): quarter-note triplets, three even hits across two beats.
- [Dotted-Eighth Displacement](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/dotted-eighth-displacement): an accent that walks across the beat while you keep the four underneath.

### Questions that come up

#### Why do I keep speeding up when I strum?

Usually because the hand stops moving between strokes, so each stroke starts from rest and arrives early, or because a chord change pulls the strum forward. Keep the down-up motion going through every beat, including the strokes that miss the strings, and practice the change against a click until it lands on time.

#### What is the most useful strumming pattern to learn first?

After straight eighth notes, the pattern counted 1, 2-and, and-4-and: down, down-up, up-down-up, with the hand missing the strings on beat 3. It fits a wide range of songs in 4/4, and learning it teaches the skill every other pattern needs, which is keeping the hand moving through a stroke you do not play.

#### Should I strum with a pick or my fingers?

Either works. A thin to medium pick, roughly 0.5 to 0.7 millimeters, gives a bright, even strum and is easier for beginners to control. Strumming with the fingers gives a softer sound. Choose one for a month so the motion has a chance to settle.

#### How do I work out the strumming pattern of a song?

Count the beat out loud while the song plays, then listen for which strums land on the numbers and which land on the ands. Tap the pattern on your leg with the down-up motion going, and only then try it on the guitar. Many songs use one main pattern with small variations at the ends of phrases.

## Barre chords and the F chord, without the death grip.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/how-to-play-barre-chords

A barre chord is leverage, not strength. Put the index finger in the right place, let your arm do the pressing, and build the F chord in four steps.

Updated October 10, 2026

To play a barre chord, lay your index finger straight across the strings just behind the fret, rolled slightly onto its thumb-side edge, and let the weight of your arm pull the fingers into the neck instead of squeezing with your thumb. For the F chord (133211), the index only has to sound strings 6, 2 and 1, because the other fingers cover the rest. Build up to it in four steps: Fmaj7, a four-string F, a five-string F, then the full barre. Check every chord string by string, and practice the full shape higher up the neck first, where it is easier, before bringing it down to fret 1.

Fingerings below list frets from string 6 (low E) to string 1 (high E), with x for a string you do not play and 0 for an open string.

### Why the F chord stops so many players

F is usually the first chord where one finger has to hold down several strings at once, and it arrives at fret 1, right next to the nut, where the strings have the least room to flex and take the most force to press. Most players try it with the open-chord technique they already have: pressing harder with the fingertip and squeezing with the thumb. That produces a sore thumb and dead strings, and it is why the barre feels like a strength problem. Stage 5 of the [GuitarHub guitar curriculum](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar) opens with a lesson called Barre Is Leverage, Not Strength, and that is the right frame.

### What actually needs to be pressed

The full F major chord is 133211:

- Index finger barred across all six strings at fret 1.
- Middle finger on string 3, fret 2.
- Ring finger on string 5, fret 3.
- Pinky on string 4, fret 3.

The ring, pinky and middle fingers fret strings 5, 4 and 3. So the barre only has to sound three strings: string 6, string 2 and string 1. Knowing that changes where you put your attention. You do not need even pressure along the whole finger. You need it at the very end (string 1), near the middle crease (string 2), and at the base (string 6).

The creases of the index finger are the usual reason a string dies. If string 2 or 1 thuds, slide the finger a few millimeters toward or away from the headstock, or move the whole barre slightly up or down across the strings so the crease falls between strings instead of on one.

### Leverage instead of squeeze

- **Index close to the fret.** Right behind the fret wire, not in the middle of the space. The closer it is, the less force a clean note needs.
- **Roll the index onto its edge.** Turn it slightly so the harder, thumb-side edge of the finger meets the strings instead of the soft flat pad.
- **Thumb low and loose.** Place it on the back of the neck roughly behind the middle finger, not hooked over the top. It balances; it does not clamp.
- **Let the arm do it.** With the elbow relaxed at your side, let the weight of the arm draw the fingers back into the strings, as if gently pulling the neck toward you. On an electric with a strap, or a guitar braced against your body, this supplies most of the pressure.
- **Use the minimum.** Press until every string sounds, then ease off until one starts to buzz, then add back just enough. That is the pressure the chord needs.

### The four-step path to F

- **Fmaj7 (xx3210).** Ring finger on string 4 fret 3, middle on string 3 fret 2, index on string 2 fret 1, string 1 open. No barre at all, and it gets the fingers used to the F shape.
- **Four-string F (xx3211).** The same shape, but the index now flattens across strings 2 and 1 at fret 1. This is a small barre, two strings wide, and a complete F major chord.
- **Five-string F (x33211).** Add the bass: ring finger on string 5 fret 3, pinky on string 4 fret 3, middle on string 3 fret 2, index barring strings 2 and 1 at fret 1.
- **Full F (133211).** Extend the index across all six strings so it also frets string 6 at fret 1.

Move to the next step only when the current one rings clean four times in a row from a cold start. In the meantime, use the step you have in your songs. Every one of them is an F chord.

### Start higher, then slide down

The full barre shape is easier around fret 5, where the strings flex more easily under the finger and the frets sit closer together. Play the same shape at fret 5 (577655) and you have A major. Once it rings, move it down one fret at a time: A flat at fret 4, G at 3, F sharp at 2, and F at 1. Each step shows you exactly which string fails first as the shape gets harder.

### Check it string by string

Strum the chord once, then pick each string from 6 to 1. Fix only the first string that fails, then check again. Common culprits: string 2 or string 1 under an index crease, string 3 when the middle finger collapses flat, and string 2 touched by the underside of the middle finger. Arching the middle, ring and pinky fingers more steeply clears the strings under them.

### The E shape and the A shape

The F chord is the E shape: an open E major chord moved up one fret with the index barre playing the role of the nut. Move it anywhere and the root on string 6 names the chord, so the E shape at fret 3 is G and at fret 8 is C. Lift the middle finger and you have the minor version: F minor is 133111.

The second barre shape is the A shape, with its root on string 5. B flat major is x13331: index barre at fret 1, and the ring finger flattened across strings 4, 3 and 2 at fret 3. B major is the same shape at fret 2, x24442. The minor version comes from the open A minor shape: B minor is x24432, with the index barre at fret 2, middle on string 2 fret 3, ring on string 4 fret 4, and pinky on string 3 fret 4.

With those two shapes, you can play every major and minor chord, placing the root on string 6 or string 5. The [first movable shape drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/movable-shape-roots) trains exactly that placement, and the [fretboard notes guide](https://guitarhub.org/learn-guitar-fretboard-notes) covers the note names on both strings and how these shapes fit into the CAGED system. Stage 6 of the curriculum, Whole Neck, builds both shapes in five positions.

### Changing into F

C (x32010) to F (133211) has an anchor. The ring finger is on string 5 at fret 3 in both chords, so it stays down. The middle finger moves from string 4 to string 3, still at fret 2, the pinky drops onto string 4 at fret 3, and the index lays flat across fret 1. Practice it with one-minute changes and the techniques in the [chord change guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-change-chords-faster), then put the change on a ladder with the [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo).

### A ten-minute barre session

- **2 minutes, squeeze and release:** form the barre shape at fret 5. At 60 BPM on the [metronome](https://guitarhub.org/practice), press for four beats, then release to light contact for four beats, without lifting off the strings.
- **2 minutes, string check:** pick each string and fix the first one that fails.
- **2 minutes, slide down:** fret 5 to fret 1, one fret at a time, checking at each stop.
- **3 minutes, changes:** C to F one-minute changes, using whichever F step you are on.
- **1 minute:** a song with an F in it.

Barre practice brings a new kind of soreness at the side of the index finger and the base of the thumb. A little tenderness is expected. Aching in the wrist or forearm is a signal to stop, and the [finger and hand pain guide](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-finger-pain) covers the warning signs and the setup changes that make barre chords easier.

### Questions that come up

#### How long does it take to learn barre chords?

Expect weeks of short daily practice rather than days, and expect the F chord at fret 1 to come last. The four-step path on this page lets you play songs with a smaller F along the way, so the weeks are spent playing music instead of waiting for one chord.

#### Is it OK to play the small F instead of the full barre?

Yes. The four-string F (xx3211) and the five-string version (x33211) are both real F major chords, and plenty of songs sound better with them. Learn the full barre as well, because the same E shape becomes every major chord up the neck once you can hold it.

#### Will lighter strings make barre chords easier?

Lighter strings need less force, so yes, and a professional setup that lowers the action and the nut slots often makes an even bigger difference. If chords at fret 1 feel much harder than the same shape at fret 5, the setup is worth checking.

#### Why does my thumb hurt when I play barre chords?

Usually because the thumb is squeezing the neck to supply the pressure. Move the thumb lower behind the neck, roughly behind the middle finger, and let the weight of your arm pull the fingers into the strings. Pain that stays after rest, or spreads to the wrist or forearm, is a reason to stop and get it checked.

## How to practice improvising, one constraint at a time.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-improvisation

Improvising is a string of small choices made in time. Practice the choosing: fewer notes, more space, and every phrase ending somewhere on purpose.

Updated October 10, 2026

To practice guitar improvisation, pick one key, one backing track and one scale position, then play over it with deliberate limits: two notes only, one string only, short phrases with rests between them, and phrases that answer each other in call and response. Then learn where each chord's tones sit, especially the third, and practice ending phrases on them. A 12-bar blues in A with the A minor pentatonic scale is the classic place to start. Record every session and keep one phrase you like.

This page is about making up phrases over chords: what to practice so that improvising stops sounding like a scale played in order. How to practice the scale itself, until the shape plays smoothly in time, is covered in the [scale practice guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-scales).

### Improvising is choosing, so practice choosing

The usual obstacle in improvising is not a lack of notes. It is too many options at once. With a whole scale under your fingers and no plan, the hand falls back on its habit, which is running the scale up and down. Constraints remove options so you can hear the effect of the ones that are left. Every drill below takes something away on purpose.

### Set up: one key, one backing, one position

Start with a 12-bar blues in A. The form, one chord per bar, is:

- Bars 1 to 4: A7, A7, A7, A7.
- Bars 5 to 8: D7, D7, A7, A7.
- Bars 9 to 12: E7, D7, A7, E7.

Use any 12-bar blues backing track in A, or record yourself playing the chords for three choruses on your phone and loop it. Start around 70 to 90 BPM.

The scale is A minor pentatonic in its first position, at fret 5: A, C, D, E and G.

- String 6: fret 5 (A) and fret 8 (C).
- String 5: fret 5 (D) and fret 7 (E).
- String 4: fret 5 (G) and fret 7 (A).
- String 3: fret 5 (C) and fret 7 (D).
- String 2: fret 5 (E) and fret 8 (G).
- String 1: fret 5 (A) and fret 8 (C).

Stage 5 of the [GuitarHub guitar curriculum](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar) covers both the twelve-bar form and a first solo built on four-bar phrases.

### The constraint drills

Give each drill at least three full choruses before moving on. The point is to stay inside the limit long enough to find what it makes possible.

- **Two notes only.** Use A (string 1, fret 5) and C (string 1, fret 8). With pitch taken away, rhythm is the only variable: long notes, short notes, repeated notes, silence. Many great blues phrases are two notes and a strong rhythm.
- **One string only.** Play the scale notes on string 2 or string 3 alone, sliding between them. Phrases on one string move horizontally along the neck, which breaks the box habit.
- **Play two bars, rest two bars.** Silence is part of the phrase. Forcing the rest also gives you time to hear the chord change coming and plan the next idea.
- **Call and response.** Play a short phrase as a question, then answer it with a phrase that starts the same way and ends differently. Many memorable solos are built from pairs like this.
- **Repeat and vary.** Play one phrase, then repeat it with one change: a different rhythm, a different last note, or the same shape over the next chord. Developing one idea through a whole chorus sounds composed, even when it is not.

### Land on the chord, not just in the key

The minor pentatonic works over the whole blues, which is why it is usually the first scale players learn for soloing. What makes a phrase sound like it knows the chord changes is where it ends. The strongest landing note is usually the third of the chord of the moment:

- Over A7, the third is C sharp, at string 3 fret 6. The scale's C at fret 5 is one fret below it, so sliding or bending from C to C sharp is the classic blues resolution.
- Over D7, the third is F sharp, at string 2 fret 7.
- Over E7, the third is G sharp, at string 4 fret 6.

Practice ending every phrase on one of those notes, timed to arrive as the chord does. The [Land on the Chord Tone drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/blues-landing-notes) gives you phrases that resolve to each third over A7, D7 and E7 and checks every note with your microphone, then asks you to improvise your own phrase to the same landing note.

When the thirds are comfortable, the [Guide Tones drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/guide-tones) takes the same idea into a ii-V-I in C, playing only the third and seventh of each chord so you hear how they move by half steps. Stage 6 of the curriculum calls this Target the Third.

### Approach notes and enclosures

Once you know your target, you can decorate the arrival. An enclosure plays the note above the target, then the note below it, then the target itself, so the line sounds like it is homing in. The [Enclosures drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/enclosures) practices four targets, C sharp, F sharp, A and E, each approached from above and below. Use it on the landing notes from the blues above.

### Add one color note

Adding a single note to a scale you already own is the quickest route to a new sound. Over an A minor chord, add F sharp, the major sixth, and the pentatonic takes on the brighter minor color of the Dorian mode. The [Add the Dorian Sixth drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/dorian-color) gives you a phrase with that note in it, then asks you to improvise with it and resolve to A or C rather than to the F sharp itself.

### Steal phrases by ear

Every improviser's vocabulary comes from other players. Pick a short phrase from a recording you love, four to eight notes, and find it on the neck by ear: hear it, sing it, find the first note, then the next. The [Eight-Note Phrase by Ear drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/phrase-by-ear) trains the process one note at a time. Then use the repeat-and-vary drill on it until it fits your own playing.

### A 25-minute improvisation session

- **5 minutes, vocabulary:** one phrase learned by ear, or one drill from the Advanced Lab.
- **5 minutes, today's constraint:** one of the five drills above, over the backing, for at least three choruses.
- **5 minutes, landing notes:** every phrase ends on the third of the current chord.
- **7 minutes, free improvisation, recorded:** no rules except to keep going through mistakes.
- **3 minutes, listen back:** mark the best phrase and write down how it starts. Start tomorrow's free improvisation by playing it.

Recording is what turns this into progress you can hear. The [phone recording guide](https://guitarhub.org/record-guitar-practice-on-phone) covers placement and what to listen for, and a monthly comparison of the same 12 bars shows changes in phrasing that are hard to notice day to day. The note names behind the landing notes are covered in the [fretboard notes guide](https://guitarhub.org/learn-guitar-fretboard-notes).

### Questions that come up

#### Do I need to know music theory to improvise?

You need a little, and you can learn it as you go. One scale shape, the names of the chords you are playing over, and where the third of each chord sits will carry you a long way. Everything else on this page is ear and habit, built by playing over chords and listening back.

#### Which scale should I improvise with first?

The minor pentatonic, in the first position. Five notes, two per string, and every note sounds acceptable over a blues or a minor rock progression. That freedom lets you put your attention on rhythm, phrasing and landing notes, which are what make improvising sound like music.

#### How do I stop sounding like I am just running up and down a scale?

Play fewer notes and leave space. Use short phrases with rests between them, repeat a phrase and change one thing, and end each phrase on a chord tone instead of wherever the scale happened to run out. The constraint drills on this page force all three.

#### Is it OK to use licks I have learned?

Yes. Learned phrases are vocabulary, the same way borrowed words are for a speaker. The skill is placing them over the right chord and changing them: start a lick on a different beat, shorten it, or end it on a different chord tone, and it becomes yours.

## Coming back to guitar after years away: a 30-day restart.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/coming-back-to-guitar

Most of what you learned is still there. The guitar needs a setup, your fingertips need two weeks, and the month needs one finish line.

Updated October 10, 2026

To come back to guitar after years away, start with the instrument: new strings, a tuning check, and a setup if the strings sit high. Then rebuild your fingertips with two short sessions a day for the first two weeks, record a fresh baseline of where you are now, and pick one song to finish by day 30. Relearning is faster than learning the first time, so most of the restart is physical: calluses, finger strength and stamina. Measure the month with a recording on day 1 and day 30, not with your memory of how you used to play.

### Week zero: the guitar

A guitar that sat in a case or a closet for years usually needs attention before it is pleasant to play. Changes in humidity and temperature can move the neck, and old strings lose their tone and corrode.

- **Restring it.** Fresh strings sound brighter, stay in tune better, and are kinder to soft fingertips than corroded ones. If you used heavy strings before, this is a good moment to go a gauge lighter.
- **Tune and recheck.** Use the [guitar tuner](https://guitarhub.org/practice) on all six strings, E, A, D, G, B, E from low to high. New strings stretch, so expect to retune several times in the first few days.
- **Check the action.** If the strings sit noticeably higher above the frets than you remember, or notes buzz, the neck has probably moved. A setup by a guitar technician adjusts it and is one of the best-value repairs an old guitar can get.
- **Electrics and pickups.** Crackling volume or tone knobs usually need cleaning. On an acoustic with a pickup, replace the battery.

### Days 1 to 7: fingertips and a fresh baseline

Your calluses are gone, and your hands remember shapes your fingertips can no longer hold for long. The classic restart mistake is a three-hour first session that ends in blisters and a week off. Play 10 to 15 minutes, two or three times a day, and stop when a fingertip feels hot or stings. The [finger pain guide](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-finger-pain) covers how calluses rebuild and the warning signs that mean stop.

In the first week, record a baseline. Three short takes on your phone, each without warming up on it first:

- A song you used to know, as far as you can get without stopping.
- The open chords you remember, each strummed and then picked string by string.
- Any scale or riff your hands still know.

These takes are the start line for this restart, not a verdict on the years away. Do not compare them with your memory of how you used to play, which is reliably more flattering than any recording. Compare them with day 30. The [phone recording guide](https://guitarhub.org/record-guitar-practice-on-phone) covers how to set up so the two takes are comparable.

### What comes back fast, and what takes longer

Relearning is faster than learning. In his memory experiments published in 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus found that relearning material he had already forgotten took less time than learning it the first time, and he named the difference savings. Returning players experience the same thing on the instrument: a chord shape or a song that took weeks the first time often returns in a few sessions.

What takes longer is the physical layer. Fingertips need a couple of weeks of short daily sessions, and speed and stamina rebuild over the month. Plan for that. Spend the first two weeks on material you already know at comfortable tempos, and save the hardest passage you used to play for after the calluses are back.

### Find your level, then pick one finish line

Your level now may not match your level when you stopped, and it may be uneven: chords intact, lead playing rusty, reading forgotten. The [find your level page](https://guitarhub.org/start) asks three questions and opens at the right place, and the [GuitarHub guitar curriculum](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar) lets you jump straight to the stage that matches, from open chords and strumming to barre chords and the whole neck.

Then choose one finish line for days 8 to 30. One song, played start to finish without stopping, at a tempo you choose, recorded on day 30. One finish line beats a plan to get everything back at once, because it gives every session the same target. The [30-day breakthrough planner](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough) turns that finish line into four weeks of practice focuses, and if you cannot tell what is holding the song back, the [practice plateau diagnostic](https://guitarhub.org/diagnose) names the most likely cause.

### Days 8 to 30: run the loop

The restart month uses the same four stages as the [GuitarHub method](https://guitarhub.org/method): baseline, isolate, reconnect, prove.

- **Baseline:** the first-week recording of your chosen song shows where it breaks.
- **Isolate:** take the first place it breaks, two beats either side, and slow it down until it is clean every time. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) sets the steps back up to song tempo.
- **Reconnect:** put the repaired spot back into the section, then the whole song.
- **Prove:** on day 30, record the same song the same way and compare it with the baseline.

### Play from memory before you look

For songs you used to know, try to play them from memory before you look up the chords or tab. Struggling to recall is not wasted time. In a 2006 study, Henry Roediger and Jeffrey Karpicke found that students who practiced recalling a passage remembered more of it a week later than students who spent the same time rereading it. On guitar, the attempt to retrieve a song strengthens it more than reading it again. Look it up after the attempt, fix what you missed, and try again from memory the next day. The [guide to memorizing songs](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-memorize-songs-on-guitar) goes further into learning the form instead of the finger path.

### Fit it into an adult week

If work and family filled the time before, they are still there. Protect one longer session a week and keep the other days short. The [practice schedule guide](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-schedule) builds a week that survives a busy Wednesday, and the [practice session builder](https://guitarhub.org/session) turns the minutes you have on a given day into timed blocks. One line per session in the [practice evidence log](https://guitarhub.org/log) shows you, within a couple of weeks, which days actually happen.

### Restart mistakes to skip

- **A marathon first session.** Blisters cost you more days than the session gained.
- **Starting with your hardest old song at full speed.** Start with the easiest song you remember and earn the hard one by week three.
- **Buying gear before playing.** A setup and new strings first. Play a month, then decide what you actually want.
- **Trying to recover everything at once.** One finish line for the month. Everything else waits for month two.

### Questions that come up

#### Will I have to start from scratch?

Rarely. Chord shapes, songs you once knew well and your sense of how the instrument works tend to come back much faster than they took to learn. What fades most is the physical layer: calluses, finger strength, speed and stamina. Rebuild that gently and you skip most of the beginner stage.

#### How long until I am back to where I was?

It depends on how far you went and how long you were away, so measure it instead of guessing. Record a baseline in your first week and the same take on day 30. The comparison tells you how fast you are coming back, and it usually shows more progress than your sense of it does.

#### Should I buy a new guitar?
