Get the one you have restrung and set up first. A setup by a guitar technician fixes most of what makes an old guitar hard to play, for a fraction of the cost of a new one. If you still want a new guitar after a month of playing, you will know much better what you want from it.

#### Should I take lessons again?

Lessons help most once you know what you want to work on. Spend the first two weeks finding your level and recording a baseline, then choose: the GuitarHub curriculum for a structured path from wherever you land, or a teacher for live feedback on the specific thing your recordings point at.

## How to practice scales so they turn into music.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-scales

Up and down a scale is a finger exercise. Sequences, intervals, a drone, rhythm and chord tones are what turn the same notes into music.

Updated October 10, 2026

To practice guitar scales so they become music, learn one shape until you can play it cold, in time, with alternate picking. Then stop playing it only up and down. Play it in sequences and in thirds, play it over a drone so you hear what each note does, play it in rhythms with rests, and pick out the chord tones inside it. Five to fifteen minutes a day on one scale, done this way, builds more usable playing than an hour of running every shape you know.

This page is about the scale itself: how to practice a shape so it plays like music instead of an exercise. Using scales to make up phrases over chords is covered in the [improvisation guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-improvisation).

### Why up and down does not transfer

Music almost never runs a scale from its lowest note to its highest in even notes. It skips, repeats, changes direction, rests and lands on particular notes. A scale practiced only as a straight run trains one path through the notes, and that path rarely appears in a song.

There is also no target in it. In their 1993 study of violinists at a music academy in Berlin, K. Anders Ericsson, Ralf Krampe and Clemens Tesch-Römer described deliberate practice as activity designed specifically to improve performance, done with full concentration, with feedback on the result. Running a scale you already know, while thinking about something else, has none of those features. Every step below adds a specific target and a way to check it.

### Step 1: one shape, cold

Choose one shape and one key. Two good starting points:

- **A minor pentatonic, first position.** A, C, D, E and G, two notes per string between frets 5 and 8: frets 5 and 8 on strings 6, 2 and 1, and frets 5 and 7 on strings 5, 4 and 3.
- **G major, three notes per string.** G, A, B, C, D, E and F sharp. The [Three Notes a String drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/three-note-legato-g-major) plays it across four strings, string 6 at frets 3, 5 and 7, string 5 at 3, 5 and 7, then strings 4 and 3 at 4, 5 and 7, and checks every note with your microphone.

Every major scale follows the same pattern of whole steps (W, two frets) and half steps (H, one fret): W W H W W W H. C major is C, D, E, F, G, A, B, with no sharps or flats. G major is G, A, B, C, D, E, F sharp.

Play the shape in eighth notes with strict alternate picking, down, up, down, up, against the [metronome](https://guitarhub.org/practice) at 60 BPM. Climb in steps of about 5 BPM, moving up only after three clean passes in a row, and drop back a step when a pass breaks. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) lays out the steps. Stage 4 of the [GuitarHub guitar curriculum](https://guitarhub.org/learn/guitar), The First Scale, runs this exact ladder from 60 to 100 BPM.

The shape is learned when you can play it cold, first thing in a session, with your eyes off the fretboard. Until then, the other steps will be about finding notes instead of making music.

### Step 2: sequences

A sequence plays the scale in short overlapping groups, so the line moves forward while changing direction. In C major, groups of three go C D E, D E F, E F G, F G A, and on up the scale. Groups of four go C D E F, D E F G, E F G A. Play each sequence ascending, then descending (C B A, B A G, A G F).

Sequences break the single straight path, force your hands to start from every note in the shape, and produce lines that already sound like melodic runs. Keep them at a tempo where the picking stays strictly alternate, which is usually slower than your straight scale tempo at first.

### Step 3: intervals

Play the scale in thirds: each note followed by the note two scale steps above it. In C major that is C E, D F, E G, F A, G B, A C, B D. Thirds are the building blocks of chords and of a lot of melody, so this one exercise makes the scale sound musical immediately. When thirds are smooth, try fourths (C F, D G, E A) and sixths (C A, D B, E C).

### Step 4: hear it against a drone

A note only has a musical meaning against something else. Let the open A string ring and play the A minor scale (A, B, C, D, E, F, G) over it slowly, holding each note for a few seconds. Notice which notes sound settled (A, C and E, the notes of an A minor chord), which pull toward a neighbor, and which add tension or color.

Then change one note. The [One Root, Two Modes drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/aeolian-vs-dorian) plays A Aeolian and then A Dorian, which differ only in the sixth, F in Aeolian and F sharp in Dorian. Hearing that one note change against a fixed root is how modes stop being a theory topic and start being sounds you can choose.

### Step 5: rhythm, not just notes

Play the same shape in different rhythms: quarter notes, eighth notes, triplets, then a long-short pattern such as a dotted eighth followed by a sixteenth. Then add rests. Play four notes and rest for four beats, or start the run on beat 2 instead of beat 1.

Finish this step by making a four-bar phrase from the shape: a short idea in bar 1, a repeat with a change in bar 2, something longer in bar 3, and a held note in bar 4. That is the moment a scale becomes a melody.

### Step 6: the chord tones inside the scale

Every scale contains chords, and every chord is a set of notes you can find inside the shape. In C major, the C chord is C, E and G, D minor is D, F and A, and G7 is G, B, D and F. Play those notes inside the scale shape, low to high, as arpeggios.

The [ii-V-I Arpeggios drill](https://guitarhub.org/advanced/ii-v-i-arpeggios) spells Dm7 (D, F, A, C), G7 (G, B, D, F) and Cmaj7 (C, E, G, B) note by note in one position. Knowing where the chord tones sit inside a shape is what lets you aim a line at the chord of the moment instead of wandering through the key.

### Step 7: connect positions

One shape covers four or five frets. To use the whole neck, learn the neighboring shape and practice the shift between them: play up one shape and slide on one string into the next. The [fretboard notes guide](https://guitarhub.org/learn-guitar-fretboard-notes) shows how the five CAGED shapes map the major scale positions across the neck, and Stage 6 of the curriculum, Whole Neck, teaches the major scale in five positions and how to connect them.

### A fifteen-minute scale session

- **3 minutes:** today's shape cold, once, at your current ladder tempo. Note whether it held.
- **4 minutes:** one sequence, ascending and descending, against the click.
- **3 minutes:** thirds, or the drone, alternating by day.
- **3 minutes:** chord tones inside the shape.
- **2 minutes:** one four-bar phrase from the shape, recorded. Keep the best one.

On a short day, do the cold pass and the four-bar phrase. That keeps both ends of the job alive: the shape your hands know, and the music you make with it. When you want to take those phrases over chord changes, the [improvisation guide](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-improvisation) picks up from here.

### Questions that come up

#### Which guitar scales should I learn first?

The minor pentatonic in its first position, then the major scale. The minor pentatonic is five notes, two per string, and it works over blues and a great deal of rock. The major scale is the reference every other scale and mode is described against, so it pays back everything you learn after it.

#### How fast should I play scales?

Only as fast as you can play them evenly, in time, with every note clean. Start with eighth notes at 60 BPM and climb in steps of about 5 BPM, moving up only after a few clean passes in a row. A ladder from 60 to 100 BPM in eighth notes is a solid first target.

#### Should I use alternate picking for scales?

Yes, as your default: down, up, down, up, regardless of string changes. It keeps the picking hand in time and makes speed possible later. Practice legato as a separate skill, picking the first note on each string and hammering the rest.

#### How do I know a scale is learned?

Play it cold, at the start of a session, with no warm-up. Start it from any note, play it in a sequence, and make a four-bar phrase with it over a chord. If all of that works without looking at a diagram, the scale is learned. If any part fails, that part is tomorrow's practice.

## Print the Quiet, turned into practice tests.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/resources/print-the-quiet

Three field guides for players who want to hear what clean tone, right-hand dynamics and a real room are doing, then prove the difference in a recording.

Updated August 31, 2026

**By Jason Colapietro, founder of Suede AI.**

[Print the Quiet](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/book/print-the-quiet) is a nine-essay series about tone, dynamics and the parts of a record that never make it onto the lead sheet. The original essays remain on Strumly in their long-form editorial versions.

These GuitarHub editions are field guides, not reprints. Each one takes a guitar-first idea from the series and turns it into a bounded test you can run with one instrument, one recording device and a short practice window. The goal is to give each idea an observable meaning.

### Start with the result you want to hear

Choose the clean-tone guide if gain is hiding uneven attack or noisy muting. Choose the Hallelujah guide if you want to study how dynamics and space can carry a part with very little gear. Choose the room guide if your recordings feel flat and you cannot tell whether the problem is the performance, the microphone position or the ambience.

Every guide ends with a before-and-after recording. That keeps the work inside the GuitarHub method: make one claim, change one variable and keep the result only if the recording supports it.

### What these pages do not claim

A famous rig is context, not a prescription. You do not need Mark Knopfler's amplifier, Jeff Buckley's Telecaster or a major studio room to learn from their records. You need a stable signal, matched playback level and enough patience to compare two takes honestly.

Read the original series for the wider history. Use these field guides when you are holding the guitar.

## Practice clean guitar tone until nothing is hiding.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/resources/how-to-practice-clean-guitar-tone

Clean tone is not a preset category. It is a test of attack, muting, pitch and dynamics. This seven-day protocol changes one variable at a time and ends with a recording you can compare.

Updated August 31, 2026

Field Guide No. 12

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

**By Jason Colapietro, founder of Suede AI.**

A useful clean guitar tone keeps the note's attack, pitch and decay readable. It may include compression, EQ, reverb or a little amplifier color. The practical boundary is simpler: when you play harder, the sound should get meaningfully louder and brighter instead of collapsing into the same saturated shape.

This guide adapts the technique argument from [The Lost Art of Clean](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/book/print-the-quiet/ptq-04-lost-art-of-clean) into a GuitarHub practice test. The original essay follows clean tone through players such as Mark Knopfler, Jimi Hendrix, Stevie Ray Vaughan and Larry Carlton. This version is about what to do in the next seven sessions, even if your rig is only a guitar and a small interface.

This is the general protocol: seven days on a phrase you choose, on whatever rig you already own. It is not a study of a particular record. If you arrived looking for what one performance does with a clean sound, the companion guide to [Jeff Buckley's Hallelujah](https://guitarhub.org/resources/jeff-buckley-hallelujah-guitar-tone) is a close reading of that recording and ends in a test of its own. This page gives you the protocol. That page gives you the example.

### Set one clean baseline

Choose a four-bar phrase with three ingredients: a chord, a short single-note line and at least one intentional rest. Keep the phrase easy enough that you can play it from memory. If the notes themselves consume all your attention, the test will measure recall instead of tone control.

Use one pickup position and one amp or model. Turn off delay and long reverb. Lower the gain until a hard strum stays mostly clear, then set the output level so the recording does not clip. Record three takes at the same tempo. Do not polish the best one. Save the middle take as the baseline because it represents the session better than an outlier.

### Listen for four things, not for “good”

- **Attack:** Do repeated notes begin at a similar volume, or does one leap forward because the pick dug deeper?
- **Muting:** Do unused strings speak between notes? Mark the exact transition where the noise starts.
- **Pitch:** Do bends and fretted chords settle in tune, or does excess pressure pull them sharp?
- **Dynamics:** Can the phrase move from quiet to loud without changing tempo or losing the smallest notes?

Pick the worst of those four categories. That is the only category you work on for the week. Tone practice turns vague when the player tries to improve the amp, the hands, the part and the mix at once.

### The seven-day clean-tone test

#### Day 1: match the attacks

Play the phrase at half speed on one string. Aim for five notes whose beginnings sound equally strong. Change pick depth before changing equipment. If fingerpicking, listen for whether the thumb and fingers produce different levels.

#### Day 2: isolate the noise

Play only the transitions. Stop after each one and let the silence reveal any open string. Decide which hand owns each mute. The fretting hand can release pressure without leaving the string, while the picking hand can cover lower strings. Write down the assignment.

#### Day 3: test pressure and tuning

Tune, fret the chord with your normal pressure and check it again. Then repeat with the lightest pressure that produces a clear note. If the normal version is sharper, the issue is not the tuner. It is the hand.

#### Day 4: build a real dynamic range

Record the phrase once as quietly as possible without losing notes and once as loudly as possible without breaking the tone apart. The two waveforms and the two playbacks should be clearly different. If they are almost the same level, reduce gain or compression before blaming the hands.

#### Day 5: find the edge of breakup

Raise the amp gain or input one small step at a time. At each step, play one quiet chord and one hard chord. Stop where the hard chord gains a little harmonic density but the quiet chord stays clear. That point is a useful edge-of-breakup setting, not a universal ideal.

#### Day 6: put space back into the phrase

Restore a short reverb or room sound if the part needs it. Match the dry and effected versions by perceived loudness. An effect that is simply louder will often win a casual comparison even when it blurs the part.

#### Day 7: retest without a warm-up take

Use the original tempo, pickup and signal chain. Record three takes from cold and keep the middle one. Compare it with Day 1 at matched playback level. Name one change you can hear and one weakness that remains.

### What to change when the test fails

If attack is still uneven, slow the phrase and reduce pick depth. If string noise remains, shrink the test to the single transition that produces it. If the phrase sounds flat, confirm that the quiet and loud versions are actually different before adding more effects. If the recording is harsh, move the microphone or change the speaker simulation before cutting a narrow EQ notch by habit.

Do not buy a new clean preset because one retest failed. A preset can change the sound, but it cannot tell you whether the right hand became more consistent. Keep the chain stable long enough for the performance variable to become visible.

### Clean guitar tone questions

#### Does clean tone mean no pedals?

No. Compression, EQ, modulation and ambience can all belong in a clean sound. Start dry enough to hear the performance, then add one effect at a time and level-match the comparison.

#### Should a clean amp be completely free of breakup?

Not necessarily. Many useful clean sounds sit just below or at the edge of breakup. The test is whether changes in touch remain audible, not whether an oscilloscope would show a perfectly unchanged waveform.

#### How do I know the practice worked?

The Day 7 recording should show the selected category improving under the same conditions as Day 1. “It felt better” is not enough. Keep the claim narrow: cleaner transitions, more even attacks, wider dynamics or better pitch under normal fretting pressure.

**One chain. One phrase. One audible change.**

## What Hallelujah teaches about guitar tone.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/resources/jeff-buckley-hallelujah-guitar-tone

Jeff Buckley's recording is useful because the guitar part leaves nowhere for touch, balance or space to hide. You can study those decisions without copying the exact rig.

Updated August 31, 2026

Field Guide No. 13

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

**By Jason Colapietro, founder of Suede AI.**

Jeff Buckley's recording of Hallelujah is a clean-guitar lesson before it is a gear lesson. The arpeggio stays exposed for most of the performance. Changes in finger attack, note length and vocal intensity remain audible because the arrangement does not cover them with drums, doubled guitars or heavy gain.

This field guide adapts the longer essay [Jeff Buckley's Hallelujah: The Tone That Won the Song](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/book/print-the-quiet/ptq-01-jeff-buckley-tone-hallelujah). The original follows the instrument, amplifier, effects, studio and mix history. This page narrows the question: what can a guitarist test in one practice session after listening closely?

This guide studies one recording rather than teaching clean tone in general. The broader question, how to practice clean tone on your own phrase over a week, is answered by [the seven-day clean-tone test](https://guitarhub.org/resources/how-to-practice-clean-guitar-tone). Use that one to build the skill. Use this one to hear what the skill is for.

### The rig matters less than the relationship

Accounts of the session generally place Buckley's Telecaster into a clean Fender-style amplifier with an Alesis Quadraverb contributing the wide ambience associated with the recording. Individual gear details have been repeated inconsistently over the years, so copying a fan-made preset is a weak starting point.

The stable lesson is the relationship among four things: a clear attack, a long but controlled decay, large dynamic movement and enough empty arrangement space for those details to matter. If any one of those changes, the part behaves differently.

### Listen in four passes

#### Pass 1: follow only the loudness arc

Ignore the chords and follow how the guitar moves from near-silence to a firmer attack. The part does not sit at one average intensity. It supports the vocal arc while remaining quieter than the voice.

#### Pass 2: follow the top note

Hear each arpeggio as a small melody rather than a chord shape being repeated. Notice whether the top note is brought forward or allowed to disappear into the pattern. This is a right-hand balance decision.

#### Pass 3: listen to the gaps

The ambience continues after the fingers release a note, but the next attack remains readable. Listen for the point where decay becomes clutter. That boundary is more useful than the name of the reverb preset.

#### Pass 4: listen for human evidence

Small noises, breaths and changes in attack were not erased into a perfectly repeated pattern. They are not excuses for careless playing. They show that the performance is a continuous decision rather than a grid of interchangeable notes.

### Run the Hallelujah restraint test

- Choose any four-chord progression you can arpeggiate without looking at a chart.
- Set a clean sound with enough headroom that a hard pluck is louder than a quiet one.
- Record the progression dry at a fixed tempo. Keep the take even if a small noise appears.
- Add one room or hall effect. Raise the decay until adjacent chords begin to blur, then back it down one step.
- Record three dynamic levels: quiet, conversational and full. Do not change the tempo.
- Play back all versions at matched volume and select the one where the top melody stays clear without the part sounding detached.

The test is not an attempt to recreate Buckley's master. It uses the same constraint that makes the recording instructive: one exposed guitar part must carry harmony, pulse and emotional movement without a wall of sound.

### What usually breaks

If the part feels mechanical, the loudness of every finger may be too similar. If it feels vague, the ambience may be masking the start of each note. If the top melody vanishes, assign one finger to bring it forward rather than turning up the entire guitar. If the quiet take loses notes, reduce compression and practice the minimum attack needed to make each string speak.

Resist adding another effect until you can name which failure it is meant to repair. More width will not fix uneven balance. More compression will not create a dynamic arc. More gain will make the part easier to sustain, but it may replace the relationship you are trying to study.

### Hallelujah guitar tone questions

#### Do I need a Telecaster?

No. A Telecaster helps explain the recorded context, but the practice test works on any guitar that can produce a clear attack and useful dynamic range.

#### Which reverb preset recreates the recording?

No preset alone recreates a room, performance, amplifier, microphone and mix. Start by finding the longest decay that still leaves the next attack readable. That is a repeatable decision on your own rig.

#### Should I remove every finger noise?

Remove noises that interrupt the phrase or reveal weak muting. Keep incidental evidence that does not steal attention. The distinction is musical, so compare a corrected take with the original instead of applying a blanket rule.

**Study the record for relationships. Test those relationships on the instrument you own.**

## Hear what the room is doing to your guitar.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/resources/recording-guitar-room-sound

A room changes the first reflection, decay and low-frequency balance before a plugin enters the chain. This experiment separates those effects from the performance.

Updated August 31, 2026

Field Guide No. 14

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

**By Jason Colapietro, founder of Suede AI.**

A guitar recording contains more than the guitar. The sound reaches a wall, floor and ceiling before some of it returns to the microphone. Those early reflections affect apparent size and tone. Later reflections form the audible decay most players call reverb.

The essay [The Room as Instrument](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/book/print-the-quiet/ptq-05-room-as-instrument) follows that idea through rooms such as Bearsville, Sound City, Electric Lady and Abbey Road. This GuitarHub version removes the studio tour and gives you a controlled test that works in a bedroom, rehearsal space or live room.

### Do not compare three different performances

A player changes touch in response to what comes back from the room. That interaction is musically valuable, but it can confuse a technical comparison. Begin with one recorded performance so microphone position and simulated ambience are the variables you are testing.

A reamped electric guitar is ideal if you have a safe line-level reamping setup. If you do not, use a small speaker, acoustic guitar or phone playback at a moderate level. Protect your hearing and do not connect a line output directly to an amplifier input unless the equipment is designed for it.

### Build three versions

#### Version A: close and dry

Place the microphone close enough that the direct sound clearly dominates. For an amplifier, start near the speaker and slightly off the center of the cone. For an acoustic guitar, start around the twelfth fret rather than directly at the sound hole. Record ten seconds and note the position.

#### Version B: farther into the room

Move the same microphone several feet back while keeping its height and direction consistent. Record the same source at the same playback level. The distant version will usually contain more room, but it may also lose direct detail or gain uneven bass because of the room's dimensions.

#### Version C: close with simulated room

Return to Version A and add a short room or convolution reverb. Do not change EQ or compression yet. Adjust the wet level until Version C feels roughly as spacious as Version B.

### Level-match before you decide

Louder examples often feel fuller and more exciting. Reduce the playback gain of the loudest version until switching among A, B and C does not create an obvious jump. You do not need laboratory precision. You need a comparison that is not being won by level alone.

Then score each version on four questions:

- Can you hear the beginning of each note without strain?
- Does the decay support the phrase or overlap the next chord?
- Does one bass note boom or disappear compared with the others?
- Does the sound feel connected to a physical space, and does that help the part?

There is no automatic winner. A dry close sound may be right for a dense arrangement. A distant microphone may give a sparse clean part believable scale. A simulated room may offer the best control in an untreated space.

### Find the useful position, not the perfect room

If Version B is harsh, move the microphone away from the nearest reflective wall or lower it below ear height. If the bass changes wildly, move the source or microphone rather than reaching for EQ immediately. Even a shift of a foot can move both away from a strong room mode.

If Version C sounds detached, shorten the pre-delay or decay and reduce the wet level. If it sounds too small, increase early reflections before extending a long reverb tail. Size and duration are related, but they are not the same control.

### Turn the result into a repeatable note

Save the winning clip with five facts: the room, source position, microphone position, playback level and any added ambience. A phrase such as “large room sound” is not reproducible. “Amp two feet from the short wall, microphone four feet back at speaker height, short room at twelve percent wet” gives the next session a starting point.

Retest on another day before treating the setup as solved. Rooms change when furniture, doors, people and volume change. The note is a useful hypothesis, not a permanent law.

### Guitar room-sound questions

#### Can a plugin reproduce a real room?

A good room or convolution reverb can reproduce important parts of a room's response and may be the best choice for the record. It does not recreate every interaction among speaker, floor, microphone and player. Compare the result instead of arguing from the tool category.

#### Is a distant microphone always more natural?

No. Distance adds room and changes frequency balance. In a poor position it can add comb filtering, noise or uneven bass. Natural does not automatically mean useful.

#### What if I only have a phone?

Put the phone in one fixed location and record the same phrase with the source close, then farther away. The phone limits fidelity but can still reveal changes in attack, decay and room balance.

**The room is not decoration. It is one more variable you can test.**

## NAM A2 turns guitar tone into an open format.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/resources/nam-a2-open-tone-format

Architecture 2 makes captured tone more efficient and portable. Its larger contribution may be a tone file that can move across software and hardware without being rebuilt for every box.

Updated August 31, 2026

Field Guide No. 15

Keep this guide as a PDF for your phone or the music stand.

**By Jason Colapietro, founder of Suede AI.**

Neural Amp Modeler Architecture 2, or A2, is the current open-source NAM architecture for capturing the sound and response of amps, pedals, studio gear and full signal chains. Often called NAM v2, it replaces A1 as the default for new captures on TONE3000 and lets one trained model run at A2-Full or A2-Lite size. The [official A2 guide](https://www.tone3000.com/guides/nam-a2-the-complete-guide) documents the architecture, benchmarks and migration path.

The benchmark gains matter because they push captured tone beyond the computer. The larger opportunity is portability: a musician can keep one open NAM file while software and hardware hosts choose the model size they can run.

### A2 fixes a computer-sized assumption

The original NAM architecture was designed around computers and digital audio workstations. A2 was developed by Steve Atkinson and TONE3000 around a wider range of processing budgets, including the limits inside compact pedals and amps. Steve Atkinson's [A2 release note](https://www.neuralampmodeler.com/post/a2-is-released) points builders to the open-source trainer, core DSP library and plugin versions that added official support.

A2-Full targets maximum accuracy in a DAW or a device with enough processing headroom. A2-Lite runs the same model at a smaller width for constrained hardware. Creators do not need to train two separate files. Slimmable training lets one model run at either size, and the host chooses the width it can support.

TONE3000 reports that A2-Full uses 30 to 40 percent less CPU than A1-Standard and that A2-Lite runs at 50 percent CPU on a 600 MHz ARM Cortex-M7. Its quantitative evaluation covered 39 tones. The published listening dataset contains 105,842 ratings from 1,184 participants, collected from April 18 through May 29, 2026, across 37 tones. The [raw MUSHRA data and test notes](https://github.com/tone-3000/a2-mushra-data) are public, so engineers and skeptical musicians can inspect the evidence rather than relying on a marketing summary.

Those are company-published results, not the final word on how every capture feels under a player's hands. Recorded evaluations can measure similarity, but they cannot reproduce every interaction among a player, an instrument and a responsive amp. The practical result still matters: a capture that once assumed a computer-sized host can now run natively on smaller hardware without conversion into a closed model format.

### Open source changes who can build the next device

The official NAM training code, C++ inference core and reference plugin are MIT-licensed. A developer can inspect the code and add native A2 support without inventing a new capture architecture or paying a NAM format license. TONE3000 describes A2 as an open protocol for tone, closer in spirit to an impulse-response or MIDI file than a preset locked to one manufacturer's product.

A proprietary capture system can be excellent and still leave the musician dependent on one company's hardware, software, account system and product roadmap. An open NAM file can move wherever native NAM support exists. A software developer can add it to a plugin. A pedal maker can add it to a device. A musician can keep the file when the playback hardware changes.

The open NAM format and the TONE3000 catalog are separate things. TONE3000's [API terms, effective July 7, 2026](https://www.tone3000.com/api/terms), say A1 and A2 are open source and free to implement in any product. The same terms place separate conditions on catalog access, creator content and commercial API integrations. Supporting the format does not grant permission to mirror the catalog or repackage its contents.

### A portable tone still needs provenance

Open code does not settle every rights question around a capture.

The software can be MIT-licensed while an individual tone carries a creator-selected license, attribution requirements or platform rules. TONE3000's current [Tone Sharing Policy](https://www.tone3000.com/policy) permits captures of analog gear, commercial software captured with explicit permission, and original tones built from software chains. It prohibits unauthorized direct captures of commercial software. Its API terms also say tones and models belong to their creators and that integrations must preserve the license attached to each tone.

Creators should treat each NAM file as a media asset with a history. A useful provenance note should identify:

- who made the capture
- the amp, pedal, cabinet, microphone or signal chain that was used
- the capture date, input level and calibration method
- whether the file uses A1 or A2
- any edits or conversions applied after capture
- the license and terms for sharing or commercial use

That record does not prove legal ownership or clear a file for every use. It gives collaborators and product builders enough context to evaluate the asset before they load, share or package it. The model file carries the sound. The provenance record carries the facts needed to use that sound responsibly.

### The A2 migration has one real catch

A2 is not backward compatible with an A1-only host. Existing A1 captures still work in software and hardware that support A1, but a host must update its NAM integration before it can load A2 natively. A NAM logo by itself does not prove native A2 playback, so musicians should check the architecture a device actually loads.

TONE3000 says it retrained its existing A1 library except for zero-download models older than 60 days and models with malformed training data. When original training recordings were available, the platform used them to produce new A2 models. Otherwise, it generated synthetic training data from the A1 model. TONE3000 labels those synthetic retrains as **Convert** in the tone pack's Models section.

That label matters. A converted model does not have the same history as a fresh A2 capture trained from the original recording. The transition will remain uneven while hosts add A2 support, and some devices may continue converting NAM files into their own internal format.

### The next step is machine-readable tone

A2 makes a tone portable. Structured metadata can make it legible.

Imagine a session tool that can find a clean bass capture, confirm the architecture, read the signal chain, check the creator's license and load the correct model size for the available processor. The tool does not need to own the tone or make a legal decision. It needs the file and its provenance to be readable.

Open audio models can become durable creative objects instead of disposable presets. Musicians can preserve the sound of a rare rig. Engineers can document the exact chain behind a record. Builders can support the same capture without forcing its creator to rebuild it for every box. NAM A2 provides the technical layer. The creator community still has to build the trust layer around it.

### How to test NAM A2 now

Start with one capture. Load an A2 model in the current [NAM Gateway plugin](https://www.neuralampmodeler.com/users). Compare it with the original gear or an A1 version at matched levels. Test how it reacts to different guitars, pickups and playing dynamics. Then save a provenance note beside the model before you share it.

NAM earns trust when musicians know what a tone is, who captured it, where it can run and what they are allowed to do with it. That matters more than claiming every listener will hear no difference.

### NAM A2 questions

#### What is NAM v2?

NAM v2 is the informal name many people use for Neural Amp Modeler Architecture 2, officially called A2. It is the current NAM architecture and the default for new captures trained on TONE3000.

#### Is NAM A2 backward compatible with A1 software and hardware?

No. Existing A1 captures remain usable in A1-compatible hosts, but software and hardware need an updated NAM integration to load A2 natively.

#### Does open source mean every NAM capture is free to use?

No. The NAM code and A2 format are open source, but individual captures can carry separate licenses, sharing terms and platform rules. Open architecture does not replace permission, attribution or provenance.

### NAM A2 in one paragraph

Neural Amp Modeler Architecture 2, often called NAM v2, is an open-source architecture for capturing the sound and response of amps, pedals, studio gear and signal chains. It supports Full and Lite playback from one model and can run in software or constrained hardware. Its larger importance is portability: a NAM A2 tone can move across products that support the open format. Creators should pair each capture with provenance and clear sharing terms because open-source software does not automatically clear every tone file for every use.

**Test one A2 capture and document its provenance.**

## Tune up. Find your tempo.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/practice

The practice room

Check your strings, then play along with the click. These tools are free to use on their own, before a lesson or during your own practice.

Keep a steady pulse

### Metronome

Use the click for chord changes, scales, or a passage you are working on. No microphone is needed.

**90** beats per minute

30–240 BPM. Tempo changes take effect after the next beat.

Choose a comfortable tempo, then start the click.

### Guitar tuner

Use standard tuning: low E2, A2, D3, G3, B3, high E4. Check every string before playing. This tuner is free to use.

**Target: string 6, Low E (E2)**

82.4 Hz · A4 = 440 Hz · open string, no fret pressed

The tuner will show the detected note and octave here.

Reference tones demonstrate pitch using a synthesized sound. Playback stops microphone capture and includes time for the sound to fade.

Pick a string, then start the tuner. Play one string at a time.

- Trace the selected string to its tuning peg before turning it. Peg directions differ between guitars.
- Pluck one string and make small adjustments. Recheck the correct octave if the reading is far away; stop if a string feels unusually tight.
- After the last adjustment, make another pass over all six strings. There is no speed requirement.

The tuner asks for microphone access when you start it. Audio is processed in this browser and is not uploaded or saved. The metronome and reference tones do not need microphone permission. Starting another audio tool stops the current one; leaving this page or hiding the tab stops the sound and microphone.

Use one string at a time. The tuner shows pitch and octave, not complete chords or a lesson score. These tools do not record lesson completion.

Your practice workspace

### Make this session count.

Your plan, session, tempo work, and evidence together. Saved in this browser.

Open the [session builder](https://guitarhub.org/session), [30-day planner](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough), [tempo ladder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo), or [practice log](https://guitarhub.org/log).

Checked steps are your practice record. Compare recordings and logged results to judge what improved. Browser data stays on this device; export your evidence log to keep a backup.

## Stop browsing. Prove one change.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough

Turn one guitar goal into four weeks of practice, evidence, correction, and the next right move. The planner is free and stays in your browser.

Not sure which change to chase? [Run the practice plateau diagnostic](https://guitarhub.org/diagnose) first. It reads nine answers back and tells you what they point at, including when they do not point at any one thing.

This is the planner rather than the guide: it turns one finish line into four weeks of focuses and a piece of evidence to record each week. Choosing a finish line narrow enough to prove, and judging the day 30 recording once you have it, are written out in [the 30-day guitar challenge](https://guitarhub.org/30-day-guitar-challenge). Read that one for the judgment. Use this one for the four weeks.

The learning loop

### Community becomes useful when every conversation changes the next practice.

The planner runs this loop for you. If you want to see what each stage asks and how you know you can move on, read [the GuitarHub method](https://guitarhub.org/method).

#### Week 1 · Baseline

Record one real attempt at your finish line and name where it breaks. No placement quiz to game.

#### Week 2 · Isolate

Cut the failure down to the smallest piece that still breaks and repair that one piece.

#### Week 3 · Reconnect

Put the repair back into the full song, the click, or the backing track the week calls for.

#### Week 4 · Prove

Record the same take beside the baseline. Founding-room members also get one highest-leverage correction, and progress proof is shared only when you choose.

## Something in your practice stopped working.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/diagnose

Answer 9 questions about how you actually practice. This scores five common blockers, names the one your answers point at hardest, and gives you one thing to do in the next session.

No account. No email. Your answers stay in this browser.

This is the diagnostic rather than the explanation: nine questions, five blockers scored, and the one worth changing next session. If you would rather read the causes and recognize your own, [why guitar practice plateaus](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-plateau) sets out six of them in prose. That page explains. This one ranks.

What it looks for

### Five ways practice stops producing change.

A plateau is rarely a lack of effort. It is usually one of these, running quietly underneath an hour that felt productive.

#### No measurable target

Sessions end on the clock or on mood, not on a specific thing that changed.

**First move:** Write one sentence naming what has to be true before you stop tonight.

#### Never at tempo

You can play it slowly. Nothing yet proves it survives at the speed the music moves.

**First move:** Find the song's real tempo, then the fastest clean tempo you have today. Write both down.

#### No feedback loop

Nothing outside your own hands is telling you whether it improved.

**First move:** Record thirty seconds today, listen back once, and write the first specific problem you hear.

#### Practicing the comfortable part

Most of the session goes to the parts that already work.

**First move:** Name the bar that breaks, then spend the first twenty minutes on nothing else.

#### Material churn

New material keeps arriving before the last piece was finished.

**First move:** Choose the one thing you will finish this month, and close everything else.

How this works

### You should know how it reached the answer.

#### Nine questions, five blockers

Every option carries fixed weights across five named blockers. The weights are the same for everyone and do not change with how you feel about the answer.

#### Scored against its own ceiling

A blocker asked about in six questions would out-score one asked about in three. So each is measured against the most its own questions could give it, and that share is what ranks them.

#### Ties break the same way every time

When two blockers land level, the earlier one in a fixed list takes it. Nothing is random. The same answers produce the same result on every run, on every device.

#### A self-report, not a measurement

The diagnostic knows what you told it and nothing else. Its job is to narrow five possibilities to one worth acting on this week. A recording is what settles whether the action worked.

If you would rather read than answer questions, these three cover the same ground in longer form.

### Now give it four weeks.

Knowing the blocker changes nothing on its own. Turn it into a plan you can run this month, or apply to the founding room and have a crew read your evidence. Applying starts a fit conversation. It takes no payment.

## You have the time. Now spend it on purpose.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/session

Most practice sessions are decided in the first ninety seconds, by whatever your hands reached for. This turns the minutes you have into an ordered set of blocks with a length, a purpose, and something specific to do in each one.

The problem this solves

### The hour was not the problem. Nobody decided what it was for.

An unplanned practice hour has a predictable shape. Ten minutes of playing what already sounds good, twenty on the thing you were working on last time until it stops being fun, then the rest on something else entirely. Nothing in that is lazy. It is what happens when the decision about where the time goes is made forty separate times, at the instrument, by someone holding a guitar.

Making the decision once, before you start, is the whole trick — and it is why the answer has to be specific about minutes. A block with no length is a suggestion. Fifteen minutes on the bar that breaks first, followed by nine on tempo, is a session. If the problem is bigger than one session and your playing has stalled generally, [why guitar practice plateaus](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-plateau) is the better place to start.

How this works

### Five steps, and no leftover minutes.

- 1 Enter the minutes you actually have Type the real number, not the one you wish you had. A session planned for an hour you do not have becomes the first block and nothing else, which is the one shape of practice that reliably wastes the time.
- 2 Pick the one thing the session is for Raise a tempo ceiling, memorize a song, repair a transition, or general upkeep. The focus decides which block gets the largest share of the time, and at short lengths it decides which blocks exist at all.
- 3 Read the split, which adds up exactly Every block is a whole number of minutes, and the blocks total the length you asked for. Nothing is rounded away and nothing is invented, so the plan on screen is the session you actually have.
- 4 Run the blocks in order, without shortening them Each block has a minimum size below which starting it costs more than skipping it. Anything that lands under that minimum is dropped and its minutes go to the blocks that survived, which is why a fifteen-minute session comes back with two blocks instead of five stubs.
- 5 Tick a block once it is finished Progress is counted in minutes rather than in boxes, so a long block moves the bar further than a short one. What you tick is stored in this browser, and the clear button removes it.

#### Why a short session comes back almost empty

Fifteen minutes divided five ways is three minutes a block, and a three-minute block is mostly the setup: finding the passage, setting the metronome, remembering what you decided last time. The builder refuses to produce that. Blocks that fall under their minimum are removed and their minutes are given to the ones that are left, so fifteen minutes comes back as two blocks that can actually be run rather than five that cannot.

It also tells you which blocks it dropped and what each one needed, because “there was no room for the cold-start test” is useful information about your week. If most of your sessions are coming back with two blocks, the answer is not a cleverer split — it is [a schedule that survives a real week](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-schedule).

#### Why the focus changes the shape, not the labels

Each focus carries its own weighting across the five blocks, and the block that repairs the thing you named is guaranteed the largest share of the session. Memorizing a song puts the second largest share on playing from memory and almost nothing on tempo work; raising a tempo ceiling reverses that. At sixty minutes both produce five blocks, and the two sessions are not the same session with different headings on it.

General upkeep is the exception, and deliberately so. With nothing named as broken there is no repair target worth the largest share, so the weight moves to playing complete music under some kind of pressure. At half an hour or less the upkeep session drops the repair block entirely rather than inventing something to fix. What that block should contain when you do have a target is [deliberate practice on guitar](https://guitarhub.org/deliberate-practice-guitar).

#### Why the tempo block is deliberately vague about numbers

This tool knows how many minutes to spend on tempo work. It does not know what tempo you are on, what you are aiming at, or how big a step your hands can absorb, so it does not pretend to. The [tempo ladder builder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) is the tool that answers those, and its rungs are what the tempo block here is for. Run the two together: this one decides the minutes, that one decides the numbers.

The rules it follows

### The split is generated from rules, not from a template.

Two players entering the same length get different sessions, because the shape is derived from the focus and from how much time there actually is.

#### The minutes add up, exactly

Every block is a whole number and the blocks total the length you entered. Rounding each block's share on its own drifts by a minute in either direction depending on the total, so the leftover is handed out deliberately instead: to the blocks whose share was cut hardest by the rounding.

#### Blocks are dropped, never shrunk

Each block has a size below which starting it costs more than it returns. A block that lands under that size is removed and its minutes go to the blocks still standing, so a short session comes back with two real blocks rather than five that are each too small to begin.

#### The focus block is always the largest

Whatever you chose to fix gets more time than anything else in the session, guaranteed rather than usually. A focus that changes the labels and not the shape of the session is decoration, and this one changes the shape.

#### Something always survives

At five minutes there is one block and it takes all five, because a plan with nothing in it is not a shorter plan. The block you get is the one your focus pointed at.

#### The session ends cold, on purpose

Wherever there is room for it, the last block puts the guitar down for two minutes and then asks for one attempt with no run-up. What you can only play while already warm has not been learned yet, it has been loaded.

#### Nothing leaves this browser

There is no account and no upload. The length, the focus, and the blocks you tick off are stored in this browser only, and the clear button removes them.

### How to use it well.

- There is no timer here. Use the clock you already have, or your phone.
- Nothing is recorded or listened to. Whether a block was really finished is yours to judge.
- The blocks are named and sized, but what goes in the repair block is chosen by you. The tool does not know which bar is broken.
- One session at a time. It plans today, not a week, and it keeps no history beyond the boxes you have ticked.

What to put inside the blocks, and what to do when one of them stops producing change:

- [All the free tools →](https://guitarhub.org/tools)
- [How to practice effectively →](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-practice-guitar-effectively)
- [How long to practice each day →](https://guitarhub.org/how-long-to-practice-guitar-each-day)
- [How to memorize a song →](https://guitarhub.org/how-to-memorize-songs-on-guitar)
- [The GuitarHub method →](https://guitarhub.org/method)
- [Designing a practice routine ↗](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine)
- [The Strumly learning path ↗](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/path)

#### Practice plateau diagnostic →

Answer a short set of questions and name the part of your practice that stopped producing change.

### The plan is the easy half. Someone hearing it is the other one.

A session builder can tell you to spend fifteen minutes on the bar that breaks first. It cannot tell you that the bar breaks because your picking hand is anticipating the change. The founding room is being assembled for that part: a small crew, a weekly recording, and one correction that changes the next session.

## One passage. One tempo at a time.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/tempo

Speeding a passage up by pushing the metronome until it falls apart teaches your hands to fall apart. This builds the ladder instead: the tempo you already own at the bottom, the tempo you want at the top, and a session for every rung between them.

How this works

### The rungs are generated from rules, not from a template.

Two players entering the same target get different ladders, because the shape is derived from the distance between your two tempos and the number of sessions you are willing to spend.

#### Steps are capped, not averaged

No rung asks for more than a tenth of the tempo you are leaving, and never more than 10 BPM. A jump from 60 is smaller than a jump from 200, because your hands feel proportion, not arithmetic.

#### Hold rungs are sessions, not rest

Some rungs repeat the previous tempo. Reaching a tempo once and owning it are different things, and the second one only comes from repetition at a speed you already reached.

#### One session goes down on purpose

Every ladder contains at least one back-off rung: drop below the top tempo you reached and climb back through the rungs you already passed. Re-covering ground is what turns a ceiling into a floor.

#### The numbers are metronome numbers

Rungs land on whole BPM from 30 to 240, the full range of the GuitarHub metronome, and on multiples of five or two wherever that does not distort the spacing. Every rung dials in exactly.

#### The baseline is a measurement

The first session is not practice. You are finding the fastest tempo you can play the passage three times in a row, cleanly. Start the ladder above that and every rung after it is guesswork.

#### Nothing leaves this browser

There is no account and no upload. Your two tempos and the sessions you check off are stored in this browser only, and the clear button removes them.

### Put your ladder to work.

- Play each rung on the free metronome in the GuitarHub practice room, or any metronome you already use.
- Assess each pass against the listed conditions. Your practice stays private; this tool uses no microphone or recordings.
- A ladder covers one passage. Build a separate one for each part that is holding a song back.
- For larger tempo goals, the builder gives you a reachable next target to complete first.

Why the rungs are shaped this way, and what to run when one of them will not pass:

- [Deliberate practice on guitar →](https://guitarhub.org/deliberate-practice-guitar)
- [The GuitarHub method →](https://guitarhub.org/method)
- [Smoother chord transitions ↗](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/smoother-chord-transitions)
- [Designing a practice routine ↗](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine)

### Where to go next.

#### Guitar tuner and metronome →

Check each open string with pitch feedback and reference tones, then practice with a steady four-beat click.

#### 30-day breakthrough planner →

Choose one finish line and turn it into a four-week practice sequence you can run this month.

#### Practice plateau diagnostic →

Answer a short set of questions and name the part of your practice that stopped producing change.

#### Practice session builder →

#### Song readiness score →

#### Practice evidence log →

Log one line per session and read what actually moved, with no streak counter and no direction under three sessions.

#### Why guitar practice plateaus →

### A ladder is the practice. The room is the correction.

The builder gives you the next tempo. Apply to the founding room for a small practice crew built around a weekly recording and focused feedback that guides your next session.

## Finished, or just comfortable?

Source: https://guitarhub.org/readiness

Score one song against the ten conditions that decide whether it holds up away from your practice chair. No account, nothing uploaded, and it stays in your browser.

The problem this measures

### The song did not fall apart because you forgot it. It fell apart because of the room.

Most songs reach a point where you would say they are done. You can play it, it sounds like the record, and you stop working on it. Then you play it for one person and it comes apart in a bar that has never given you trouble.

The notes were not the problem. The problem was a condition you never practiced in: cold hands, a listener, full tempo set by something other than you, or a mistake in bar four with nothing rehearsed for what comes next. This tool asks about those conditions one at a time, weights them by how much damage each one does, and hands back the single thing worth fixing before you play it for anybody. If your whole practice has stalled rather than one song, start with [why guitar practice plateaus](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-plateau) instead.

### Score one song against ten checks that break under pressure.

Answer each check honestly. Two of the ten carry more weight than any other check, because two of them end a performance rather than dent it. Your songs stay in this browser.

Name a song above to start. Pick one you would call finished. The checks are most useful on a song you already believe you can play.

How this works

### What the number is, and how to use it.

- 1 Name the song Type in one song you would call finished. It is stored under that name in this browser, so you can come back and score it again after you have done something about the result.
- 2 Answer the ten checks Each check is a yes or no about something that has either happened or has not. None of them ask how well you play. If you are unsure whether you can start it cold, the honest answer is no.
- 3 Read the score and the band The score is the weighted total of the checks you ticked, shown from 0 to 100. The band names what that total means: practice-room only, good-day only, nearly there, or stage-ready.
- 4 Do the one action it hands back The tool returns the heaviest check still open, with an instruction you can run in a single practice session. One thing this week, rather than a list of ten.
- 5 Score it again afterwards Change an answer only once the thing has actually happened. The score is worth something only for as long as the checks stay honest.

#### Why two checks weigh more than the others

Starting cold and playing through a mistake carry three points each. The rest carry two or one, for nineteen points in total. That split is a judgment rather than a finding: those two failures end a performance, and the other eight only make it worse. A song can pass eight checks and still stop dead in the first bar.

The practical effect is that ticking the two heavy checks scores higher than ticking three light ones. The score does not reward collecting the easy boxes, which is the same reason the [GuitarHub method](https://guitarhub.org/method) puts a recording at the end of every week.

#### Why it hands back one action instead of a list

Ten open checks is a to-do list, and a to-do list is how a song stays unfinished. The tool sorts what is left by weight and returns the top one with an instruction you can run in a single session. When two are tied it takes the earlier one, because the order they are listed in is roughly the order a song needs them. If you want that same idea across a whole month rather than one song, the [30-day challenge](https://guitarhub.org/30-day-guitar-challenge) and the [breakthrough planner](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough) run it week by week.

#### What the score cannot tell you

It cannot hear you. It counts what you told it, and it only knows about the ten things on the list. It has nothing to say about tone, feel, dynamics, or whether the song suits you at all. A score of 100 means the ten failure modes here have been tested, not that the performance is good.

Read a low score as a map of what has not been tested yet, rather than a verdict on your playing. For turning that map into a weekly routine, Strumly has a [guide to designing a practice routine](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine) and a [staged learning path](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/path).

### Where to go next

#### The GuitarHub method →

The four-stage loop the whole site runs on: baseline, isolate, reconnect, prove, with an exit test for each stage.

#### 30-day breakthrough planner →

Choose one finish line and turn it into a four-week practice sequence you can run this month.

#### Why guitar practice plateaus →

Why progress stalls once the beginner gains run out, and what to change when it does.

#### The 30-day guitar challenge →

How to run a 30-day challenge that ends with a recording you can compare, not a streak you kept.

### One song, tested properly, beats five nearly done.

Score the song, do the one action, and score it again. If you want a human layer around that work, the founding room is being assembled as a small crew with a weekly studio. Applying starts a fit conversation and takes no payment.

## A streak proves you showed up. This proves something changed.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/log

One line per session: the day, what you worked on, the tempo or pass rate you actually reached, and an honest sentence about whether it moved. Then a read on the last 7 and 30 days — which stays silent about any focus that has not earned a verdict yet.

The problem this fixes

### You know you practiced. You do not know whether it worked.

Most practice records answer the easy question. They count days, minutes, and sessions — all things you can produce without playing anything better at the end of them. A month of that leaves you with a number that went up and a passage that did not.

The hard question is whether anything moved, and it needs two things a streak never asks for: a specific focus, and a number attached to it. Log those, and after three sessions on the same focus the comparison starts to mean something. Log them for a month and you can tell which of the things you changed was the thing that worked. That is the same loop the [GuitarHub method](https://guitarhub.org/method) runs on, and the reason [deliberate practice](https://guitarhub.org/deliberate-practice-guitar) asks for a measurement rather than a duration.

What the log can support

### Evidence, not a streak.

There is no consecutive-day counter here, and there is not going to be. A streak goes up on a session that changed nothing and resets on a week off that changed a lot. These numbers only move when the playing does.

Nothing logged yet. Log 3 sessions on the same focus and this turns into a direction — before that it stays a list, because 2 points would only draw a line through a good day and a bad one.

### The data is yours

No account and no upload. Export writes a plain JSON file you can read in any text editor, keep as a backup, or open on another machine. Importing adds those sessions to this browser — anything identical is skipped rather than duplicated.

How this works

### Five fields, and one rule about them.

- 1 Log the session while it is still true Pick the day you practiced and write it down before the evening rewrites it. The log will not accept a date in the future, because a record of what has not happened yet is the one thing it must never hold.
- 2 Name the focus the same way every time One passage or one skill, not a whole song. Capitals and extra spaces are ignored, so the sessions group together, but a focus called something different each week never accumulates enough sessions to show you anything.
- 3 Record the number you actually reached Either the fastest tempo you played it cleanly, in beats per minute, or your clean run-throughs as a share of your attempts out of 100. Not the fastest you attempted, and not the one good take.
- 4 Write the one honest line A single sentence on whether it moved. No change is a perfectly good entry, and a more useful one than a good mood, because it is the entry that tells you next week whether the thing you changed was the thing that worked.
- 5 Read the summary, including where it refuses to answer You get sessions logged, distinct focuses, and the best number per focus over the last 7 and the last 30 days. A focus with fewer than three sessions is reported as not enough evidence yet, rather than given a direction.

#### What the log refuses to do

A practice tool earns its answers by being willing to give none. These six refusals are enforced in the code that computes the summary, not in the copy describing it.

##### No streak counter

Deliberately absent, and it is not an oversight. A streak measures attendance: it goes up on a session that changed nothing, and it drops to zero on a week off that changed a lot. It is a number that always moves, which is exactly why it feels like evidence and is not.

##### No direction under three sessions

Two points draw a straight line through any pair of numbers, including a good day next to a bad one. Under three sessions on a focus, the tool returns not enough evidence yet. That rule lives in the code rather than in this paragraph, so nothing built on top of it can talk its way past it.

##### A rise with a falling floor is not a rise

If your average went up but your worst session went down with it, that is a wider spread, not progress, and the log says so. The same goes the other way: an average that held while the individual sessions swung is reported as no clear direction, not as holding steady.

##### A decline is shown, not buried

When the later sessions average below the earlier ones, the log says that in a sentence. A tool that only ever reports good news is a tool whose good news means nothing.

##### Tempo is never averaged with a pass rate

If a focus switched from beats per minute to clean passes, only the sessions using the most recent measure feed the comparison, and the count left out is shown next to it. Averaging the two would produce a confident number about nothing.

##### Nothing leaves this browser

There is no account, no upload, and no network call. Sessions are stored in this browser only. Export writes a plain JSON file you keep, importing it adds those sessions back, and the clear button removes the lot.

#### Where the number comes from

Pick whichever measure suits the thing you are working on. A passage with a speed ceiling wants a tempo — build the steps with the [tempo ladder](https://guitarhub.org/tempo) and log the rung you reached. Something that falls apart at random wants a pass rate: ten attempts, six clean, log 60. If you are unsure which failure you are looking at, the [song readiness score](https://guitarhub.org/readiness) names it, and [practicing with a metronome](https://guitarhub.org/practicing-guitar-with-a-metronome) covers how to take a tempo reading you can trust.

### How to read it.

- It cannot hear you. Every number in it is one you typed, and the log is worth exactly as much as your honesty about them.
- It does not know why anything changed. It can tell you the tempo moved; it cannot tell you that your left hand is late because your right hand is early.
- It is not a practice plan. Use the tempo ladder or the 30-day planner to decide what to do, and this to record what happened.
- A direction over three sessions is a small piece of evidence, not a finding. More sessions on one focus make it worth more.

What to run when the log says a focus has stopped moving:

- [Why practice plateaus →](https://guitarhub.org/guitar-practice-plateau)
- [All the free tools →](https://guitarhub.org/tools)
- [Designing a practice routine ↗](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/guides/designing-a-practice-routine)
- [A staged learning path ↗](https://strumly.suedeai.ai/path)

#### Practice session builder →

#### Tempo ladder builder →

### The log tells you it stopped moving. It cannot tell you why.

That part still takes another set of ears. The founding room is being assembled for it: a small crew, a weekly recording, and one correction that changes the next session. Applying starts a fit conversation. It does not charge you or create a commitment.

## Free guitar practice tools that run in your browser.

Source: https://guitarhub.org/tools

The tools GuitarHub publishes, in one place: what each one is for, who it helps, and which part of the practice loop it belongs to. None of them ask for an account, and what you type into them stays in your browser.

The common thread

### The same conditions, on each one of them.

These are not a funnel with the good part behind a form. They are small, finished tools, and the conditions below are the same for each of them.

#### Free, with nothing behind it

These practice tools are free. They have no payment step, trial, or locked second half.

#### No account

Open any tool and use it without signing in or entering an email address.

#### Runs in your browser

Plans, diagnoses, ladders, and summaries are computed on the page. The tuner processes microphone sound on your device; it does not upload audio.

#### Stores no data on a server

Plans and logs stay in this browser's local storage. Tuner readings and metronome playback are temporary and stop when you leave. These standalone tools do not upload practice history.

The last one is a claim you can check rather than trust. There is no analytics script and no third-party tracker on this site, which the page source will tell you faster than we can. The tuner listens only while you run it, measures pitch on your device, and never records or uploads audio; the planning tools never touch the microphone. When a tool tells you to record a baseline, record it on your phone and keep it yourself.

[What happens to anything you type →](https://guitarhub.org/about)

### The tools.

Each one does a different job inside the same loop, which is why there is no single “start here” button. Open the one that matches the sentence you would use to describe the problem.

#### [Guitar tuner and metronome →](https://guitarhub.org/practice)

Check each open string with pitch feedback and reference tones, then practice with a steady four-beat click.

**What it is for**

Check the pitch and octave of one open guitar string at a time, hear synthesized standard tuning references, and use a four-beat metronome at your chosen tempo. The microphone stays off until you start the tuner.

**Who it helps**

Players tuning up before a lesson or practicing chord changes, scales, and short passages with a steady click.

#### [30-day breakthrough planner →](https://guitarhub.org/breakthrough)

Choose one finish line and turn it into a four-week practice sequence you can run this month.

**What it is for**

You choose one finish line, say where you are as a player, and say how many days a week and how many minutes a session you actually have. It returns four weeks, each with a focus, the actions that serve it, and the recording that ends the week.

**Who it helps**

Players who practice regularly and still reach the end of a month unable to say what changed. Also anyone whose month keeps splitting across five goals at once.

#### [Practice plateau diagnostic →](https://guitarhub.org/diagnose)

Answer a short set of questions and name the part of your practice that stopped producing change.

**What it is for**

Nine questions about how you practice now, not how you mean to. Each answer scores five named blockers against their own maximum, and the result is the one your answers point at hardest, with a prescription and a first action.

**Who it helps**

Players who are putting in the hours, know something has stopped working, and cannot name which part of the routine it is.

#### [Practice session builder →](https://guitarhub.org/session)

Turn the minutes you actually have into timed blocks, weighted toward the one thing you are fixing.

**What it is for**

You give it the minutes you actually have and the one thing the session is for. It returns ordered, whole-minute blocks that add up exactly, drops anything too short to be useful, and keeps completed blocks in this browser.

**Who it helps**

Players who already know what needs work but lose the session deciding what to do next, or whose available time rarely matches a canned routine.

#### [Tempo ladder builder →](https://guitarhub.org/tempo)

Turn one difficult passage into a tempo ladder with a starting speed, a target, and steps between them.

**What it is for**

You give it the tempo you already play a passage cleanly and the tempo you want. It returns an ordered set of sessions between them, with the step size capped, sessions that hold a tempo instead of adding to it, and a pass condition on every rung.

**Who it helps**

Anyone whose speed work is pushing the metronome up until the passage falls apart, then starting over the next day from a number they cannot remember.

#### [Song readiness score →](https://guitarhub.org/readiness)

Check a song against the parts that break under pressure before you call it finished.

**What it is for**

Ten yes-or-no checks about things that have either happened with a song or have not, weighted into a score and a band. It hands back the heaviest check still open, with one instruction you can run in a session.

**Who it helps**

Players deciding whether a song is finished, and anyone about to play one standing up, in front of a person, or into a camera.

#### [Practice evidence log →](https://guitarhub.org/log)

Log one line per session and read what actually moved, with no streak counter and no direction under three sessions.

**What it is for**

You record the date, one focus, a tempo or clean-pass rate, and one honest note. It compares like with like over 7 and 30 days, and refuses to claim a direction until one focus has at least three sessions.

**Who it helps**

Players who can say how often they practiced but cannot show whether the passage, transition, or song they chose is actually moving.

### Which one to open first.

Find your sentence on the left. The stage on the right is where that tool sits in the four-stage loop the whole site runs on: baseline, isolate, reconnect, prove.

[The GuitarHub method →](https://guitarhub.org/method)

“I have my guitar ready and need to tune up or set a steady tempo.”

During practice. Open the tuner and metronome without starting a lesson.

“I practice most days and cannot say what stopped producing change.”

Baseline. It ends with a named blocker to record against.

“I know what I want to fix and the month keeps dissolving.”

The whole loop, laid out one stage per week.

“I know what to work on and need it to fit the time I have today.”

Isolate. It turns the target into blocks you can run now.

“One passage holds together up to a speed and then does not.”

Isolate. The stage where the fragment gets repaired.

“I think this song is finished and I am not sure I believe it.”

Reconnect and prove. What survives outside practice.

“I finished the session and need to know whether the work is moving.”

Prove. It carries the evidence into the next baseline.

### How the tools work.

Each tool does one job, on your device. That is what keeps them free without taking anything from you in exchange, and these are the operating details worth knowing before you start.

- The tuner listens only after you start it and allow microphone access. It detects one note at a time; it does not verify complete chords or award a lesson score.
- The metronome and synthesized reference tones do not need microphone permission. Starting another audio tool stops the current one, and hiding or leaving the page stops playback and listening.
- State does not follow you between devices or browsers. No account carries it. A plan built on your laptop is not on your phone.
- Clearing your browser data deletes what you entered, and it cannot be restored from here.
- They need JavaScript. The results are computed on the page rather than fetched, so the tools produce no results without it.
- Planning tools depend on your own answers. The tuner reports pitch; it cannot assess your posture, complete chord fingering, or overall playing technique.

### The thinking behind them.

Every tool here is an argument about practice with a form attached. The guides are the argument written out, including the parts a form cannot make.

Phone placement, levels, a day 1 versus day 30 comparison, and the five things to listen for in every take.

#### Learn the fretboard notes and CAGED →

The musical alphabet, strings 6 and 5, octave shapes, and the five CAGED shapes that connect the whole neck.

#### How to practice strumming →

A hand that never stops, counted eighths, five patterns in order, and a click on beats 2 and 4.

#### Barre chords and the F chord →

Leverage instead of grip strength, a four-step path to a full F, and the E and A shapes up the neck.

#### How to practice improvising →

Constraint drills, phrases that answer each other, and landing on chord tones over a 12-bar blues in A.

#### Coming back to guitar after years away →

A 30-day restart: set up the guitar, rebuild your fingertips, record a fresh baseline, and finish one song.

#### Practicing scales so they become music →

One shape learned cold, then sequences, thirds, a drone, rhythm and chord tones, in a 15-minute daily plan.
